books.title: The Legend of Nessie
books.art_why: A legendary creature and sightings from AD 565 to 1934 cannot be photographed, so drawings suit the myth and past events.

pages.text: Word Origins The word loch means lake or a narrow arm of the sea that stretches inland. It comes from the language of Scotland, called Scottish Gaelic (GAY-lick). Introduction Is the Loch Ness Monster a myth or a legend? People have described seeing something strange emerging from the dark waters of Loch Ness in Scotland. They describe an animal similar to the descriptions of ancient dragons or sea serpents. The monster has a dark body, long neck, sheep-like head, and two or more humps on its back. The monster, called Nessie, is named after the loch, or lake, in which it lives.
pages.brief: A long-necked creature with a sheep-like head and two dark humps rises from the dark water of a Scottish loch, shown as people describe it. Steep green shores and misty water surround the creature in the cold lake.

pages.text: Strange creatures of the sea are found in many legends, myths, and stories. Scottish myths have been passed down about a water spirit, called a kelpie, that looks like a horse. When sailors first started sailing beyond the sight of land, they talked about seeing monsters at sea. Some of those monsters were described as being so large that they could swallow a ship! According to legend, these huge, horrible beasts guarded treasure at the bottom of the sea. Could Nessie be one of these monsters of myth or legend? This monster of legend lived in the “Sea of Darkness.”
pages.brief: On an old sailing ship beyond sight of land, sailors point at a huge sea monster large enough to swallow a ship. Nearby, a kelpie, a water spirit shaped like a horse, stands in the dark Sea of Darkness, guarding treasure on the sea bottom.

pages.text: The Loch Called Ness The body of water that is rumored to be home to the legendary Loch Ness Monster is large. In fact, it’s the largest body of fresh water in the British Isles. Loch Ness is 24 miles (39 km) long, only 1 mile (1.6 km) wide, and over 800 feet (244 m) deep in some places. It’s much deeper than the seas that surround the British Isles. Loch Ness was formed during the last ice age. At that time, the land now called Scotland split in two, and earthquakes made a trench. Then glaciers covered that trench until about 12,000 years ago. When the ice melted, it filled the trench with water to form a loch. British Isles.
pages.brief: A long, narrow Loch Ness stretches 24 miles through the land, only 1 mile wide and over 800 feet deep. Melting glaciers fill a deep trench cut by earthquakes, forming the loch about 12,000 years ago.

pages.text: Loch Ness’s water is very cold. Peat, a layer of dead plant material, is thick in the water of Loch Ness. The peat allows light to travel only as deep as a few yards. As a result, sunlight can’t warm the water, making it too cold for people to swim in. The top 100 feet (30.5 m) warms up to 54 degrees Fahrenheit (12°C) in the summer. The rest stays at 42 degrees Fahrenheit (6°C) all year round. Because of this, most life in the loch, such as fish and seals, stays close to the surface. A gray seal might be mistaken for a monster when seen in a loch.
pages.brief: Sunlight reaches only a few yards into Loch Ness's dark, peat-stained water. A gray seal swims near the surface with fish, while the deep water below stays cold all year. The surface water is warmer in summer but still too cold for swimming.

pages.text: Monster Sightings For over 1,400 years, curious people have taken Nessie sightings seriously. Scientists have even used NASA’s computers, along with underwater cameras and other equipment, to test the loch. But long before this testing began in the 1970s, other sources saw the “monster” in the loch. The first recorded sighting was in ad 565 by an Irish missionary named Saint Columba. The report says he asked his servant to swim across the loch to get a boat. A creature came to the surface, roared, and opened its mouth. Columba commanded it to go back, be quiet, and not touch the man. It did, and every sighting since then has been quiet and peaceful. This man claimed he had seen and even filmed Nessie.
pages.brief: Saint Columba stands on the shore in AD 565 as his servant swims across the loch. A creature surfaces, roars, and opens its mouth. Columba commands it to go back and be quiet. Later, a man with a film camera watches the water.

pages.text: Urquhart Castle overlooks some of the deepest known parts of Loch Ness. People kept Nessie sightings quiet until the 1930s, when cameras became popular. Nessie hunting took off with a flash. People wanted to catch Nessie, at least in a picture. Thousands of people who live in the area have signed a statement promising that they’ve seen the monster. Most sightings have occurred near the Urquhart (ER-kert) Castle ruins. The castle ruins are located near the midpoint of the loch, where the water is deepest.
pages.brief: Urquhart Castle ruins overlook the deepest part of Loch Ness. In the 1930s, people with cameras gather near the ruins, hoping to photograph Nessie. A crowd of local people stands by the water, watching for the monster.

pages.text: Sightings of strange water creatures are not unique to Loch Ness. People have reported seeing similar creatures in at least 265 lakes and rivers around the world. Some people think the creatures must be a type of saltwater mammal or fish. Some think the Nessie sightings are of a prehistoric reptile that somehow survived over millions of years. They say that when the trench was created during the last ice age, a prehistoric beast or group of beasts became landlocked. Some people believe the Loch Ness Monster might be related to the plesiosaur, which lived millions of years ago and is now extinct.
pages.brief: A plesiosaur, a prehistoric reptile with a long neck, swims in an ancient sea. In a landlocked lake, a similar long-necked creature surfaces. Around the world, people report similar water creatures in many lakes and rivers.

pages.text: Operation Deep Scan used boats lined up across Loch Ness to search for evidence of the legendary monster. Fact or Fiction? Some accept the reports of Nessie as fact. The believers cite the similarity of descriptions of Nessie, the number of eyewitness reports, and possible sonar evidence. Others think of the reports as legends to keep children away from the deep, cold waters of the loch. The nonbelievers cite the lack of hard scientific evidence that proves Nessie is real. Some people have tried to make the world believe Nessie is real by creating hoaxes. These hoaxes are tricks that keep the legend of the Loch Ness Monster alive.
pages.brief: Boats line up across Loch Ness for Operation Deep Scan. On shore, some people believe the eyewitness reports and sonar evidence, while others call Nessie a legend. A parent keeps children away from the deep, cold water.

pages.text: This photograph was printed in a newspaper in 1934, but later, people learned it was a hoax. A few of the most famous hoaxes are based on photographs. People thought a photo of three humps was the real monster. It turned out to be a picture of three bales of hay covered in black tar. A famous photograph from 1934 turned out to be a fake sea-serpent head attached to a toy submarine. Another hoax in 1934 got people excited when they saw a giant footprint in the mud on the banks of the loch. A man had used a stuffed hippopotamus foot to make the footprint.
pages.brief: A 1934 newspaper photograph shows three dark humps in Loch Ness. Behind the hoax, three hay bales covered in black tar float in the water. A fake sea-serpent head sits on a toy submarine, and a stuffed hippopotamus foot presses a giant footprint into mud.

pages.text: Scientists got involved, despite all the hoaxes. They wanted to learn whether Nessie was real and put an end to the mystery. There was enough consistent evidence that people couldn’t explain. For example, sonar picked up a long object moving 480 feet deep in the loch. That is too deep for most fish. They decided to map the entire loch. In 1987, scientists launched “Operation Deep Scan.” They used 24 boats to map the bottom and sides of the loch with sonar equipment. Sonar uses sound to identify the shapes of objects. A sound is sent out from a sonar machine. When the sound hits an object, the sound bounces back as an echo. Scientists measure the time it takes for the sound to bounce back, which helps them create a picture. A sonar machine used in the loch shows objects that can’t be seen under the murky water. Some sounds from “Operation Deep Scan” were echoes from the loch’s steep sides. But they could not explain at least one echo from a “large and moving” object 200 feet down. No one knows for sure what the object was. Was it Nessie?
pages.brief: Twenty-four boats stretch across Loch Ness in 1987, mapping the bottom with sonar. Sound waves bounce off the steep sides and return as echoes. Deep below, sonar picks up a large, moving object 200 feet down that scientists cannot explain.

pages.text: Divers launch this “creature camera” into Loch Ness to try to capture underwater photographs of the legendary monster. Studying the loch has turned up other findings. In 1981, the Loch Ness Project found fish called red-bellied Arctic (ARK-tick) char. They had been living at a depth of 700 feet (213 meters) for over 12,000 years—since the last ice age. Experts had thought the waters were too cold for life below a few hundred feet. The discovery of red-bellied Arctic char surprised them.
pages.brief: Divers lower a creature camera into the dark water of Loch Ness. Deep below, red-bellied Arctic char swim at 700 feet, where experts thought the water was too cold for life. The fish have lived there for over 12,000 years.

pages.text: Do you see Nessie? Conclusion Maybe the Loch Ness Monster will one day lose its legendary status. It might someday be identified as a new species (SPEE-sheez) of fish. But for now, Nessie remains a mystery. That mystery might be its greatest appeal. The legend continues to capture people’s imaginations.
pages.brief: Children and adults stand at the loch shore, looking out and imagining Nessie. A shadowy long-necked creature swims in the water, and a small fish nearby hints that Nessie might be a new species. The mystery still captures imaginations.

books.title: What the Boys Found
books.art_why: Prehistoric Stone Age cave art and a 1940 discovery — no photograph of these events or paintings is possible, so drawn reconstruction art suits it.

pages.text: What the Boys Found An Art History Mystery by Dina Anastasio.
pages.brief: The opening title page of an art history mystery set in southern France — a plain, unadorned page that will lead the reader down into a hidden cave and the prehistoric paintings on its walls.

pages.text: The area near the Dordogne and Vezere rivers contains more than 100 prehistoric sites. Discovery in the Woods Have you ever been out for a walk and stumbled over a mysterious hole? Did you hesitate, look down into the darkness, and wonder what was under there? Well, that’s just what happened to four teenage boys near Lascaux (la-SKO) manor in southern France on a warm September day in 1940.
pages.brief: Four teenage boys out walking in the woods near Lascaux manor in southern France on a warm September day in 1940 stop at the edge of a mysterious dark hole, hesitating and looking down into the darkness, wondering what lies beneath them.

pages.text: Marcel Ravidat (RAH-vee-dah), three friends, and a dog were exploring the woods around the town of Montignac (MON-tee-nyack), when they discovered the hole. Several years before, a large pine tree had been struck by lightning and tumbled over, exposing a gaping entrance to what turned out to be one of history’s most interesting treasures.
pages.brief: Marcel Ravidat and three friends explore the woods around Montignac with a dog. Ahead of them lies the gaping entrance exposed when a large pine tree was struck by lightning and tumbled over, opening a hole in the ground.

pages.text: As the dog barked excitedly, Marcel and his friends dropped to their knees and peered into the hole. Without a light, it was impossible to make out what lay below, but they could tell that something hollow and thrilling was hidden there. They had a feeling that the opening was something other than a burrow or a tunnel created by a mole or a groundhog. The boys could barely contain their excitement. What had they found? Was this a cave, or perhaps a long-buried tomb? They felt they had to follow their instincts and continue their exploration. They made plans to return with a light and some shovels.
pages.brief: The dog barks excitedly as Marcel and his friends drop to their knees and peer into the dark hole. Without a light they can make nothing out, but they sense something hollow and thrilling below, and plan to come back with a lantern and shovels.

pages.text: Exploring the Cave A few days later, Marcel and his friends returned to the hole with a lantern. Digging quickly, they enlarged the hole, and one by one they slipped into it, fell onto a pile of rocks, and looked around. Their light was very dim, and it took several minutes to become accustomed to the darkness in this underground space. They saw that another entrance, almost a doorway into a shadowy space beyond, was behind some rocks. They looked at each other, nodded and shrugged, then held the lantern higher and moved into a large, dark space.
pages.brief: Marcel and his friends return days later with a lantern. They dig the hole wider, slip in one by one, land on a pile of rocks and blink in the dim light until their eyes grow used to the darkness, then move past a rocky doorway into a large dark space.

pages.text: The boys continued to explore the cave together, going deeper and deeper into the ground until they encountered a deep, narrow passage too small for all of them to fit through. After talking it over, they decided that Marcel should go forward alone. He would take the lantern and enlarge the passageway, then return for the others. Carrying the lantern, a shovel, and some rope, Marcel squeezed through the space, digging as he went. After a while he lowered the rope and dropped down a shaft into a cavernous room below.
pages.brief: Deep underground the boys reach a narrow passage too small for all of them. Marcel goes on alone with a lantern, a shovel and rope, squeezing through and digging as he goes, then lowering the rope and dropping down a shaft into a cavernous room below.

pages.text: Holding the lantern higher, he peered through the darkness at the walls surrounding him. The walls were covered with bas-relief (images that are carved out of a surface making the image raised from the surface) paintings of animals. Marcel moved closer. Images of horses, cows, stags, and bison seemed to dance and gallop and swim across the walls of the cave. Marcel could barely contain himself. He hurried out of the room and climbed up. As he made his way back to his friends, he noticed other pictures on the walls of the passageway. The Great Hall of the Bulls is the largest room in Lascaux’s caves, and Stone Age paintings cover its walls.
pages.brief: Marcel holds the lantern high and stares at the walls: horses, cows, stags and bison seem to dance, gallop and swim across the rock. Climbing back, he notices more painted animals in the passageway, and the great hall of the bulls opens around him.

pages.text: The Great Hall of the Bulls is named for the paintings of bulls, but horses and stags are more common in the cave. 2 A stag with antlers 3 A horse.
pages.brief: Inside the great hall named for its bulls, painted horses and stags crowd the rock walls more thickly than the bulls themselves. A stag lifts its antlers and a horse stands painted on the stone, lit only by lantern light in the dark chamber.

pages.text: More Questions, More Exploration By the next morning, the news of the boys’ discovery had spread throughout the village. Villagers descended upon the cave and found other rooms filled with new and exciting carvings. Clearly, these works of art were very, very old, and before long archaeologists came to the cave to study them. Archaeologists are scientists who study ancient cultures using the objects that people leave behind. The archaeologists looked at the pictures very carefully, and the longer they looked, the more questions they asked. The Lascaux cave entrance.
pages.brief: By the next morning villagers crowd into the cave, finding more rooms filled with carvings, and archaeologists arrive to study the art. The scientists examine the painted walls carefully, and the Lascaux cave entrance stands open behind them as questions pile up.

pages.text: The Scene of the Dead Man shows a man, bison, bird, and spear with a rhinoceros fleeing to the left. Who painted these mysterious paintings, and how old were they? Why were they painted in underground caves? Why did the artists paint only large birds and animals, such as horses and bulls, and ignore small creatures such as snakes and fish? How could such perfect art be created in such a dark space? There were tiny holes in the wall halfway up to the high ceiling. Why? What purpose did they serve?
pages.brief: On one wall the scene of the dead man shows a man, a bison, a bird and a spear, with a rhinoceros fleeing to the left. Archaeologists study the images and ask who painted them, why underground, and how such perfect art was made in the dark.

pages.text: These paintings were clearly very old. But how old? The archaeologists began by trying to figure out when the paintings were created. To do so, they tried several different methods. Many scientists started by looking at the paintings themselves. They analyzed the dyes, paints, or other materials used to create colors. If the artists used charcoal, scientists might be able to date them using the radiocarbon method (things that contain carbon can be dated by measuring how much the carbon has changed). But they found that these pictures could not be dated in this way. A scientist cleans a mammoth’s tooth before dating it using the radiocarbon method. Mammoths appear in Lascaux’s artwork.
pages.brief: Scientists try to date the paintings by analyzing the dyes and paints, hoping charcoal in the art will allow radiocarbon dating, but it does not work. In a laboratory a scientist cleans a mammoth's tooth before dating it, a mammoth like those in the cave art.

pages.text: Tools like these might have been used by the artists of Lascaux. The scientists had to lower their eyes to find the answers to their questions. On the ground, below the pictures, they found flint and bone fragments used to carve the pictures and pigments used to create colors. Like fossils, the materials were sealed in the layers of the ground. After a great deal of study, the scientists finally understood what the boys had found. The pictures on the wall had been created by Stone Age people who lived about 17,000 years earlier.
pages.brief: Scientists lower their eyes to the ground beneath the pictures and find flint and bone fragments used for carving, and pigments used to make color, sealed in layers of earth. From these they work out that Stone Age people painted the walls about 17,000 years earlier.

pages.text: The Back-to-Back Bison in the Main Gallery show how Lascaux’s artists tried to make their artwork three-dimensional. Who Painted the Caves? Still, like other caves in the area, the Lascaux cave held many more secrets. Scientists wondered who these artists were. Why had they carved and painted pictures so far underground? Scientists in 1940 already knew a great deal about Stone Age people. Stone Age men were hunters who killed and ate large animals such as bison. They were also people who believed in the magical powers of their leader, the Shaman.
pages.brief: Back-to-back bison in the main gallery show how Lascaux's artists tried to make their artwork three-dimensional. Meanwhile scientists puzzle over the painters themselves: Stone Age hunters who killed bison and believed in the magical powers of their leader, the Shaman.

pages.text: Scientists wondered if the pictures on the walls of the Lascaux cave could possibly have been carved and painted by a Shaman. Could this mystical leader have gone underground to try to communicate with spirits of people who had lived before? Could he have painted the pictures to ensure a successful hunt? Or could the hunters themselves have created the pictures as a way to bring them luck on their hunt? In other nearby caves, scientists found small and large footprints. Did this mean that children helped the artists or came to visit the Shaman with their parents? These stags appear to be swimming across the wall in the cave’s Main Gallery.
pages.brief: Scientists wonder whether a Shaman went underground to communicate with spirits or to ensure a good hunt, or whether the hunters painted for luck. In nearby caves they find small and large footprints, perhaps children helping or visiting with their parents; stags appear to swim across the main gallery wall.

pages.text: One question really befuddled the scientists: How were the artists able to see? It was very dark deep inside the cave, and no one believed that Stone Age people used lighting that could be carried into the cave. So, did the Stone Age people come first and the people who did the paintings follow much later, after fire had been discovered? As with many questions that seem to have no answers, this one was solved by accident. Someone found a piece of sandstone that was hollowed out on one side. Inside the hollowed out circle was some left-over carbon. When the carbon was analyzed and dated, scientists found traces of animal fat. People in the Stone Age burned animal fat in the scoop of this early lamp to light the cave.
pages.brief: Deep in the dark cave one question baffles the scientists: how did the artists see? By accident someone finds a hollowed piece of sandstone holding leftover carbon; when it is analyzed it shows traces of animal fat, the fuel burned in this early lamp to light the cave.

pages.text: The lighting mystery was solved. Stone Age artists lit their workspace by burning lamps filled with animal fat. But other questions remained. How did the artists manage to carve and paint the glorious pictures at the top of the Painted Gallery? The ceiling in the gallery is very, very high and really impossible to reach. Could those holes halfway up the wall hold the answer? This painting shows how artists would have used scaffolding to reach high places. Scientists estimated the size of the artists. They guessed how far the artists were from those high paintings. When they were finished guessing, they deduced the answer. The holes were used for a temporary scaffold that the artists climbed or stood on as they painted.
pages.brief: With the lighting mystery solved, scientists face the very high ceiling of the painted gallery, impossible to reach. They estimate the artists' size and guess how far they stood from the paintings, then deduce that the small holes halfway up the wall held a temporary scaffold the artists climbed or stood on.

pages.text: These shapes appear in the Main Gallery in shades of red, yellow, and violet. What were Stone Age artists like? How did they create color? What tools did they use? What were they thinking? Luckily the artists left all kinds of clues behind on the ground below their masterpieces. Can you guess what tools they used to carve the stone walls inside the cave?
pages.brief: Red, yellow and violet shapes cover the walls of the main gallery. Scientists ask what the Stone Age artists were like, how they created color and which tools they used, and they search the ground below the masterpieces for the clues the painters left behind.

pages.text: Other rock faces were impossible to carve at all and had to be painted. Most of the pictures are painted with red and black pigments made from minerals and metals found in the earth. Scientists understood why the colors of Lascaux’s paintings remained on the rock walls for 17,000 years. Q: Can you guess why the colors didn’t fade? See answer on page 23. Other caves The Cussac cave (top left) in France’s Dordogne region contains engravings that might be older than those at Lascaux. A cave near Vallon-Pont d’Arc in France (bottom left) shows animals that no longer live in the area. What animals do you see in each image?
pages.brief: Some rock faces could not be carved at all and had to be painted, mostly with red and black pigments made from minerals and metals in the earth, which is why the colors never faded. Engravings in the Cussac cave and animals near Vallon-Pont d'Arc show other old art.

pages.text: Understanding the Cave Art What else do the caves tell us? Do we know what the carvings and paintings mean? One thing that the caves tell us is that men, women, and children have always drawn pictures and always will. Stone Age people did not live in these caves. They went down into the earth and created pictures that represented something in their lives. Whether they went there just to draw or to be near their ancestors who lived before or to seek help from their Shaman, we may never know. But they were still creating art. This is the only rhinoceros to appear in the Lascaux artwork, even though rhinos lived all over France during the Stone Age.
pages.brief: Stone Age people did not live in these caves; they went down into the earth to create pictures that represented something in their lives, to draw or to be near their ancestors or to seek the Shaman's help. A lone rhinoceros, the only one at Lascaux, appears on the rock.

pages.text: A: The colors on the rock walls didn’t fade because the pigments were created from minerals and were protected in the cave from rain, wind, snow, and sun. When we look at paintings created fifty years ago or even today, can we understand what the artist was thinking? And do we really need to know, or is it enough to look at a picture and say, “Wow! That’s beautiful”?
pages.brief: The colors survived because the pigments came from minerals and the cave sheltered them from rain, wind, snow and sun. Looking at paintings old or new, people can simply stand before a picture and call it beautiful without ever knowing what the artist was thinking.

books.title: Coral Reefs
books.art_why: Coral reefs and modern places, boats, and people exist today, so photographs are possible.

pages.text: Coral Reefs.
pages.brief: A broad underwater view of a coral reef fills the page, showing many kinds of coral growing together in clear water, with the reef forming a large natural structure beneath the ocean surface. The scene focuses on the reef itself.

pages.text: Many kinds of corals, fish, and other sea creatures live on coral reefs. Introduction Just below the surface of Earth’s tropical oceans lie huge undersea communities known as coral reefs. These places of wonder and beauty support an incredible variety of life. Coral reefs are home to thousands of living organisms that depend on each other for food, shelter, and safety. Day and night, thousands of animals swim about, hunting, eating, and avoiding being eaten. Almost one-quarter of all plants and animals in the ocean live around coral reefs. Fish, sea turtles, sea stars, and many other animals make reefs their home. Visitors include seabirds and dolphins.
pages.brief: Just below the surface of a tropical ocean, a huge coral reef community teems with many kinds of corals, fish, sea turtles, and sea stars. Above the water, seabirds fly and dolphins swim near the reef, showing the variety of life that depends on it.

pages.text: What Is Coral? At first glance, coral may look like oddly shaped rocks or spiny plants. In fact, corals are tiny animals called polyps (PAH-lips). Most polyps are very small—between the size of a pinhead and the size of a pea. One branch or mound of coral can have thousands of these tiny polyps. Each polyp has a tubelike body and a mouth surrounded by tiny tentacles. Polyps are eating machines. At night, they open their tentacles to catch tiny animals and get the nutrients they need. Coral polyps stay in one place on a surface and stay there forever.
pages.brief: A close-up of a coral branch shows thousands of tiny polyps packed together, each with a tubelike body and a mouth ringed by small tentacles. At night, the polyps open their tentacles to catch tiny animals drifting in the water.

pages.text: Hundreds of kinds of coral live in the ocean. Most belong to one of two types. Hard corals, also known as stony corals, form hard skeletons. Over time, many millions of these hard skeletons build up and form reefs. Most kinds of stony coral live together with a variety of plantlike algae (AL-jee). The algae help supply food for the corals and for many of the fish that live around the reef. Elkhorn coral looks like the broad antlers of an elk. (Elk don’t have horns.)
pages.brief: A hard, stony coral reef shows branching elkhorn coral with broad, antler-like branches growing among other stony corals. Tiny plantlike algae live with the corals, helping supply food for the corals and for fish around the reef.

pages.text: Sea pens become smaller and hide in sand if creatures get too close (top). Sea fans branch up and out like wide fans. Their shape helps them trap tiny organisms to eat (bottom). The second common type is soft coral. These corals grow flexible, woody cores instead of hard skeletons. They often look like trees, bushes, or other plants. Soft corals can bend with the currents. Some soft corals have algae growing in their bodies, but others do not.
pages.brief: A sea pen pulls smaller and hides in the sandy seafloor as a creature comes too close. Nearby, soft sea fans branch up and out like wide fans, their shape helping trap tiny organisms to eat while currents bend them. These soft corals have flexible woody cores.

pages.text: Golden butterflyfish and a school of red bigeye fish swim past soft corals in Egypt’s Red Sea. A Busy Underwater Community Most people think of brightly colored fish when they think about coral reefs—and with good reason. Over four thousand species of fish live on reefs. The reefs provide them with food as well as protection from predators. Some fish live off the algae and plankton around the reef. Some eat other fish that live there. A few types of fish even eat the coral itself. Shrimp, lobsters, and crabs also consider reefs a favorite dining spot. Sea urchins and sea stars catch clams and smaller shellfish hidden among the coral branches. Waving sea anemones, which look like graceful flowers, hide in shallow openings, waiting for their next meal to drift past. Large holes in reefs make good homes and hiding spots for eels. No space is wasted on a busy reef.
pages.brief: Golden butterflyfish and a school of red bigeye fish swim past soft corals in Egypt’s Red Sea. Around them, the busy reef holds shrimp, lobsters, crabs, sea urchins, sea stars, waving sea anemones, and eels hiding in large holes among the coral.

pages.text: Coral reefs don’t just support thousands of species of organisms. They also help protect shorelines from floods and storms. By protecting the coast, reefs reduce erosion, property damage, and loss of human life. Coral reefs also feed and shelter animals that provide much of the world’s seafood. In doing so, they help the economies and diets of many countries. Diving tours and sport fishing also bring visitors—and income— to areas near coral reefs. Reef plants and animals are used in medicines, too. Coral reefs are a valuable natural resource. Reefs like this one in the Caribbean Sea protect the land from damage. Medicines from Coral Reefs Scientists have made medicines from reef organisms, and more are likely on the way. Corals produce a substance now used in the treatment of asthma and arthritis. Medicines that treat several different types of cancer come from coral reefs, too. Scientists are also studying other reef organisms that may treat skin conditions as well as infections.
pages.brief: A reef in the Caribbean Sea lies between open water and a shoreline, its coral structure protecting the land from storm waves and erosion. Nearby, scientists study reef organisms, and medicines made from corals are used to treat asthma, arthritis, and some cancers.

pages.text: The Coral Reef Zone NORTH AMERICA ASIA EUROPE AFRICA SOUTH AMERICA AUSTRALIA ANTARCTICA Most coral reefs are found near the equator. Where Are Coral Reefs? Most reefs are located close to shore in warm tropical waters. They also form where warm currents flow from the tropics, such as in Florida and parts of Japan. Corals grow best in warm water that is between 21 and 29 degrees Celsius (70–84°F). Since algae need sunlight to make food, most corals live near the water’s surface. Even with these conditions in place, coral reefs cannot survive in many areas. They do not grow well near the mouths of rivers, where dirt, trash, and fresh water flow into the sea. Fresh water can kill corals. Dirt and trash can damage or even smother reefs. Because corals grow very slowly, a reef takes a long time to increase in size or recover from damage. Some living coral reefs began growing twenty-five million years ago.
pages.brief: A world map shows the tropical zone near the equator, where most coral reefs grow close to shore in warm water. The map highlights warm ocean areas and shallow sunlit waters, while river mouths and muddy freshwater areas are shown as places where corals do not grow well.

pages.text: Three types of coral reefs exist. The first type, fringing reefs, are located close to shore. They usually follow the natural shoreline, or fringe, of the land. The second type is barrier reefs. They create a deep lagoon, or area of water, between the reef and the shore. The world’s largest barrier reef is the Great Barrier Reef in Australia. It is 2,300 kilometers (1,429 mi.) long and is made up of over three thousand reefs and islands. The Great Barrier Reef is home to nearly two thousand species of fish.
pages.brief: A fringing reef follows the shoreline close to land. Farther out, a barrier reef creates a deep lagoon between the reef and the shore. The Great Barrier Reef in Australia stretches long and is made up of thousands of reefs and islands, with many fish species living there.

pages.text: The Great Barrier Reef The Great Barrier Reef is between six and eight thousand years old, but coral reefs have been growing in this same spot for about five hundred thousand years! Many changes in sea levels occurred during that time, and low sea levels caused earlier reefs to die. New reefs formed during times of higher sea levels, including after the last ice age ended. Scientists think the current Great Barrier Reef is at least the sixth one to form in that location. Atolls are the third type of reef. They form in a circular pattern around a sinking island or an aging island volcano. As an island sinks or an island volcano ages and breaks apart, the remaining land disappears beneath the ocean’s surface. When that happens, the growing reef forms a circle around a central lagoon.
pages.brief: The Great Barrier Reef stretches across the ocean, with many coral reefs and islands. Nearby, an atoll forms a circular ring of coral around a central lagoon where a sinking island or aging volcano has disappeared beneath the surface.

pages.text: Threats to Coral Reefs Coral reefs are fragile, and many things can damage them. Large, powerful waves caused by a hurricane can destroy reefs. So can a tsunami (soo-NAH-mee). Most damage is caused by people, however. Poor water quality caused by human pollution is a likely factor in coral diseases. These diseases can wipe out an ancient coral reef in weeks. Another likely factor, also caused by people, is higher ocean temperatures as a result of global warming.
pages.brief: Large, powerful hurricane waves and a tsunami surge over a fragile coral reef, breaking coral. Polluted water flows toward the reef, and higher ocean temperatures stress the corals, showing how human pollution and global warming can damage ancient reefs.

pages.text: Global Warming Global warming is an increase in the average temperature of Earth’s atmosphere and oceans large enough to change long-term weather patterns. Global warming today is mainly the result of human activities such as clearing land for farming, industrial processes, and burning coal, oil, and gas. These activities create large amounts of carbon dioxide gas. This gas enters Earth’s atmosphere and traps heat close to Earth’s surface. Global warming is causing many problems. They include wildfires, extreme weather, and threats to coral reefs and other natural communities. Scientists expect the problems to get worse unless we reduce the activities that create so much carbon dioxide. Another problem that is killing corals is known as bleaching. Today, the most common cause of bleaching is ocean temperatures becoming too warm. When this happens, the algae that live in coral polyps undergo a chemical change that harms the polyps. The polyps get rid of the algae to stop the damage. Algae provide coral polyps with food as well as color. When corals get rid of algae, they lose their main source of food and begin to starve. They also lose their color, which makes them look bleached. Corals can sometimes recover from bleaching. But if the cause of bleaching continues, both the corals and the reef will die. Bleaching now affects three-quarters of coral reefs.
pages.brief: Factories, cleared farmland, and burning coal, oil, and gas release carbon dioxide that traps heat near Earth’s surface. In warm ocean water, coral polyps expel the algae that give them food and color, leaving the reef pale and bleached.

pages.text: Coral reefs around the world are turning white from bleaching. The same human activities that cause too much carbon dioxide in Earth’s atmosphere also cause too much carbon dioxide in oceans. This process makes ocean water more acidic. When this happens, corals can’t take in calcium carbonate, which keeps their skeletons healthy. Instead, the stony skeletons that support corals and reefs dissolve. People cause harm to coral reefs in other ways, too. Fishing methods that use poisons and explosives have destroyed over half the reefs in the Philippines. Coastal homes and other buildings create soil erosion and fresh water that pours into oceans. Fresh water damages coral, and it may also contain chemicals as well as waste.
pages.brief: Coral reefs turn white as bleaching spreads. In more acidic ocean water, stony coral skeletons dissolve. Near coastal homes and buildings, soil erosion and fresh water pour into the sea, while destructive fishing with poisons and explosives has damaged reefs in the Philippines.

pages.text: Ships and smaller boats have caused scars in Florida’s barrier reef. Another danger to coral reefs is breaking off chunks of them, whether by accident or on purpose. Some people take pieces home to keep or sell. Since 2011, the area of threatened reefs has increased by 30 percent. Even if we could stop global warming now, scientists predict that more than 90 percent of coral reefs will die by 2050. If we stand by and do nothing, though, we could lose them all. Boaters damaged this elkhorn coral.
pages.brief: Ships and smaller boats leave scars across Florida’s barrier reef, and chunks of elkhorn coral have been broken off by accident or on purpose. Some people take coral pieces home to keep or sell, adding to the threats facing reefs that scientists say may largely die by 2050.

pages.text: Protecting Coral Reefs Many countries have taken steps to preserve nearby reefs. In the United States, a government group makes maps of coral reefs. Satellite images help scientists watch for problems. Floating buoys measure sea levels, water temperature, wind speed, and air temperature. All this information helps scientists better understand reef damage and work to reduce it. Coral Nurseries Scientists can grow pieces of healthy coral in nurseries. The pieces may be rescued from boat damage or coastal construction projects. Scientists hang the pieces from bars, place them in baskets, or fasten them to stands on the ocean floor. They later move the pieces to damaged reefs to help them become healthy again.
pages.brief: A government group maps a coral reef while satellite images help scientists watch for problems. Floating buoys measure sea level, water temperature, wind speed, and air temperature. In a coral nursery, scientists hang healthy coral pieces from bars, place them in baskets, or fasten them to stands on the ocean floor.

pages.text: In Florida and on the Great Barrier Reef, it is against the law to take fish, plants, or coral from protected areas. People and boats are not allowed near many fragile reefs. But these efforts are only a start. Half of the world’s reefs have already been destroyed. Most of those that remain are threatened. It is up to all of us to help save coral reefs. Even if you don’t live near an ocean, you can help by doing your part to reduce global warming. Use less energy, walk or bike more, and recycle as much as you can.
pages.brief: In Florida and on the Great Barrier Reef, protected waters hold fish, plants, and coral that people may not take, and boats stay away from fragile reefs. On land, people help by using less energy, walking or biking more, and recycling as much as they can.

pages.text: Indonesian people plant mangrove trees to help protect nearby coral reefs. You can also help by learning how communities around the world support resilient reefs. These reefs stay healthy or recover when faced with climate-related challenges. Community members plant crops that provide shade for coral reefs, which helps them stay cool. Other people grow plants that help prevent erosion and keep pollution from entering the ocean. Still others protect fish that help reefs continue to have a balanced ecosystem. Each of us can do something to help coral reefs remain a beautiful natural wonder for centuries to come. What can you do?
pages.brief: Indonesian people plant mangrove trees along the shore to help protect nearby coral reefs. Community members also plant crops that provide shade for the reefs and grow plants that prevent erosion and keep pollution from entering the ocean, while others protect fish for a balanced ecosystem.

books.title: Alaska
books.art_why: Alaska is a real modern place, so photographs suit it.

pages.text: Alaska BEAUFORT SEA BERING SEA Alaska Anchorage Fairbanks Canada GULF OF ALASKA PACIFIC OCEAN Juneau Welcome to Alaska At the very top of North America lies a vast, wild, and unique land: Alaska. Located on the Arctic Circle, Alaska is west of Canada and between the Pacific and the Arctic Oceans. Alaska is a land of adventure. Alaska’s name comes from Alyeska. The word means “great land” in the language spoken by one Indigenous Alaskan group, the Aleuts. Alaska is special for many different reasons, including its beauty, people, and natural resources. Read on to learn all about Alaska.
pages.brief: A broad, wild Alaskan landscape near the Arctic Circle at the top of North America, between the Pacific and Arctic Oceans and west of Canada, showing the vast, unique, beautiful scale of a land of adventure.

pages.text: Matanuska Glacier features ice caves surrounded by the crystal blue water of supraglacial lakes—lakes located atop glaciers. The Land Alaska is enormous, covering over 660,000 square miles (1.7 million sq km). The coastline of Alaska is longer than the coastline of any other U.S. state. Because it is so big, Alaska includes many different landscapes. Alaska has around one hundred thousand glaciers of different sizes. It isn’t all snow and ice in Alaska, though. Land of the Midnight Sun The most northern part of Alaska is known as the “land of the midnight sun.” Above the Arctic Circle, the Sun doesn’t fully set for 24 hours during the summer solstice. But during the winter solstice, the Sun doesn’t fully rise for 24 hours. The amount of sunlight varies as Earth’s tilt causes the Arctic Circle to turn toward and away from the Sun. Summer temperatures can be above 90ºF (32ºC), while winter temperatures can drop below –58ºF (–50º C). Every year on summer solstice, an Alaskan baseball team plays a game at midnight.
pages.brief: Blue ice caves and crystal-blue supraglacial lakes atop Matanuska Glacier spread across a wide Alaskan landscape; far to the north, an Alaskan baseball team plays a midnight game under the summer sun that does not set.

pages.text: Most of the land in Alaska is in what many Alaskans call “the Interior.” The Interior is full of mountains, glaciers, and Arctic tundra. The weather is freezing cold, and it can also be quite dry. Very few people live there. Alaska is home to seventeen of the tallest twenty peaks in the United States. Denali, the tallest mountain in North America, towers 20,310 feet (6,190 m) above sea level. The mountain’s name means the “tall or high one” in the language of the Indigenous Koyukon people. Their lands include the sides of the mountain. A father and his children hunt caribou during the early fall.
pages.brief: A father and his children hunt caribou in the early fall across the Interior, where cold, dry mountains, glaciers, and Arctic tundra stretch out; Denali towers above them as the tallest mountain in North America.

pages.text: Alaska’s People and Its History Alaska has the largest area of any U.S. state but the fourth- smallest population. In 2020, the population of Alaska was about 733,000. Most of Alaska’s people live in the cities. Anchorage, the largest city, has the state’s largest port. Alaska’s capital is Juneau (JOO-noh). No roads lead to this city—people can only get there by sea or by air! Indigenous Athabascan girls wear kuspuks— oversized shirts with hoods. Land Area by State Alaska Texas Wisconsin Virginia Massachusetts Rhode Island Population by State Texas Virginia Massachusetts Wisconsin Rhode Island Alaska.
pages.brief: Indigenous Athabascan girls wear oversized hooded kuspuks in an Alaskan community, while Anchorage’s busy port and Juneau’s sea-and-air access show where most people live in this large state with a small population and a capital without roads.

pages.text: Between 15 and 18 percent of Alaskans— nearly one out of every five people—identifies as Indigenous. In fact, Alaska has the largest Indigenous population of any state. There are 231 federally recognized Native groups in Alaska today. They include the Tlingit (TLING-kuht), Haida, and Tsimshian (TSIM-shee-an) of the southeast coast. The Aleuts live in southwest Alaska, and the Iñupiaqs (i-NYOO-pee-ahks) and Yupiks live on the northern coast. Many Athabascan-speaking nations live in the interior. Russian fur traders were among the first Europeans to take over Alaska in the 1740s. Russians enslaved Alaska Natives and ruled over them harshly. By the 1800s, American fur traders were also in Alaska. In 1867, the United States bought Alaska from Russia. An Indigenous woman brings in a haul of salmon from Alaskan waters.
pages.brief: An Indigenous woman brings in a haul of salmon from Alaskan waters, with the southeastern, southwestern, northern, and interior homelands of Tlingit, Haida, Tsimshian, Aleut, Iñupiaq, Yupik, and Athabascan peoples around her as Russian and American fur traders arrive.

pages.text: Most of the land had long belonged to Indigenous peoples, however. Gold was discovered in the late 1800s. Soon thousands of miners from all over the world came through Alaska. The arrival of so many miners thirsty for wealth led to the deaths of thousands of Indigenous people. Alaska became an important location for U.S. military bases during World War II (1939–1945). Then it became the 49th U.S. state on January 3, 1959. Over time, the U.S. government and Alaska Natives worked together to reach agreements. The Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act (ANCSA) of 1971 recognized that Alaska Natives have the right to 44 million acres (18 million hectares) of land. That’s around 10 percent of the state’s land. The act also saw that 962 million dollars went to Alaska Natives. Alaskan Flag Children were invited to create the state flag for Alaska. Seventh grader John Benson, an Indigenous Alaskan student, created the winning design. The seven stars forming the constellation of the Big Dipper symbolize the strength of the bear. The eighth star represents the North Star.
pages.brief: A seventh-grade Indigenous Alaskan student, John Benson, created the winning Alaska flag design, showing seven Big Dipper stars for the bear’s strength and an eighth star for the North Star; gold miners arrive after gold is discovered, and Alaska later becomes the 49th state.

pages.text: The Wildlife Alaska is famous for its snowy mountains, giant forests, and crystal-clear lakes. This wild land is home to wolves, moose, and bald eagles. Whales, seals, sea lions, and many types of fish live in its waters. Many animals in Alaska have thick fur or blubber to keep warm in very cold conditions. Some Alaskan animals, such as snowy owls and mountain goats, remain white all year. Their color helps them to camouflage against winter snow. However, other animals, such as the willow ptarmigan (TAR-mi-gan), change color from summer to winter. In summer, they are speckled brown to blend in with the ground. In winter, they turn white. Ptarmigan in the summer Ptarmigan in the winter.
pages.brief: A snowy owl and mountain goat stay white against winter snow, while a willow ptarmigan is speckled brown in summer and white in winter; wolves, moose, bald eagles, whales, seals, sea lions, and fish share Alaska’s snowy mountains, giant forests, crystal-clear lakes, and waters.

pages.text: Thousands of wolf packs roam the state. They hunt animals such as moose, which often weigh more than 1,000 pounds (454 kg). Wolves also hunt caribou, of which there are around 750,000. They move each year from the forest to the coast. A pack of gray wolves travels together in Denali National Park. Three types of bears live in Alaska. They include brown, black, and polar bears. Mainly sea animals, polar bears are great swimmers usually found near sea ice. A young polar bear spread out on the ice might be waiting to use its front paws to pounce on a seal in an ice hole.
pages.brief: A pack of gray wolves travels together in Denali National Park, hunting moose and caribou; brown, black, and polar bears live in Alaska, and a young polar bear spreads out on sea ice, ready to use its front paws to pounce on a seal at an ice hole.

pages.text: Workers maintain the 800-mile (1,288 km) Trans-Alaska Pipeline. The Natural Resources In 1968, oil was discovered on Alaska’s northern coast. This discovery completely changed Alaska’s economy. The oil industry relies on the Trans- Alaska Pipeline. It is a giant oil pipe that stretches across the entire state from north to south. It takes oil from wells on the northern coast to an ice-free port on the Pacific coast. From there, ships carry the oil to the rest of the United States to power homes, vehicles, and more. However, the pipeline has been steadily carrying less oil since the 1980s. Do You Know? The state of Alaska makes so much money from oil that it doesn’t charge income tax or sales tax like most other states.
pages.brief: Workers maintain the 800-mile Trans-Alaska Pipeline stretching from northern oil wells to an ice-free Pacific port, where ships carry oil to power homes and vehicles; since the 1980s, the pipeline has been steadily carrying less oil across the state.

pages.text: Many Alaskans make their living from oil. However, the oil industry harms the state’s wildlife and natural beauty. Many Alaska Natives and others want to set aside huge areas of Alaska. They want to protect it from ever being drilled for oil or changed by humans in any way. Others say doing so would be a waste of resources that could help many people. The oil industry has many risks. Hundreds of oil spills happen each year along the pipeline. The largest disaster took place in 1989. An oil tanker hit a reef, sending 11 million gallons (42 million liters) of oil into the ocean. Fishing is also an important industry in Alaska. Alaskan boats catch cod, salmon, and crab. Alaska has the largest fish business in the country—it sells more fish every year than any other state. Each net on this fishing boat can catch more than 20,000 pounds (9,072 kg) of salmon.
pages.brief: An Alaskan fishing boat hauls a net heavy with salmon, cod, and crab, while oil from a 1989 tanker spill spreads across the ocean after the ship hits a reef; Alaskans debate protecting wild land from drilling against the risks of oil spills and the value of resources.

pages.text: Alaska’s Beauty One of the fastest-growing parts of the Alaskan economy is tourism. Alaskans depend on the hundreds of thousands of people who visit their state from all over the world. Visitors arrive on cruise ships and airplanes. They go whale-watching, hike through national parks, and visit Alaskan cities. Alaska is vast and wild. During the darkest days of winter, the sky above Alaska sometimes fills with colorful light. This is called the aurora borealis, or northern lights. They shine when Earth’s magnetic field pulls tiny particles from the Sun. Oxygen molecules located around 60 miles (97 km) above Earth produce green light, the most common color of the aurora borealis.
pages.brief: Tourists arrive by cruise ship and airplane to whale-watch, hike through national parks, and visit Alaskan cities; above the dark winter landscape, the aurora borealis fills the sky with colorful light, including common green light produced by oxygen high above Earth.

pages.text: An iceberg from a glacier floats in an Alaskan river (left). Tourists aboard a cruise ship visit Glacier Bay National Park. Alaska is a special land, but it also faces some problems. It is warming faster than any other state. Scientists studied the length of the snow season between 1997 and 2018. They found that it has gotten shorter over time. Climate change is melting Alaska’s glaciers, which is damaging for Alaska Natives and native wildlife. While Alaska’s future isn’t certain, it remains an amazing place of great beauty and adventure.
pages.brief: An iceberg from a glacier floats in an Alaskan river, while tourists aboard a cruise ship visit Glacier Bay National Park; Alaska is warming faster than any other state, the snow season is shorter, and melting glaciers threaten Alaska Natives and native wildlife.

pages.text: No Ordinary Bird What type of bird cannot fly and has strong flippers instead of wings? What type of bird spends its whole life swimming or walking? It’s no ordinary bird, that’s for sure—it’s a penguin! Penguins are amusing to watch. Their dark backs and white bellies make them look as if they are dressed up for a fancy party. On land, most are clumsy and walk with a strange waddle. But in water, they are swift and graceful. The movie March of the Penguins sparked great interest in emperor penguins. There are also sixteen other types of penguins. Read on to learn more about these amazing birds. Where do you think these gentoo penguins are going?
pages.brief: Several gentoo penguins stand together on land, their dark backs and white bellies making them look dressed up. Most waddle awkwardly, while others move toward the water, where penguins swim swiftly and gracefully. Their strong flippers replace wings, and they cannot fly.

pages.text: Where Penguins Live All penguins live in the southern hemisphere. Many live in places with very cold weather. Four species of penguins live on the ice around Antarctica—the coldest place on Earth. Another three species live on islands near Antarctica. But not all penguins live in cold, harsh places. The little blue penguin lives along the coasts of Australia and New Zealand, where forests, not ice fields, border the ocean. And the Galapagos penguin lives off the west coast of South America near Ecuador, which lies on the equator!
pages.brief: A group of penguins stands on Antarctic ice in a very cold place. Elsewhere, a little blue penguin walks along a forested coast near Australia and New Zealand, where trees border the ocean. A Galapagos penguin stands near Ecuador, close to the equator, in a much warmer place.

pages.text: Africa Where Penguins Live ATLANTIC OCEAN South America Antarctica INDIAN OCEAN PACIFIC OCEAN Australia Equator South America Galapagos Islands Imagine you are in a spaceship high above Antarctica. From that height, you can see the southern areas of Africa, Australia, and South America. The large “Where Penguins Live” map, from that same view, shows where most species of penguins live. The small maps show where Galapagos penguins live.
pages.brief: A high view from a spaceship looks down on Antarctica and the southern parts of Africa, Australia, and South America. Beside it, a large map of the southern hemisphere shows where most penguins live, and smaller maps focus on the Galapagos Islands.

pages.text: Penguin Bodies Unlike most birds, penguins spend most of their lives in the ocean. Their streamlined bodies and webbed feet help them move through the water with ease. Some penguins can swim as fast as 40 kilometers per hour (25 mph) for short distances. Instead of wings with long feathers, penguins have powerful flippers similar to those of seals, dolphins, and sea turtles. Penguins use their flippers like boat oars to push water and move forward. They steer with their feet and tails. This king penguin uses its flippers to zoom through the water.
pages.brief: A king penguin zooms through blue water, its streamlined body and webbed feet moving easily. Its powerful flippers push the water like boat oars, while its feet and tail steer. It can swim as fast as forty kilometers per hour for short distances.

pages.text: Penguins have two layers of feathers—a stiff outer layer and a soft layer underneath. Their small, stiff outer feathers are packed closely together. Penguins rub their beaks on oil glands at the base of their tails and spread the oil on their outer feathers. Their oily coats keep out water and keep in heat. Underneath penguins’ outer feathers is a layer of down—warm, fluffy feathers that hold warm air close to the body. A thick layer of fat adds another layer of insulation. If a penguin gets too hot, it fluffs up its feathers to let body heat escape. It may eat snow to cool off, too. Eating snow also helps a penguin get enough water in its body. Most penguins molt, or replace old feathers with new ones, once each year. Around age two, young penguins grow their adult feathers.
pages.brief: A penguin rubs its beak on oil glands at the base of its tail, then spreads the oil over its stiff outer feathers. A close view shows the soft down underneath and the thick layer of fat. The penguin fluffs its feathers and eats snow to cool down.

pages.text: Toboggan tracks Tobogganing is much faster than walking. Penguins are awkward on land. Because their legs attach far back on their bodies, it is difficult for them to walk smoothly. But penguins often must travel on land for long distances. When they get tired of walking, they slide on their stomachs. This way of moving is called tobogganing. Do You Know? Why don’t penguins’ feet freeze when they walk on ice? Warm blood keeps penguins’ feet from freezing. Fat and feathers keep penguins’ core body temperature high, even when their feet are only a few degrees above freezing. As warm blood flows to their feet, it passes very close to cold blood that is flowing from the feet back to the heart. As it flows by, the warm blood heats the cold blood so that it doesn’t lower the penguins’ core temperature to a dangerous level.
pages.brief: A penguin lies on its belly and slides across the snow, pushing with its feet. Its legs are set far back on its body, so walking is awkward, but tobogganing is much faster. Its warm feathered body rests on the cold ice.
