They range from the little blue and yellow-eyed penguins to the tall emperor and king penguins.

pages.text: Wowser! The smallest penguin is the little blue penguin. 8 It is about the size of a large duck. The largest penguin is the emperor penguin. 7 It is about the same height and weight as an average third grader!
pages.brief: A little blue penguin stands beside a large duck, showing that it is about the same size. Nearby, a tall emperor penguin stands next to an average third grader, matching the child in both height and weight.

pages.text: Penguin Parents and Chicks Spring comes in late September south of the equator. This is when most penguins move onto land to start families. They build nests in huge nesting areas called rookeries. Depending on the species of penguin, the rookery may be on snowy ice, a rocky cliff, or a hillside. A group of penguins that nests together is called a colony. A colony may contain hundreds or even thousands of one species of penguin. They make noises—grunts, croaks, hisses, and trumpeting sounds—as well as movements such as stretching, bowing, and pointing their beaks toward the sky. A penguin colony is very loud (and dirty!), with lots of activity.
pages.brief: A huge colony of penguins gathers on a rocky hillside in spring. Hundreds of nests fill the rookery. The penguins stretch, bow, and point their beaks toward the sky, making grunts, croaks, hisses, and trumpeting sounds. The noisy, dirty colony is full of activity.

pages.text: All these noises and movements help penguins pick mates. Each pair builds a nest together using grass, moss, feathers, or pebbles. Emperor and king penguins use their feet as a nest, cradling the egg on top of their feet. Eggs must stay warm or they won’t hatch. The smaller Antarctic penguins sit on their eggs for about five weeks. The eggs of emperor and king penguins take about eight weeks to hatch. During that time, a parent’s body keeps the egg warm. King parents take turns egg-sitting, but an emperor father cares for the egg while the mother leaves to get food. He may go without food for four months before his mate returns to care for the hatched chick. During this time, he and other male emperor penguins face some of the harshest weather on Earth. A flap of skin on this king penguin’s body keeps its egg warm.
pages.brief: A king penguin stands upright with a single egg cradled on top of its feet, a flap of skin keeping the egg warm. Nearby, pairs build nests from grass, moss, feathers, or pebbles. An emperor father may care for his egg through harsh weather for months without food.

pages.text: This gentoo penguin chick eats food brought up from its parent’s stomach. Penguin chicks are covered with down when they hatch. They cannot swim until they grow waterproof feathers, so they must stay on land. Since there is no penguin food on land, one parent cares for the chick while the other parent goes to the ocean to eat. That parent brings back food for the chick. As a chick grows, it leaves its nest and lives in a group with other chicks. They crowd together to stay warm, and their parents bring them food. Chicks recognize their parent’s voice. Even with thousands of penguins in the colony and all the noise they produce, each chick knows the sound of its own parent’s call, and they will find each other. When chicks grow their adult feathers, they are ready to go to sea and hunt their own food. They eat well and grow quickly. Penguins between the ages of two and eight have chicks of their own.
pages.brief: A gentoo penguin chick, covered in down, opens its beak as a parent brings up food from its stomach. Other chicks crowd together nearby to stay warm. The chick cannot swim until it grows waterproof adult feathers, so it stays on land.

pages.text: Hunters and Hunted Penguins are meat eaters, and their diet includes fish, squid, crab, and other ocean animals. Among their favorite foods are tiny animals called krill, which are related to shrimp. The largest penguins—emperors and kings— mostly eat fish and squid, which are more filling than krill. Most penguins find their food near the ocean’s surface, but larger penguins may dive deep in the ocean to find food. Like other birds, penguins have no teeth. Some seabirds, including penguins, have a fringe of spines inside their mouths. The spines help penguins hold onto slippery food that might be trying to escape. You can see the spines along the sides of this rockhopper penguin’s mouth.
pages.brief: A rockhopper penguin swims among fish, squid, crab, and tiny krill, its mouth open. A fringe of spines along the sides of its mouth helps it hold slippery food. Larger penguins may dive deep, while most penguins find food near the ocean surface.

pages.text: Penguins are the main source of food for leopard seals. Penguins are hunted by sharks and orcas, but their worst enemies are leopard seals, which can swim very fast. To escape, penguins must get out of the water quickly. They gain speed by swimming deep; then they paddle very fast, shooting up onto land as if they’ve been shot from a cannon. Safe on land, adult penguins have few enemies, so they don’t need to fly to escape. Antarctic penguins must keep their chicks safe from other birds. Smaller birds will eat penguin eggs, and larger seabirds may eat the eggs and attack the chicks. But no birds hunt healthy adult penguins.
pages.brief: A leopard seal chases penguins through the water. The penguins dive deep, then paddle fast and shoot up onto land. On land, adult penguins stand near chicks while seabirds are nearby; smaller birds may eat eggs, and larger seabirds may attack chicks.

pages.text: Penguins and People Because penguins can’t fly, they have no way to escape people who hunt them. Long ago, sailors hunted penguins for food, and the practice continues in some areas. Penguins are also killed and used for fishing bait. Huge numbers of penguins gather to breed in certain areas, and they need a plentiful food supply. Penguins compete for ocean food with people who conduct large fishing operations in many of the same areas. Without a dependable food source, fewer adult penguins survive, so fewer chicks survive. Penguins also get tangled in fishing nets and die. Conservation groups are working to convince large fishing companies to limit their fishing near penguin rookery sites during the breeding season. Do You Know? The great auk, a flightless penguinlike bird in the northern hemisphere, became extinct in the 1800s because of hunting.
pages.brief: Penguins swim near a fishing boat and a large net; some become tangled in the net. Long ago, sailors hunted penguins for food, and people still hunt them in some places or use them as bait. Conservation groups work to limit fishing near rookeries during breeding season.

pages.text: Oil pollution is another threat to penguins’ safety. Because they spend so much of their time swimming in the water, penguins are at greater risk than most other birds of coming in contact with an oil spill. They can’t fly above a polluted area to see and avoid it. When oil from a spill coats birds’ feathers, it prevents their natural insulation from working properly, causing them to quickly get too cold. Penguins have a thick layer of fat beneath their skin that gives them extra protection against the cold. When penguins are rescued and cleaned, their fat layer helps them to survive more often than other birds. Still, many more penguins die than can be rescued and cleaned.
pages.brief: Oil from a spill coats penguins swimming in the ocean, making their feathers lose insulation and letting them get cold. A thick layer of fat beneath their skin gives extra protection. Rescuers clean oiled penguins, but many more die than can be rescued.

pages.text: Warmer ocean temperatures have caused the food supply of black-footed penguins to move south. The penguins must swim farther to get food, and fewer survive. Global warming is creating new dangers for penguins. As the air and water in the Antarctic region warm up, the ice mass shrinks. Normally, algae build up on the ice in winter. When spring comes, the ice melts and krill eat the algae. Less ice means less algae and less food for krill. With less krill to eat, fewer Antarctic penguins survive. Scientists are also studying other ways that global warming is affecting penguins. They have seen the numbers of many penguin species drop by nearly half in the past fifty years. The effects of global warming are most easily seen in polar regions. Like polar bears in the northern hemisphere, penguins are messengers of a planet in trouble. Penguins, like all birds— and all wildlife—need our help to survive.
pages.brief: A black-footed penguin swims far across warming ocean water to find food. In the Antarctic, shrinking ice leaves less algae for krill, so fewer krill are available. Scientists watch as penguin numbers fall, showing that these birds are messengers of a planet in trouble.

books.title: Camouflage
books.art_why: All subjects are real animals and natural settings; photographs suit a camouflage science book.

pages.text: Chameleon Introduction Most animals have enemies. In order to survive, they have to defend themselves. Some animals use speed and strength to survive. Others, like alligators, use their powerful jaws and sharp teeth. Some, like rattlesnakes and black widow spiders, use venom. Others, such as turtles, have hard body coverings. But other animals must rely on the color and pattern of their body covering for survival.
pages.brief: A chameleon perches on a branch. An alligator shows open jaws and sharp teeth; a rattlesnake and black widow spider are nearby; a turtle is tucked inside its hard shell. The scene is a natural habitat with several animals that survive by different defenses.

pages.text: The use of coloring and patterns to disguise and conceal is called camouflage. Many kinds of animals use camouflage in order to survive. Predators—animals that hunt—use it to sneak up on their prey without being seen. Prey use it to hide from predators. The snake’s patterns and color can help it hide. Camouflage comes in many forms. Some animals have permanent color patterns that help them to hide. Others have color patterns that change with the seasons. Still others have color patterns that change with the surface the animal is on. And still others use patterns that change during different stages of life. Let’s take a look at different forms of camouflage.
pages.brief: A patterned snake rests among leaves and rocks, its colors merging with the background. Nearby, a predator crouches low as if sneaking toward hidden prey. The scene suggests different kinds of camouflage: markings that hide an animal, colors that change with seasons, surfaces or life stages.

pages.text: Do You Know? A polar bear can swim up to 60 miles without resting. Polar bears blend in with their surroundings. Blending or Concealing Coloration Have you heard the joke about the student who turned in a blank sheet of white paper for his art project? His teacher asked him how he could call that art. “It’s not a blank sheet of white paper,” he replied. “It’s a polar bear in a snowstorm.” The polar bear is an example of blending coloration—its white fur blends in well with its snowy surroundings. This gives the polar bear an advantage when hunting. It is less visible and can sneak up on seals, walruses, and other animals that it hunts.
pages.brief: A white polar bear stands in a snowy landscape, its fur blending into the white surroundings. It watches toward seals and walruses in the distance, less visible as it hunts. Snow and pale light make the bear hard to pick out from the scene.

pages.text: Blending coloration is quite common in nature. Many desert creatures, including snakes, lizards, and desert foxes, are the color of sand to match their surroundings. Many insects are green to blend in with the plants they live and feed on. Lions match the color of the dry grasslands of the African plains where they live. Other big cats with color patterns, such as leopards, cheetahs, and tigers, blend in with the light and dark of their woodland homes. This snake’s color blends with the rocks.
pages.brief: A desert snake, lizard and fox are sand-colored against dry ground. Green insects rest on plants, a lion stands in dry African grassland, and a leopard, cheetah and tiger move among woodland light and shadow. A snake lies on rocks, its color blending with the stone.

pages.text: A special kind of blending can happen when one kind of animal is found living in many different places. Let’s look at earless lizards as an example. Earless lizards living on the white sands of New Mexico are white. Other earless lizards that live nearby on black volcanic rock are almost black. Still other earless lizards in nearby desert areas are light yellow to blend well with sand. Earless lizards.
pages.brief: Three earless lizards are shown in different places: one white on pale sand in New Mexico, one almost black on dark volcanic rock, and one light yellow on desert sand. Each lizard's color matches the ground beneath it, helping it blend into its surroundings.

pages.text: Arctic foxes change color for winter and summer. Seasonal Blending Many animals have fur or skin that blends in with their environment. But what do you do when the color of your environment changes? Some animals that live in colder climates change color with the seasons. Arctic hares and Arctic foxes in the far north have brown fur in the summer and white fur in the winter. This helps them to hide year round. If the land around them is white, they’re white. If it’s dark, they’re dark, too.
pages.brief: An Arctic fox and an Arctic hare stand in a northern landscape. In summer they have brown fur among dark ground; in winter their fur is white against snow. The scene shows the same animals changing color with the seasons to stay hidden year round.

pages.text: Arctic birds such as ptarmigans (TAR-mi- gans) and snowy owls also change color with the seasons. Ptarmigans start to grow speckled brown summer coats in the spring. The males stay white longer so that they’re more visible to predators. While the predators are busy chasing the more visible male, the female hides in her nest and warms her newly laid eggs. Ptarmigans in summer and winter.
pages.brief: A male ptarmigan stays white against summer ground while a female ptarmigan, speckled brown, sits low in her nest warming newly laid eggs. A snowy owl is nearby in the seasonal landscape. The male's greater visibility draws predators while the female hides.

pages.text: Chameleons can change color. Color Change Perhaps one of the best-known examples of color change is the chameleon. Many people believe that chameleons change color to hide. But most chameleons change color to display emotions to other chameleons. However, because many chameleons happen to be green, brown, or gray, they are well hidden in nature. Do You Know? Chameleons have the widest range of color of all the color-changing animals. They change color based on their temperature and mood, or to communicate with other chameleons.
pages.brief: A chameleon clings to a branch, its skin showing green, brown and gray tones. Another chameleon faces it as the first changes color, displaying mood or communicating. The surrounding leaves and twigs match the chameleon's natural colors, so it is well hidden in nature.

pages.text: The octopus is also known for its ability to change color. It can change both the color and texture of its skin. When an octopus moves onto a rock, it changes color to match the rock. Its skin becomes bumpy to match the rock’s surface. The octopus blends in with its surroundings. Crab spiders change color, too. They are able to match the color of white, pink, or yellow flowers. They sit on flowers and are almost invisible until an unsuspecting beetle, fly, or bee comes by for a sip of nectar. The crab spider then attacks it.
pages.brief: An octopus moves onto a rock, its skin turning bumpy and matching the stone. Nearby, a crab spider sits on a white, pink or yellow flower, almost invisible as a beetle, fly or bee comes for nectar. The spider waits to attack.

pages.text: This white weasel blends in with the snow. Camouflage in Young Animals Some animals have camouflage patterns when they are young, but lose these patterns when they grow big and strong enough to outrun their enemies. When young, their parents must leave them alone for periods of time to go find food. If the young are camouflaged, they are less likely to be eaten by a predator while their parents are away.
pages.brief: A white weasel stands in snow, its fur blending with the white ground. Nearby, young animals with camouflage patterns wait alone while a parent is away finding food. Their markings help them stay hidden from predators during the time they are left by themselves.

pages.text: Young deer have spots to help them blend in with the leaves. Camouflage patterns are well known in baby deer. Similar light-colored spotting also occurs in the young of tapirs (a hoofed mammal) and wild boars. Topi antelopes of the African desert blend in with the sand while they are young. When they grow strong enough to flee their enemies, they develop black markings. Even some young predatory animals use camouflage to hide. Lion cubs have spots that help them blend in.
pages.brief: A young deer with light spots stands among leaves, blending into the woodland. Young tapirs and wild boars show similar light spotting. A young topi antelope is sand-colored on African desert ground, while a lion cub with spots rests nearby; older animals develop darker markings as they grow.

pages.text: Some animals are even camouflaged before birth. Many animals are at risk of being eaten when they are in the egg stage. Birds that nest on the ground are at great risk for having their eggs stolen when they leave the nest. Oystercatcher eggs are the color of pebbles along the beaches where they live. The eggs of other ground-nesting birds have streaks and blotches to break up the egg-shaped outline to help them blend with their surroundings. Speckled eggs blend in well with the rocks.
pages.brief: Oystercatcher eggs rest on a pebbly beach, colored like the surrounding stones. Other ground-nesting bird eggs have streaks and blotches that break up their egg-shaped outline. The speckled eggs lie among rocks and sand, blending with the ground where the birds nest.

pages.text: Many insects look like plant parts. Disguise Disguise is another kind of camouflage. A disguised animal looks like another animal or object. Some of the best masters of disguise are leaf insects and stick insects. A leaf insect has wings that look exactly like leaves. Stick insects look so much like sticks that it’s almost impossible to tell the insect from the stick that it rests on. Some insects are the shape and color of flowers. Tropical mantids, of which the praying mantis is one, have bodies that look just like orchids. They are always ready to gobble up an insect that thinks it’s about to get a taste of nectar.
pages.brief: A leaf insect rests with wings that look exactly like leaves, and a stick insect stands so still it resembles a twig. Nearby, a tropical mantid has a body shaped and colored like an orchid, waiting to gobble up an insect that comes looking for nectar.

pages.text: Trickery While disguise involves the visible features of an animal, trickery involves behavior. Some animals try to trick or fool other animals by pretending they are dead or by using some other trick. When frightened, some chameleons lie on the ground without moving. This behavior causes the chameleon to look like a piece of dead wood. Many kinds of small beetles play dead when they are disturbed. They fall to the ground and look like grains of soil, fooling birds who might otherwise eat them. Chameleon.
pages.brief: A chameleon lies motionless on the ground, its body looking like a piece of dead wood. Nearby, small beetles fall to the soil and lie still, resembling grains of dirt. The still poses fool birds and other animals that might otherwise eat them.

pages.text: Many predator animals will not eat an animal that is already dead. They prefer to eat only fresh meat. So many prey animals play dead to avoid being eaten. When threatened, a hognose snake turns upside-down and throws back its head, holding its mouth open. It pretends to be dead and tricks its predator into leaving it alone. A hognose snake playing dead.
pages.brief: A hognose snake lies upside-down with its head thrown back and mouth open, pretending to be dead. A predator watches nearby but prefers fresh meat and leaves the still snake alone. The snake's trick helps it avoid being eaten when threatened.

pages.text: Fireflies use light to attract mates. Fireflies are experts at a very clever kind of trickery. When a firefly wants to mate, it flashes its light. Each species of firefly flashes its own kind of signal pattern. Sometimes the female of one species will imitate the signal of another species to trick the males of that species. She flashes the signal of the other species, and when a male arrives, she eats him.
pages.brief: Fireflies glow in the dark, each species flashing its own signal pattern to attract mates. A female of one species flashes the signal of another species; when a male of that species arrives, she eats him. The scene shows this clever trickery among glowing fireflies.

pages.text: Disruptive Coloration Another kind of camouflage is called disruptive coloration. This kind of camouflage helps to break up an animal’s outline and hide its true shape. The stripes of tigers and zebras are two examples of this kind of camouflage. Two African antelopes also have stripes that help break up their outlines. The stripes of all these animals blend in with shadows and make the animals less visible. Zebras have disruptive coloration.
pages.brief: A tiger and a zebra stand in a shadowy natural setting, their stripes breaking up their outlines and hiding their true shapes. Two African antelopes with stripes are nearby. The patterns blend with shadows and make all these animals less visible to predators.

pages.text: Io moth with eyespots Flash Coloration and Other Surprises Until now, we’ve been talking about how animals use color and behavior patterns to be less visible. But some animals survive by being more visible. Some animals escape predators by startling them. Some do it by making a sudden noise or by baring their teeth. Others startle by flashing a bright color at the predator. This is called flash coloration. A related kind of camouflage involves eyespots. Some moths have spots on their wings that look like the eyes of large animals. When the moth flashes its eyespots, this can startle a predator and give the moth an extra second or two to fly away before being eaten.
pages.brief: An Io moth rests with wings closed, then flashes bright eyespots that look like the eyes of a large animal. The sudden display startles a predator, giving the moth an extra second or two to fly away before being eaten.

pages.text: Poisonous frog Warning Coloration Other animals have bright coloring to warn other animals that they taste bad or are poisonous. The bright colors remind predators of the bad experience they had the last time they tried to eat one of these yucky animals. Fish, frogs, snakes, and many kinds of insects use warning coloration. A few animals survive simply because they look like some other bad tasting or poisonous animal. They disguise themselves using the same colors, just to keep predators away. Some flies and moths survive because they have black and yellow body stripes like stinging wasps and bees. Some also make a buzzing sound like a bee.
pages.brief: A bright poisonous frog sits among leaves, its vivid colors warning predators that it tastes bad. Nearby, a fish, snake and insects show similar warning colors. A fly and moth with black and yellow stripes resemble stinging wasps and bees, and a buzzing sound adds to the trick.

pages.text: A famous example of warning coloration is the monarch butterfly, which is bright orange and black. Monarchs taste so bad that a bird will often vomit after eating one. But the viceroy doesn’t taste bad. However, it has developed similar markings to look like the monarch. It is more likely to be left alone by predators since it looks like the foul-tasting monarch. Viceroy Monarch.
pages.brief: A bright orange and black monarch butterfly rests on a plant while a bird watches. Nearby, a viceroy butterfly has similar markings but does not taste bad. Because it looks like the foul-tasting monarch, predators are more likely to leave the viceroy alone.

pages.text: Camouflaged eggs How Did Camouflage Develop? From one generation of living things to the next, little changes happen in physical traits such as colors and patterns. Sometimes when animals have babies, some of the babies are born with slightly different features. The difference may give this new animal an advantage toward survival. For example, it may be faster or have a color or pattern to better blend with its surroundings. With such an advantage, this animal is more likely to survive to produce its own babies. These babies are likely to also have the same trait and will be more likely to survive.
pages.brief: A group of young animals and camouflaged eggs show small differences in color and pattern. One young animal has a marking that blends better with its surroundings, giving it an advantage. It is more likely to survive, have babies, and pass that helpful trait on.

pages.text: An animal whose camouflage does not work well will be eaten by a predator. Only animals with the best traits survive to produce offspring. Those offspring tend to have the same traits as their parents. In this way, the successful camouflage is passed on from one generation to the next. This process works for predators as well. Predators with the best traits will be the ones that have regular meals, stay strong, and are more likely to survive and reproduce. Their traits then get passed on to their offspring, who in turn are also more likely to survive and reproduce. Over thousands of years, weak and less protected animals failed to survive. This has allowed animals with the best traits for survival to live on and reproduce. Polar bear.
pages.brief: A polar bear stands in its snowy habitat, showing a successful trait passed from parents to offspring. Nearby, less protected animals are hidden or exposed in a natural setting. Over thousands of years, animals with the best camouflage and hunting traits survive and reproduce while weaker ones do not.

pages.text: The rhinoceros does not need camouflage. Conclusion Only a few animals have no need for camouflage. These animals may have no natural enemies and eat plant food that cannot escape. The only threat to these animals comes from humans. Land animals such as elephants, rhinoceroses, and hippopotamuses do not need to camouflage themselves from natural enemies. In the ocean, only certain huge whales that eat plankton have no need of camouflage. For other animals, camouflage plays an important role in the struggle to stay alive.
pages.brief: A rhinoceros stands in open grassland, not trying to hide. An elephant and a hippopotamus are nearby, all large plant eaters with no natural enemies. In the ocean, a huge whale feeds on plankton. These animals do not need camouflage except against threats from humans.

pages.text: TRY THIS! Wear neutral-colored clothing for a day. Notice how many people pay attention to you as you do normal activities such as going to school or going to a store. On another day, wear bright red clothing and do similar activities. Notice if you get more attention when you wear bright colors. TRY THIS! Go out into nature with a family member. Wear clothing that is only shades of green or brown. Stand in the middle of a wooded area and see if your companion can see you from 20 paces away. Now put on a brightly colored T-shirt you’ve brought with you. Stand the same distance away and see if your companion sees you.
pages.brief: A child walks to school and a store in neutral-colored clothing, noticing how few people pay attention. Later the same child wears bright red and gets more attention. In a wooded area, a family member tries to spot the child from 20 paces in green or brown, then in a bright T-shirt.

pages.brief: A nature scene brings together examples of camouflage: an animal blending into its background, dark blotches, a disguised insect, disruptive patterns, moth eyespots, a flash of bright color, parent and offspring, a predator with prey, and warning colors.

books.title: Galapagos Wonder
books.art_why: The book shows real Galapagos animals, plants, landscapes, and people in the world today, so photographs fit best.

pages.text: Introduction Imagine a place where thousands of black lizards stretch out on lava rocks to soak up the morning sun. Imagine a place where giant tortoises feed on cactus plants that grow as big as trees. Imagine an island on the equator where penguins swim and fur seals rest on coral beaches. Welcome to the Galapagos Islands. These islands have fascinated people since the first visitors arrived in 1535. The unusual landscapes and wildlife spark our imaginations. Formed from fire, these islands remind us of the raw power of our planet. And they remind us of rapidly disappearing, unspoiled places where nature remains mostly untouched by development and technology.
pages.brief: Imagine thousands of black lizards stretched on lava rocks soaking up morning sun, giant tortoises feeding on cactus plants as big as trees, and penguins swimming while fur seals rest on coral beaches. The Galapagos Islands rise from volcanic fire, an equatorial place of unusual landscapes and wildlife that sparks imagination.

pages.text: Location The Galapagos Islands are located in the Pacific Ocean and are part of the country of Ecuador. They lie along the equator, about 966 kilometers (600 mi) off the coast of South America. There are five major islands and many smaller ones of various sizes. The climate of the islands is surprisingly cool for their location on the equator. This is due to a current of cold water that flows north from Antarctica. The cold water explains why animals usually found in colder climates, such as penguins and sea lions, can live in the Galapagos.
pages.brief: The Galapagos Islands lie in the Pacific Ocean along the equator, about 966 kilometers off South America. Five major islands and many smaller ones sit in the water. A cold current flows north from Antarctica, explaining why penguins and sea lions can live in this equatorial place.

pages.text: Geology The Galapagos Islands were created by volcanic activity. They continue to be among the most active volcanic islands in the world. Scientists believe that the islands are located over a “hot spot” beneath the earth’s crust. Hot spots contain more heat than other areas. The heat melts rock, which rises up through the crust as lava. The lava flows onto the sea floor where it turns into solid rock. Over time, the rock piles up above the surface of the water and forms an island.
pages.brief: Beneath the ocean floor, a hot spot heats and melts rock. The melted rock rises through the earth’s crust as lava, flows onto the sea floor, and hardens into solid rock. Over time the rock piles up above the water’s surface and forms a volcanic island.

pages.text: First Contact The Galapagos Islands were first discovered in 1535. A ship carrying the bishop of Panama to Peru was blown off course. The bishop recorded his observations of the islands in a letter to the king of Spain. At that time, there were no humans living on the islands. During the 1700s and 1800s, the Galapagos became a refuge for pirates and whalers because of its remote location. Giant tortoises were a favorite food source. These gentle creatures were easy to capture and keep. Their numbers went from several hundred thousand to only about 15,000 by the year 1800.
pages.brief: A ship carrying the bishop of Panama to Peru is blown off course to the Galapagos in 1535; the bishop observes the islands. Later, pirates and whalers anchor near the remote shores, and giant tortoises are captured and kept as a food source, their numbers falling sharply by 1800.

pages.text: Darwin’s Visit The most famous visitor to the Galapagos Islands was Charles Darwin. The British naturalist sailed there in 1835 and collected many wildlife specimens. He also wrote detailed accounts of his observations. Darwin was amazed by the amazing diversity, or variety, of life on the islands. He noticed that similar species, or kinds, of animals developed different traits on different islands. Because of his work, we now understand much more about variety in nature.
pages.brief: Charles Darwin, a British naturalist, sails to the Galapagos in 1835. He collects wildlife specimens and writes detailed accounts of his observations. On the islands he studies the amazing diversity of life and notices similar species with different traits on different islands.

pages.text: Wildlife Scientists and tourists alike have been amazed by the diversity of native animal and plant life on the Galapagos Islands. New species are often discovered there. A 1996 expedition took scientists deep under water to study the ocean around the islands. Many new species were discovered. These included jellyfish, deep-sea moray eels, sea cucumbers, and a deepwater red octopus. The scientists discovered a new species of marine life on almost every day of their expedition.
pages.brief: Scientists and tourists marvel at the native animals and plants of the Galapagos. On a 1996 expedition, scientists go deep underwater around the islands and discover new species, including jellyfish, deep-sea moray eels, sea cucumbers, and a deepwater red octopus, finding new marine life almost every day.

pages.text: Reptiles Some of the most famous animals in the Galapagos are its reptiles. The islands were named for one of the most well-known reptiles, the giant tortoise. These herbivorous (ur-BIV-or-us) animals can live 150 years or more. Males can grow to 1.8 meters (6 ft) long and can weigh up to 300 kilograms (660 lbs). Fourteen different kinds of Galapagos tortoises used to exist. Several kinds have become extinct, and the others are now protected. Galapagos tortoises are divided into two groups. The difference is the shape of their shell, or carapace. One group has a round, dome-shaped shell, a short neck, and short legs. The other group has a saddle-shaped shell that is raised in front, a long neck, and long legs.
pages.brief: Giant tortoises, the reptiles for which the islands are named, feed on plants. Some have round, dome-shaped shells with short necks and legs; others have saddle-shaped shells raised in front with long necks and legs. These herbivores can live over 150 years, and males can grow very large.

pages.text: Marine iguanas are another well-known Galapagos reptile. Some people think they look like small dragons because of their leathery skin, curved claws, and back spines. These tropical lizards can grow to a length of 1 meter (3.3 ft). They are the only lizards in the world that spend time in the sea. Their main food source is red and green algae. They can stay under water feeding on it for up to an hour.
pages.brief: Marine iguanas with leathery skin, curved claws, and back spines look like small dragons. These tropical lizards grow up to 1 meter long and are the only lizards that spend time in the sea. They feed underwater on red and green algae for up to an hour.

pages.text: Do You Know? Marine iguanas have special glands connected to their nostrils. The glands help them get rid of extra salt that comes from drinking seawater. It may seem as though these animals sneeze a lot, but they’re just getting rid of salt. Marine iguanas have dark skin that helps them absorb the sun’s heat after being in the cold ocean water. Marine iguanas also change their position to control body temperature. They often sun themselves on lava rocks as the Sun rises in the morning. When the heat becomes too strong, they raise up on their legs. This protects their underside from the hot rocks and allows air to move around them. After a day in the cold ocean water, they pile up together at night to save body heat.
pages.brief: Marine iguanas sneeze out extra salt from glands connected to their nostrils. Their dark skin absorbs the sun’s heat after cold ocean water. They sun themselves on lava rocks in the morning, raise up on their legs when rocks get too hot, and pile together at night to save body heat.

pages.text: Mammals Many Galapagos mammals are animals normally found far from the equator. Galapagos sea lions are the marine gymnasts of the islands. Their playful tricks amuse tourists, who sometimes receive friendly nips from these animals. Sea lions live in large colonies. Female sea lions, known as cows, gather on beaches to nap. Adult males, or bulls, are territorial and very aggressive during the mating season. Galapagos fur seals are rarer than sea lions. Fur seals were hunted nearly to extinction because their thick fur was valuable. Unlike sea lions, fur seals live in smaller groups and prefer steep, rocky shores. They fear humans and are difficult to approach. Sea lion Fur seal.
pages.brief: Galapagos sea lions, playful marine gymnasts, amuse tourists and live in large colonies; females nap on beaches while territorial males guard them during mating season. Rare Galapagos fur seals, once hunted for thick fur, gather in smaller groups on steep, rocky shores and are shy, difficult to approach.

pages.text: Birds Many of the most interesting animals on the islands are birds. Frigate birds are among the most striking birds in the world. They can measure up to 1 meter (3.3 ft) tall and have a wingspan up to 2.1 meters (7 ft). During the mating season, hundreds of males gather to attract the attention of females. Each male blows up his bright red throat sac like a balloon. He stretches out his wings and shakes them while making repeated sharp cries. Do You Know? A male frigate bird can blow up its throat sac to the size of a soccer ball.
pages.brief: Frigate birds stand up to 1 meter tall with wingspans up to 2.1 meters. During mating season, hundreds of males gather to attract females. Each male blows up his bright red throat sac like a balloon, stretches and shakes his wings, and makes repeated sharp cries; the sac can grow to soccer-ball size.

pages.text: Galapagos penguins are among the most surprising native animals on the islands. We usually think of penguins as living close to Antarctica. Galapagos penguins are the most northern penguin. They weigh only 2 to 2.5 kg (4.5–5.5 lb) and stand 40 to 45 cm (16–18 in) tall. One of their big challenges is to stay cool in the tropical heat. They do this by holding out their wings so that air moves around the sides of their bodies. They also keep their feet in the shade or take a dip in the cool ocean water. Galapagos penguins swim underwater at high speeds. They use their wings as propellers and their feet as rudders. They feed on small fish that they catch by hunting in groups. They live in colonies and mate for life.
pages.brief: Galapagos penguins, the most northern penguins, stand 40 to 45 centimeters tall and weigh only 2 to 2.5 kilograms. In tropical heat they hold out their wings to let air move around them, keep their feet shaded, or dip in cool ocean water. They swim fast, hunt small fish in groups, and mate for life.

pages.text: Plant Life The plant life on the Galapagos Islands is just as remarkable as the animal life. There are about 560 kinds of native plants. Almost one-third of them are found nowhere else on Earth. The scalesia (ska-LEE-zee-yuh) tree is a unique Galapagos plant. It is a member of the daisy family and can grow to a height of 24 meters (78 ft). It grows in humid areas at higher elevations. It’s often covered with tropical flowers called orchids.
pages.brief: The Galapagos have about 560 kinds of native plants, and almost one-third grow nowhere else on Earth. The unique scalesia tree belongs to the daisy family, can grow 24 meters tall in humid areas at higher elevations, and is often covered with tropical flowers called orchids.

pages.text: The prickly pear cactus grows low to the ground on many of the islands. On the island of Santa Fe it grows into trees! The pads, flowers, and fruit of this cactus are a favorite food of land iguanas. They often roll the cactus pads on the ground to remove the spines before eating them. These creatures often sit under a tree waiting for a pad to drop to the ground.
pages.brief: The prickly pear cactus grows low to the ground on many Galapagos islands, but on Santa Fe it grows into trees. Land iguanas eat its pads, flowers, and fruit; they roll cactus pads on the ground to remove spines, and often sit under a tree waiting for a pad to drop.

pages.text: Threats to Survival Almost all of the island chains in the world have lost many of their native plants and animals. The Galapagos Islands have lost few native life forms so far, though serious threats exist. The most serious problems come from non- native species introduced by humans. Cats, dogs, pigs, goats, horses, donkeys, cattle, and rats have all been brought to the islands. Many of them have become feral, or wild, and have multiplied very quickly. Feral animals eat tortoise eggs, baby tortoises, and other native animals. They also eat plants that native animals would otherwise eat. The islands have many programs to destroy the non-native animals and restore the native ecology. And scientists are raising tortoises in captivity to try to boost their numbers and increase their survival rates.
pages.brief: Non-native animals brought by humans—cats, dogs, pigs, goats, horses, donkeys, cattle, and rats—have become feral on the Galapagos and multiplied quickly. They eat tortoise eggs, baby tortoises, other native animals, and native plants. Island programs work to remove non-native animals and restore native ecology, while scientists raise tortoises in captivity to boost their numbers.

pages.text: Another serious problem is the increasing number of people on the islands, both residents and visitors. In 1940, only 600 people lived on the islands. But in 1949, many people moved to the islands after a major earthquake in Ecuador. Tourism in the Galapagos Islands skyrocketed in the 1980s, bringing more residents and many more visitors. By 1997, the population on the islands had grown to about 15,000. With more people come many risks. New harmful species are more likely to be brought to the islands. More resources are being used for building materials and firewood. More animals are being hunted, both on land and in the ocean. Pollution from tourist and supply boats is increasing. In 2001, an oil tanker got stuck in shallow water off one of the islands, causing a huge oil spill. Experts from around the world worked with the government of Ecuador, local scientists, and others in a huge cleanup effort. The oil tanker Jessica.
pages.brief: More residents and visitors bring risks to the Galapagos: new harmful species, more use of resources for building and firewood, more hunting on land and in the ocean, and pollution from tourist and supply boats. In 2001, the oil tanker Jessica gets stuck in shallow water and causes a huge oil spill; experts join Ecuadorian scientists in a cleanup effort.

pages.text: To help preserve the Galapagos Islands, the government of Ecuador made 95 percent of the land a national park in 1959. In 1986, a law was passed to protect 69,930 square kilometers (27,000 sq mi) of the ocean around the islands. Strict laws now limit tourism on the islands. Visitors must travel with a guide who is trained to keep conservation in mind at all times. Visitors are not allowed to bring food or drink because it might introduce non-native plant seeds, insects, or bacteria to the islands. The laws also protect animals and plants from human interference, such as touching, feeding, or littering. Boat tours are carefully controlled to help protect the wildlife.
pages.brief: Ecuador made 95 percent of the Galapagos land a national park in 1959 and later protected a vast area of ocean around the islands. Strict laws limit tourism: visitors travel with trained guides, cannot bring food or drink that might introduce non-native seeds or insects, and must not touch, feed, or litter around wildlife. Boat tours are carefully controlled.

pages.text: The Charles Darwin Foundation was created in 1959. It helps the government of Ecuador make smart decisions about conservation on the islands. This foundation runs the Charles Darwin Research Station on Santa Cruz Island so that scientists and the public can continue to learn about these amazing islands. Many educational programs, both on the islands and around the world, help teach the public about Galapagos conservation efforts.
pages.brief: The Charles Darwin Foundation, created in 1959, helps the government of Ecuador make conservation decisions. It runs the Charles Darwin Research Station on Santa Cruz Island, where scientists and the public learn about the islands. Educational programs on the islands and around the world teach people about Galapagos conservation efforts.

pages.text: Conclusion Today, many animal and plant species around the world are facing extinction. The Galapagos Islands are one of the last places on Earth with so many rare life forms in such a small area. Many are found nowhere else on Earth. Scientists and other people who value nature are working to keep the Galapagos Islands safe for future generations. These islands are a natural treasure that must be preserved and protected.
pages.brief: Many animal and plant species around the world face extinction, but the Galapagos Islands remain one of the last places with so many rare life forms in a small area, many found nowhere else. Scientists and people who value nature work to keep the islands safe for future generations, preserving and protecting this natural treasure.

pages.text: Explore More At the Library Ask your librarian to help you find books on the Galapagos Islands. You can find books of Galapagos photographs, history, and modern science. You can also look for books on individual plants and animals from the Galapagos. You may even find travel books in which people describe their trips to the islands, some of them written long ago. On the Internet A. In the address window, type www.google.com. B. Type Galapagos in the search window and click on “Google Search.” C. Read the colored links. Click on one that looks interesting. When you want to explore other links, click on the “Back” button at the top left to return to the Google search page. D. Try other searches, such as Charles Darwin, Galapagos tortoise, or frigate bird.
pages.brief: In a library, a librarian helps a child find books about Galapagos photographs, history, modern science, individual plants and animals, and travel stories. Nearby, a child uses a computer to explore Galapagos topics, links, and other searches such as Charles Darwin, Galapagos tortoise, or frigate bird.

books.title: Speed
books.art_why: Real animals, vehicles and machines can be photographed, and this is not a biography of a named person.

pages.text: Introduction What is speed? Speed is the time it takes to go a certain distance. For most things, speed is measured in kilometers or miles per hour. For example, a speed of 16 kilometers (10 mi) per hour means that something is moving fast enough to travel 16 kilometers in one hour. This speed is recorded as 16 kph (10 mph). Speed can also be measured in other units of time and distance. It can be measured in meters per second or meters per minute. It can be measured in centimeters or inches per second, minute, or hour.
pages.brief: A long straight route stretches across open ground with distance markers spaced along it, while a clock face shows one hour passing; a small object travels past several markers to show how speed measures distance over time.

pages.text: Faster objects are usually measured in larger units of distance and shorter units of time. Slower things, on the other hand, are usually measured in smaller units of distance and larger units of time. For example, a snail’s speed might be measured in centimeters per hour. The movement of a glacier might be measured in meters per month. Light— the fastest thing in the universe—moves at 299,338 kilometers per second (186,000 mps). The marlin (pictured here) and sailfish are among the fastest fish in the world.
pages.brief: A snail creeps slowly across a leaf, a glacier inches forward over land, and in the sea a marlin and a sailfish dart through the water; far above, a beam of light flashes across the sky.

pages.text: People have always seemed to be fascinated by speed. We seem to love things that move fast. It doesn’t matter if it is a cheetah chasing a gazelle, a horse galloping around a track, or human runners dashing toward a finish line. We simply think that fast things are cool. Perhaps that is why some of the most popular Olympic events, from the first games on, have been contests involving speed. Footrace in early Greek Olympic games.
pages.brief: In an ancient Greek stadium, runners in an early Olympic footrace sprint toward a finish line; a cheetah chases a gazelle, a horse gallops around a track, and human runners dash forward, all showing how people love fast movement.

pages.text: Who Is Fastest? When we watch a track meet or other sporting event, we cheer for the fastest runners. But compared with other living things, humans are not all that fast. In fact, the fastest humans run at speeds of only about 35.4 kilometers per hour (22 mph).
pages.brief: At a track meet, human runners sprint along a running track while spectators cheer for the fastest runners; compared with other living things, humans are not very fast, reaching only about 35.4 kilometers per hour.

pages.text: Speed is important for the survival of most living things. The cheetah, which runs at speeds of up to 113 kilometers per hour (70 mph), is the fastest living thing on land. The cheetah depends on its speed to capture food. For many animals, survival often depends on being faster than the animal that is chasing you.
pages.brief: A cheetah runs at full stretch across open grassland, its body low and long as it chases food; its great speed helps it survive, while other animals survive by being faster than the animal chasing them.

pages.text: Fish swim much faster than humans due to their more streamlined bodies. The fastest fish is the sailfish. It zips through the water at speeds of up to 113 kilometers per hour (70 mph). The fastest living thing moves through the air. It is the peregrine falcon. This falcon reaches speeds of 435 kilometers per hour (270 mph) as it dives to capture other birds in flight. Even sailfish and cheetahs are slow compared to the falcon. But humans are not limited by our bodies in order to move from place to place. We use our brains to come up with ways to travel faster. Let’s look at some of these ways. A lithograph of Maud S, the fastest trotter in the world, in 1874.
pages.brief: A sailfish zips through the water with its long bill forward, a peregrine falcon dives after another bird in flight, and a trotting horse named Maud S runs on a track, showing three of the fastest living things.

pages.text: A man riding the “Accelerator,” an early bicycle (1819). It could travel uphill at the same speed as a man walking. Downhill it could travel as fast as a galloping horse. Bicycles Humans are the only animals that build mechanical things. We keep inventing new ways to go faster and faster. Long ago we found that by building and riding bicycles, we could go faster than riding a walking or trotting horse. A bicycle didn’t take up as much space as a horse. We didn’t need to feed and water it, and we didn’t have messes to clean up.
pages.brief: A man rides an early two-wheeled bicycle along a road; uphill he moves at the same speed as a man walking, while downhill he travels as fast as a galloping horse. The bicycle is called the Accelerator.

pages.text: When we ride a bicycle, the air in front of us seems to push back. This is called air resistance. As we ride faster, the air seems to push back harder. In 1899, a bicycle racer named Charles Murphy had the idea of reducing air resistance by riding his bicycle behind a train. By riding behind a train, Murphy was able to go 98.5 kilometers per hour (60 mph). Since then bicyclists have tried riding behind race cars to go even faster. Some have reached speeds of more than 241 kilometers per hour (150 mph)!
pages.brief: A bicycle racer crouches low on his bicycle and rides close behind a moving train, using the train to reduce air resistance; the air pushes back hard as he speeds along the track. He is trying to go faster.

pages.text: Boats When humans first started using boats, speed was governed by how fast the river flowed, how quickly and hard we paddled, and how hard the wind blew. By using sails, we were able to go faster than paddling. Because of drag (pull) of the water on the boat, sailors were limited in their speed. As boat designs improved, sailors were able to go faster, but never faster than the speed of the wind and the current.
pages.brief: People paddle a small boat on a river; later a sailboat moves with the wind, its sail full; water drags against the boat’s hull, limiting how fast sailors can go on rivers and seas. The current also pushes the boat.

pages.text: The invention of the steam engine brought about huge changes in travel. When the steam engine began to be used to power ships, people could go even faster. They were able to go faster than the wind and water. They could travel into the wind and against the current of the water. The SS United States, powered by a steam engine, was the fastest ocean liner ever. It crossed the Atlantic Ocean at an average speed of 35 knots (65 kph, or 41 mph). Its top speed was 44 knots (80.5 kph, or 50 mph).
pages.brief: A large steam-powered ocean liner, the SS United States, moves across the Atlantic Ocean, cutting through waves under its own power; steam engines let it travel faster than the wind and the current. It crosses the ocean at an average speed of 35 knots.

pages.text: The drag of the water on the bottom of the boat slows it down. Modern racing boats are designed to barely touch the water as they skim over the surface. This is called hydroplaning. A hydroplane boat can go as fast as 354 kilometers per hour (220 mph). The fastest boat in the world is a jet- powered hydroplane. It has gone 510.2 kilometers per hour (317 mph). A hydroplane on the St. Clair River.
pages.brief: A hydroplane races over the St. Clair River, barely touching the water as it skims the surface; spray flies behind it, and the boat moves far faster than ordinary boats slowed by water drag. It is jet-powered.

pages.text: An early steam locomotive Trains The steam engine was first used to power boats and tractors. When the train was invented, the steam engine was used to power it, too. These trains carried people and products faster than boats or wagons could. Early trains reached speeds of up to 65 kilometers per hour (40 mph). Some passengers, used to much slower horse-drawn carriages, fainted when traveling at these speeds.
pages.brief: An early steam locomotive pulls train cars along tracks, carrying people and products; inside, a passenger looks alarmed by the speed, while another passenger faints after riding faster than a horse-drawn carriage. It reaches up to 65 kilometers per hour.

pages.text: For years, train speed was limited by the train’s wheels rolling over steel rails. This problem was solved when magnetic trains were invented. At high speeds, magnetic trains don’t even touch the tracks. Modern trains, called bullet trains, with new powerful engines, now travel at speeds of nearly 320 kilometers per hour (200 mph). There are plans for even faster trains. These trains will travel through tubes at over 800 kilometers per hour (500 mph). A high-speed train in Japan.
pages.brief: A sleek high-speed bullet train speeds along tracks in Japan; nearby, a magnetic train glides above its track without touching it, and a planned train shoots through a long tube at even greater speed. Bullet trains travel nearly 320 kilometers per hour.

pages.text: Automobiles When automobiles were first invented, they were very slow and fragile. The first car was not much more than a small horse buggy rolling on bicycle wheels, with a small, noisy engine powering it. It was kind of like a golf cart with a lawn mower engine. Can you imagine a golf cart as your family car?
pages.brief: An early automobile looks like a small horse buggy on bicycle wheels, with a noisy little engine; beside it, a golf cart with a lawn mower engine shows how simple and slow the first cars were.

pages.text: Some early cars also had steam or electric power. The first recognized land-speed record for an automobile was set in 1898. An automobile powered by an electric motor went 63.13 kilometers per hour (39.24 mph). Imagine going down a bumpy dirt road in a golf cart at almost 64.4 kilometers per hour (40 mph). The driver must have had quite a thrilling ride!
pages.brief: An early electric automobile speeds down a bumpy dirt road, its driver holding on tightly as it sets the first recognized land-speed record for a car, going almost 64.4 kilometers per hour. The ride must be thrilling.

pages.text: Sir Malcolm Campbell in one of his Bluebird cars trying to set a new world land speed record on Daytona Beach, Florida, 1934 As engineers, designers, and builders improved cars, the cars went faster and faster. In the early 1900s, there were no paved roads to drive fast on. People found that they could drive on the hard- packed sand on ocean beaches at low tide. For many years, the fastest speed records were set on beaches. People discovered that they also could drive fast on dry lake beds in the desert. Places like the Bonneville Salt Flats in Utah and the Black Rock Desert in Nevada are flat, open areas extending for miles. Vehicles are safely driven at high speeds over these dry lake beds.
pages.brief: Sir Malcolm Campbell drives his Bluebird car across hard-packed sand on Daytona Beach at low tide, trying for a land-speed record; beyond the beach, flat dry lake beds stretch open for miles. The sand is firm enough for fast driving.

pages.text: The land speed record for wheeled vehicles is held by a jet car that is powered by two jet fighter engines. In October of 1997, Andy Green became the first human to go faster than the speed of sound in a land vehicle. He went 1,228 kilometers per hour (763.035 mph) in a jet car called the Thrust SSC. It went from a complete stop to 965.6 kph (600 mph) in 16 seconds. Andy Green driving his Thrust SSC at 1,228 kph (763 mph)
pages.brief: Andy Green drives the jet-powered Thrust SSC across a flat desert, two jet fighter engines blasting behind him; the car races faster than the speed of sound, reaching 1,228 kilometers per hour. It went from a stop to 965.6 kph in 16 seconds.

pages.text: Aircraft Humans have always wanted to fly like birds. Over the centuries, inventors have tried many different ways to fly. The first airplanes used engines that drove propellers. About 40 years later, the jet engine was invented, and the speed of aircraft really increased. The speed record now for aircraft is 3,367 kilometers per hour (2,193 mph). Can you imagine flying all the way across the United States in one hour and 15 minutes? An average jet airliner now takes about five and a half hours to make the trip.
pages.brief: An early propeller airplane flies through the sky; a modern jet aircraft streaks past, faster than the propeller plane; the jet record is 3,367 kilometers per hour, crossing the United States in about an hour and fifteen minutes.

pages.text: If you want to move really fast, become an astronaut. In order to escape the gravitational pull of the earth, rockets must go over 45,062 kilometers per hour (28,000 mph).
pages.brief: A rocket blasts off from Earth, flames roaring beneath it as it climbs fast enough to escape the planet’s gravitational pull; an astronaut rides inside, traveling over 45,062 kilometers per hour to reach space. It is the fastest way for people to travel.

pages.text: Conclusion It is unlikely that, in the future, cheetahs will run faster or sailfish will swim faster. Nor is it likely that falcons will fly faster. Even humans are not likely to run much faster than they do now. But that won’t stop humans from finding other ways to go faster.
pages.brief: A cheetah runs, a sailfish swims, a falcon flies, and a human sprints, each moving as fast as it can; the scene suggests that these natural speeds are near their limits, so people will look for other ways to go faster.

pages.text: At one time, humans wanted to travel at the speed of sound. Eventually, we found ways to make planes that traveled faster than sound. Today, rockets blasting off for space travel several times greater than the speed of sound. No doubt, humans will continue to find ways to go faster over land and water and through the air. Humans probably will not be satisfied until we are traveling at the speed of light. At that speed, we could circle the globe more than seven times in a single second. It is hard to imagine moving at such an incredibly fast speed.
pages.brief: A rocket blasts into space and a supersonic plane streaks through the sky above Earth; a beam of light circles the globe more than seven times in a single second, showing the incredible speed humans may one day seek.

books.title: Roadside Oddities
books.art_why: Real roadside attractions, buildings, and monuments exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: Billboards for The Thing make some travelers curious. What Is The Thing? Driving between Texas and Arizona, you can’t miss the signs for The Thing. Giant billboards at the side of the road ask, “The Thing? What is it?” Others say, “You’ll never forget it” and “It’s a wonder!” They call it the “Mystery of the Desert.” Whatever else it is, The Thing is one of thousands of roadside attractions around the world. Roadside attractions are weird and wonderful. Designed to capture attention, they invite people to stop and check them out.
pages.brief: Giant roadside billboards stand beside a desert highway between Texas and Arizona. A few travelers slow their car and look up at the billboards, curious. The billboards tower over the dry landscape, inviting people to stop and check out the strange attraction called The Thing.

pages.text: World’s Largest Baseball Bat The world’s largest baseball bat towers over a five-story building in Louisville, Kentucky. You couldn’t use this bat in a baseball game—it’s 120 feet (37 m) tall and weighs more than 68,000 pounds (30,844 kg). It’s a huge replica of the bat used by the famous baseball player Babe Ruth. Another attraction at the museum is the Big Glove, a sculpture weighing more than 17 tons (15 mt). After you see these oddities, you can go on a tour of the Louisville Slugger Museum and Factory to learn how the regular- sized bats are made. Do giants play baseball?
pages.brief: A towering baseball bat stands beside a five-story building in Louisville, Kentucky, dwarfing everything around it. Nearby, a giant sculpted baseball glove rests on display. The bat and glove are huge replicas, and visitors can tour the Louisville Slugger Museum and Factory to learn how regular-sized bats are made.

pages.text: Ears of corn make a mural that’s good enough to eat. The Corn Palace At the Corn Palace in Mitchell, South Dakota, they create art out of various colors of corn. Every year, the outside of the building is decorated with art made out of local grains and grasses. Each year has a different theme that is reflected in the murals. The Corn Palace is also the world’s largest bird feeder. When winter begins, the birds and squirrels eat the murals!
pages.brief: The Corn Palace in Mitchell, South Dakota, shows a large building covered with colorful murals made from different colors of corn, local grains, and grasses. The outdoor artwork changes with a yearly theme. In winter, birds and squirrels gather at the building to eat the murals, making it the world's largest bird feeder.

pages.text: Barney Smith poses with some of his unusual creations. Barney Smith’s Toilet Seat Art Museum Do you have a spare toilet seat lying around the house? If so, you can bring it to Barney Smith’s Toilet Seat Art Museum, which opened in 1992 in San Antonio, Texas. (It has since moved to just north of Dallas.) Barney Smith turned toilet seats into something wonderful. Born in 1921, he made more than 1,400 toilet seat works of art that tell stories about his life.
pages.brief: Barney Smith, an older man born in 1921, poses with some of his unusual creations, which are decorated toilet seats. Each seat tells a story about his life. The museum in San Antonio, Texas, opened in 1992 and later moved north of Dallas, displaying more than 1,400 works of toilet seat art.

pages.text: A big elephant needs a big drink of water. Lucy the Elephant In 1881, James V. Lafferty built the world’s largest elephant to attract people to the land he was selling. The six-story building in Margate City, New Jersey, is covered with 12,000 square feet (3,658 sq m) of metal. The building has been used in many ways over the years, including for school trips. Lucy the Elephant is one of America’s oldest roadside attractions. You can still climb inside her.
pages.brief: A six-story elephant-shaped building called Lucy the Elephant stands in Margate City, New Jersey. Its surface is covered with 12,000 square feet of metal. The huge elephant was built in 1881 to attract people to land being sold. Visitors can still climb inside one of America's oldest roadside attractions.

pages.text: Boll Weevil Monument You’ve probably heard of monuments for presidents, but have you ever seen one for a bug? The Boll Weevil Monument in Enterprise, Alabama, is one of the only statues in the world dedicated to a pest. In 1915, the bug destroyed the city’s cotton crops, forcing farmers to grow different types of plants, such as peanuts. In the end, growing crops other than cotton helped the people of Enterprise, so they decided to honor the weevil. The woman originally held a fountain above her head. The fountain was replaced with a boll weevil in 1949.
pages.brief: In Enterprise, Alabama, a monument honors a boll weevil, one of the only statues in the world dedicated to a pest. A woman figure stands holding a large boll weevil above her head. The monument remembers how the bug destroyed cotton crops in 1915 and pushed farmers to grow peanuts and other plants.

pages.text: Sign Post Forest was started by a homesick soldier. Sign Post Forest If you’re driving along the Alaska Highway, you’ll find a forest that isn’t made of trees. Sign Post Forest in Watson Lake, Canada, is made of more than 100,000 signs. It began in 1942 when Carl K. Lindley repaired a damaged signpost. He decided to add a new sign to the signpost with the distance to his hometown—Danville, Illinois. After Lindley hung his sign, others did the same, and the tradition continues today. People come from around the world to add their signs to this attraction.
pages.brief: In Watson Lake, Canada, along the Alaska Highway, a forest of more than 100,000 signs covers posts and frames. It began in 1942 when homesick soldier Carl K. Lindley repaired a damaged signpost and added a sign showing the distance to his hometown, Danville, Illinois. Travelers from around the world still add their own signs.

pages.text: Carhenge Stonehenge Inset: Stonehenge is a mysterious ring of stones erected more than four thousand years ago. It stands 90 miles west of London, England. Carhenge In Alliance, Nebraska, you can visit a replica of England’s Stonehenge. It isn’t built with old stones but rather with thirty-nine old cars. Artist Jim Reinders and his relatives built Carhenge during a family reunion in 1987. Some cars were placed in deep pits, while those high above the ground were joined together. Some local folk originally wanted the site turned into a junkyard. Now more than eighty thousand people visit it each year.
pages.brief: In Alliance, Nebraska, thirty-nine old cars stand in a circle like England's Stonehenge. Artist Jim Reinders and his relatives built Carhenge during a 1987 family reunion, placing some cars in deep pits and joining others high above the ground. An inset view shows the ancient stone ring of Stonehenge, which stands 90 miles west of London.

pages.text: London Bridge Inset: In this 1890 photo, London Bridge still spanned the River Thames. London Bridge In what city can you find London Bridge? In Lake Havasu City, Arizona, of course. While a number of roadside attractions are replicas, this one is the real deal. The London Bridge was first built in 1831. Robert P. McCulloch bought it for $2,460,000 in 1968. He had to spend another $7 million to have the bridge taken down and rebuilt in Arizona. Before builders took it down, each brick was numbered so they would know exactly where to put it. Tourists can now stroll across the bridge.
pages.brief: London Bridge spans a waterway in Lake Havasu City, Arizona. The real bridge was first built in 1831, then bought by Robert P. McCulloch in 1968 and rebuilt in Arizona after each brick was numbered. An inset shows the bridge in an 1890 photo still spanning the River Thames in England. Tourists stroll across it.

pages.text: World’s Largest Basket When you’re going on a picnic, you often pack a picnic basket, but not one that’s seven stories tall! Employees at the Longaberger Basket Company in Newark, Ohio, used to work inside the world’s largest basket. The building is a replica of Longaberger’s Medium Market Basket. When it was first built, a local pilot flew his small plane through the handles!
pages.brief: In Newark, Ohio, a seven-story building shaped like a giant picnic basket stands outside. It is a replica of Longaberger's Medium Market Basket, and employees of the basket company used to work inside it. When the building was new, a local pilot flew a small plane through its handles.

pages.text: World’s Largest (You Name It) 1 World’s largest tire, Allen Park, Michigan 2 World’s largest chest of drawers, High Point, North Carolina 3 World’s largest violin, Cape Breton Island, Nova Scotia, Canada • World’s largest artichoke, Castroville, California • World’s largest ketchup bottle, Collinsville, Illinois • World’s largest cuckoo clock, Sugarcreek, Ohio • World’s largest ear of corn, Olivia, Minnesota • World’s largest rubber stamp, Cleveland, Ohio Do You Know? Not all roadside attractions are made by people. General Sherman Tree in Sequoia National Park is the world’s largest tree by volume. It is estimated to be between 2,300 and 2,700 years old.
pages.brief: A collection of giant roadside objects appears: a huge tire, an enormous chest of drawers, a towering violin, a giant artichoke, a ketchup bottle, a cuckoo clock, an ear of corn, and a rubber stamp. Nearby, the General Sherman Tree stands in Sequoia National Park, the world's largest tree by volume and estimated to be 2,300 to 2,700 years old.

pages.text: A Map to Amazement AK SD NE OH UNITED STATES KY AZ AL ATLANTIC OCEAN TX GULF OF MEXICO MEXICO 1 The Thing 2 World’s largest baseball bat 3 The Corn Palace 4 Barney Smith’s Toilet Seat Art Museum 5 Lucy the Elephant 6 Boll Weevil Monument 7 Sign Post Forest 8 Carhenge 9 London Bridge 0 World’s largest basket Stop and Look There are many different types of roadside attractions, from giant museums to a person’s garage. The one thing they have in common is that they all spark people’s interest and cause them to stop. Do you want to know what The Thing is, off Interstate 10 in Arizona? You’ll just have to pull off the road to find out!
pages.brief: A map of the United States shows many roadside attractions spread across the country, with the Atlantic Ocean and Gulf of Mexico visible at the edges. The locations suggest a journey from Texas and Arizona to Ohio and beyond. The page invites travelers to pull off the road and discover what The Thing is.

books.title: Wild Horses
books.art_why: Prehistoric and historical scenes need drawn reconstruction, matching the keyword check.

pages.text: How Many Wild Horses Are There Out West? Oregon 6,162 Wyoming 8,706 Nevada 46,974 Utah 5,316 Colorado 2,116 California 8,702 Arizona 558 New Mexico 200 PACIFIC OCEAN The Bureau of Land Management (BLM), a government agency, handles most wild horses in the West. The BLM also manages the wild lands that most of these horses live on. In 2020, an estimated 95,000 wild horses and burros (wild donkeys) roamed public lands. That is more than triple the amount that the lands can support. Introduction Long ago, huge herds of horses ran across the plains of the American West. There may have been millions —so many that early maps simply named the area “Wild Horses.” Thousands of horses still run free. They roam the West in herds, usually far from people. These wild horses are called mustangs.
pages.brief: A sweeping view of western public lands with many wild mustangs and burros grazing in separate herds, far from any town. A broad map-like landscape suggests several western states and the Pacific coast, while the horses roam open plains and dry country.

pages.text: Where Did Wild Horses Come From? Between two and four million years ago, wild horses roamed North America. At the time, a land bridge connected North America and Eurasia (which included what is now Asia and Europe). The traditional story of wild horses has been that they took the land bridge to Eurasia and eventually became extinct in North America during the last Ice Age. The Bering Land Bridge AMERICA NORTH EURASIA The Bering Land Bridge is also called Beringia.
pages.brief: An Ice Age scene two to four million years ago: wild horses roam North America near a wide land bridge connecting the continent to Eurasia. Some horses cross the bridge toward Asia and Europe, while others remain on the northern plain.

pages.text: Wild horses run across parts of Wyoming today much as they did long ago. Millions of years later, in the 1500s, Spanish colonizers brought horses back to North America. However, Native peoples have oral traditions that tell a different story about how horses never left North America. Scientists have uncovered some evidence to support these traditions. Examples include artwork showing horses made after the Ice Age and before the 1500s. Scientists are testing the DNA from wild horses alive today. They are comparing it to DNA from Ice Age horses and horses throughout history.
pages.brief: Modern wild horses run across Wyoming grassland. Nearby, a Native storyteller shares an oral tradition beside artwork of horses made after the Ice Age, while scientists collect DNA samples from a living wild horse to compare with Ice Age horses.

pages.text: If horses were living in North America all along, the Spanish brought even more with them. Some were left behind. Others ran off. Horses learned to live as wild animals across the American plains. Native peoples of the plains tamed some of them. Cowboys used horses to move cattle across the land. White settlers moving west into lands traditionally lived in by Native peoples used horses to help them build homes. Once again, many tamed horses ran off. Others were left behind when people no longer needed them. These horses also joined herds in the wild. This painting shows a member of the Osage Nation taming a wild horse.
pages.brief: On the American plains, a member of the Osage Nation tames a wild horse. Around them, Spanish horses run loose, cowboys drive cattle on horseback, and white settlers use horses while building homes in lands traditionally lived in by Native peoples.

pages.text: A wild stallion in Montana prepares to charge. Stallions often charge other stallions that intrude into their territory. Life of a Wild Horse Wild horses live in herds, or bands. An adult male horse, called a stallion, leads each herd. The stallion is the mate of several female horses, or mares, who stay with the herd.
pages.brief: A wild stallion in Montana lowers his head and prepares to charge another stallion that has intruded into his territory. Behind him, a band of mares stays together on the open range, with the stallion leading the herd.

pages.text: Young horses are called foals. When the foals are a few years old, they leave to join a new herd. By playing together, young male horses learn how to grow into stallions that can start their own herds. Young females leave their herds to become the mates of these new stallions.
pages.brief: Several foals play together in a wild herd. Young male horses chase and nuzzle one another, learning skills they will need to become stallions, while young females stand nearby before leaving to join a new herd and become mates.

pages.text: Wild horses mainly eat grass, but sometimes they also browse for leaves. One mare leads the herd to food, water, and shelter. The stallion follows behind to watch for danger. Each herd stays together to raise young horses and help the group. Wild Horses by the Sea Wild horses live on some islands off the East Coast of the United States. Two wild herds live on opposite ends of Assateague Island, located off the coast of Maryland and Virginia. Life by the ocean is hard. These horses eat tough marsh plants and know how to survive the stormy weather.
pages.brief: A mare leads her herd across grassland toward food, water, and shelter, while a stallion follows behind watching for danger. On Assateague Island off Maryland and Virginia, two wild herds at opposite ends graze on tough marsh plants near the stormy ocean.

pages.text: Protecting Wild Horses In the West, people once depended on tame horses. As more and more settlers built homes in the West, towns and cities grew. By the early 1900s, some people began to think of wild horses as pests. Wild horses were killed so cows and sheep would have more grass to eat or sold for meat. In 1971, a law was passed to protect wild horses from harm by humans. That law is the Wild Free-Roaming Horses and Burros Act. (Burros are wild donkeys.) Velma Johnston, who asked thousands of children to write letters to change the wild horse law, stands with a mustang in 1976.
pages.brief: Velma Johnston stands beside a mustang in 1976, after asking thousands of children to write letters that helped change the wild horse law. In the background, towns and farms spread across the western land where cattle and sheep graze.

pages.text: Since then, the number of free wild horses in the United States has grown twice as large. Now, thousands of wild horses roam free in ten western states. Wild horses are important to the cultures of many Native peoples in North America. Many sanctuaries, places where horses are kept safe and given land to roam, are run by Native people and others who want to protect these beautiful creatures. Night Hawk Flying works with a rescued wild mustang at Stoney Brook Farm in Connecticut in 2019.
