pages.text: The Spanish killed so many Taíno people that there was a shortage of workers. So, the Spanish began forcibly transporting enslaved people from Africa to Puerto Rico. Enslaved people were crowded into cargo holds to make the dangerous voyage. Many did not survive the journey. Those who did were completely cut off from their homes, families, and cultures, with no hope of escape or return. The Spanish also brought the disease of smallpox to the islands. Because of the living conditions forced upon the Taíno by the Spanish, smallpox spread rapidly. By 1519, nearly 90% of the Taíno had been killed by the disease. By 1600, the remaining Taíno people had fled to the mountains or married Spanish and African people. Many modern Puerto Ricans have a mix of Taíno, African, and European ancestry because of this history. Meanwhile, the promise of gold continued to draw Spanish settlers to the island. Puerto Rico soon became the busiest port in the Caribbean. Its location along major trade routes made it a valuable territory. The Spanish built many forts to protect the island and prevent other countries from invading it.
pages.brief: Enslaved African people are crowded into a cargo hold on a dangerous voyage to Puerto Rico. Smallpox spreads among the Taíno, killing nearly 90 percent by 1519. Survivors flee to the mountains or marry Spanish and African people. Spanish settlers continue arriving for gold, and Puerto Rico becomes the busiest port in the Caribbean, protected by forts.

pages.text: War and Industry Spain’s rule did not last, though. In 1898, the USS Maine, an American ship, sank near Cuba. Many people in the United States thought Spain had shot at the ship, causing it to sink. The United States declared war on Spain. By the end of the year, Spain had lost the Spanish-American War and all its foreign territories. The Treaty of Paris gave the United States sovereignty over Puerto Rico. Puerto Ricans were granted United States citizenship in 1917. They do not have all of the rights of citizens in the fifty states, however. Those living in Puerto Rico cannot vote in federal elections. They do not have a voting representative in Congress. Puerto Ricans have held votes to see how people feel about becoming a state. In 1998, 2012, and 2017, a majority were in favor of becoming the United States’ fifty-first state. Statehood Puerto Ricans have voiced their support for statehood, but the decision isn’t theirs alone. Puerto Rico’s own legislature must first give its consent and create a state constitution that meets federal approval. Then the United States Congress would need to pass a law admitting Puerto Rico as the nation’s fifty-first state. pro-statehood demonstrators.
pages.brief: The USS Maine sinks near Cuba, and the United States declares war on Spain. After Spain loses the Spanish-American War, the Treaty of Paris gives the United States sovereignty over Puerto Rico. Puerto Ricans receive U.S. citizenship in 1917 but cannot vote in federal elections or have a voting representative in Congress. Pro-statehood demonstrators gather.

pages.text: The Puerto Rican islands have been used extensively by the U.S. military. During World War II (1939–1945), nearly two-thirds of the main island was used as a U.S. naval base. For sixty years, the navy held exercises on Puerto Rico. Fire and bombing exercises were done on the island of Vieques, causing damage and pollution to the environment. Today, many of the areas once used for military drills are now wildlife refuges. There have been other changes as well. In the mid-twentieth century, the government began a program to bring industry to Puerto Rico. This program, Operation Bootstrap, helped the economy shift from a focus on farming to manufacturing and tourism. Life on the U.S. Mainland vs. Puerto Rico United States Mainland Island of Puerto Rico English is the most widely used language. Both Spanish and English are the most widely used languages. Gasoline is sold by the gallon. Gasoline is sold by the liter. Olympians compete under the United States flag. Olympians compete under the Puerto Rican flag. Adult citizens can vote in presidential elections. Adult citizens cannot vote in presidential elections. Many working adults pay federal income tax. Many working adults do not pay federal income tax.
pages.brief: During World War II, nearly two-thirds of Puerto Rico's main island serves as a U.S. naval base. For sixty years the navy holds fire and bombing exercises on Vieques, damaging the environment; later some areas become wildlife refuges. In the mid-twentieth century, Operation Bootstrap shifts the economy from farming toward manufacturing and tourism. A comparison shows mainland and island life.

pages.text: The Coqui Frog The tiny coqui (koh-KEE) frog is a cultural symbol of Puerto Rico. Images of the coqui can be found in Taíno carvings that date back centuries. The coqui inhabits the forests and is named for its high-pitched call. This little frog is so ingrained in Puerto Rican culture that when locals want to explain their heritage, they say, “Soy de aquí como el coqui!” (I’m from here, as is the coqui!) Life in Paradise Tourists help support the island’s economy in a big way. San Juan is a major port for cruise ships. The beauty and temperate climate of Puerto Rico draw millions of visitors from the mainland United States and beyond. Nature lovers go to explore El Yunque (JOONG-ke), the only tropical rainforest that is part of the U.S. National Forest System. Tourists also enjoy celebrating the culture of the island. From bomba y plena to salsa, music and dancing are everywhere. Tasty food that is part of cocina criolla (koh-SEE-nah kree-OH-yah) cooking mixes flavors from traditional African, Spanish, and Taíno dishes. Pasteles (pah-STE-less), made from green- banana dough that is stuffed with meat and wrapped in banana leaves, are a Christmas treat in Puerto Rico.
pages.brief: A tiny coqui frog sits in a Puerto Rican forest. Tourists visit San Juan's cruise port and explore El Yunque, the only tropical rainforest in the U.S. National Forest System. Music and dancing, from bomba y plena to salsa, fill the scene. Pasteles made from green-banana dough and meat wrapped in banana leaves are a Christmas treat.

pages.text: Castillo Serrallés The rich history and architecture of San Juan, the island’s capital, make it a popular destination for visitors. Parts of the city are enclosed by huge walls built by the Spanish for protection from invaders. The city of Ponce is known for its beautiful fountains. Ponce’s Castillo Serrallés (kahs- TEE-yoh se-rah-YES), a former Spanish castle, serves as a museum for the sugar cane and rum industries. These industries helped establish Puerto Rico as a major trading port. San Juan is home to the largest rum producers in the world. Outdoor activities such as surfing and boating are quite popular, but Puerto Ricans are also big fans of baseball. The first organized baseball game in Puerto Rico was played in January 1898—before the island became part of the United States! The sport’s popularity has produced standout players who have had successful careers in the American major leagues. Carlos Beltrán.
pages.brief: The Castillo Serrallés in Ponce, a former Spanish castle, serves as a museum for the sugar cane and rum industries. San Juan's capital area is enclosed by huge Spanish-built walls, and the city is home to the world's largest rum producers. Surfing and boating are popular, and Puerto Ricans play baseball; Carlos Beltrán stands out as a major-league player.

pages.text: Hurricane Maria was the worst natural disaster in Puerto Rico’s history. Paradise Lost? Puerto Rico’s tropical location places it in the path of not only warm trade winds but also tropical storms. The late summer and early fall months are storm season in the Caribbean. Over the years, Puerto Rico has been battered by the fierce winds and heavy rains of hurricanes. One of the worst storms was Hurricane Maria in 2017. It was the tenth-strongest Atlantic hurricane ever recorded. Maria was a Category 4 storm when it hit the island on September 20. Winds of 249 kilometers per hour (155 mph) tore buildings to shreds. Flooding decimated coastal villages. The hurricane killed at least 2,975 people and was the deadliest natural disaster to affect a U.S. territory in one hundred years.
pages.brief: Hurricane Maria, a Category 4 storm, hits Puerto Rico on September 20, 2017, with winds of 249 kilometers per hour (155 mph). The fierce winds tear buildings to shreds, and flooding decimates coastal villages. It is the tenth-strongest Atlantic hurricane ever recorded and the deadliest natural disaster to affect a U.S. territory in one hundred years, killing at least 2,975 people.

pages.text: Thousands of homes were damaged or destroyed. Airports and roadways were covered with debris and were heavily damaged. It took nearly a year for power to be restored for many residents on the island. Access to clean water was a problem for many. After Hurricane Maria, residents of Puerto Rico had to collect clean water at distribution points around the island. Some criticized the U.S response to the hurricane as slow and less comprehensive than its efforts to assist after other, less severe hurricanes that struck the mainland that year. On January 6, 2020, a 6.4 magnitude earthquake struck southern Puerto Rico. It was followed days later by many large aftershocks. These caused widespread damage and further complicated recovery efforts. In spite of these challenges, Puerto Ricans are busy rebuilding their homes and infrastructure. They are working together to solve problems in vibrant, creative ways. For example, some communities are switching to solar power without waiting for government assistance.
pages.brief: Thousands of homes are damaged or destroyed after Hurricane Maria. Airports and roadways are covered with debris, power takes a year to restore for many, and residents collect clean water at distribution points. On January 6, 2020, a 6.4 magnitude earthquake strikes southern Puerto Rico, followed by aftershocks. Puerto Ricans rebuild and communities switch to solar power without government help.

pages.text: Conclusion Puerto Ricans know how to deal with hardships. The island is a land rich in resources. The most valuable resource, though, is its people. In the face of multiple natural disasters, Puerto Ricans have not given up. The spirit and love they feel for their homeland has shined even brighter. Some Notable Puerto Ricans Pablo Casals (1876–1973) was a world- famous cellist. He was born in Spain but made Ceiba, Puerto Rico, his home in the late 1950s. He founded the Puerto Rico Symphony Orchestra and established a music conservatory. Isolina Ferré (1914–2000) was the daughter of a prominent politician. She became a Catholic nun and is known as the “Mother Teresa of Puerto Rico.” She established clinics and schools for people living in poverty. In 1999, she received the Presidential Medal of Freedom from President Bill Clinton for her work. Roberto Clemente (1934–1972) was a successful professional baseball player for the Pittsburgh Pirates. He spent the off-season doing charitable work in the Caribbean and Latin America. He died in a plane crash while delivering aid to earthquake victims in Nicaragua. Each year, Major League Baseball presents the Roberto Clemente Award to a player who, like Clemente, is personally involved in helping others. Isolina Ferré Pablo Casals Roberto Clemente.
pages.brief: Puerto Ricans face hardships but keep rebuilding, love for their homeland shining brighter. Three notable Puerto Ricans are shown: cellist Pablo Casals, who founded the Puerto Rico Symphony Orchestra; Isolina Ferré, a Catholic nun who established clinics and schools for people in poverty; and baseball player Roberto Clemente, who died in a plane crash while delivering aid to earthquake victims.

books.title: The Secrets of Skara Brae
books.art_why: A prehistoric Stone Age village: no photographs exist of Neolithic life, and this is not a biography of a famous person.

pages.text: The Secrets of Skara Brae.
pages.brief: Wide view of the ancient stone village of Skara Brae on Orkney: low stone houses sunk into a grassy mound, thick curved walls, a narrow stone passage running between them, open treeless ground and grey sea beyond. Wind moves the grass. No people are present.

pages.text: Introduction William Watt was walking the grounds of his Scottish estate in February 1850. A terrible storm had struck the Orkney Islands, which sit off the northeastern coast of Scotland. The people of Orkney were used to storms, but this one was especially rough. Shrieking winds and high tides had reshaped the land, ripping grass from the earth and piling sand in fields. As Watt surveyed the damage, something caught his eye. He noticed stone walls protruding from a mound where the grass had been peeled away. Watt knew that local legends told of ancient burial tombs hidden underground. Could those stories be true? Watt was curious. He hired a scholar named George Petrie to excavate and examine the site. Petrie’s work was the first step in revealing the secrets of the settlement known as Skara Brae. Ancient people built homes into the stone mounds at Skara Brae.
pages.brief: February 1850 on William Watt's Scottish estate: Watt, in a heavy coat, stands on storm-damaged ground where grass has been torn away and sand piled in ridges. He stares at stone walls jutting from a low mound. Grey sky, bent bare ground, the Orkney coast behind him.

pages.text: What’s in a Name? The site was originally called Skerrabra or Styerrabrae —the name of the mound under which the entire village was buried. The name “Skara Brae” is thought to be a variation. However, no one knows what the people who actually lived there called it. The Winds of Orkney Excavating the Skara Brae site was no easy task. This flat, treeless island offered little protection from strong sea breezes blowing in from the west. The winds eat away the shoreline and carry sand far inland. Petrie conducted his work in these blustery conditions. He gradually uncovered the remains of four ancient buildings. Each one had curved stone walls nearly 2.4 meters (8 ft.) thick. Petrie was astounded not only by the good condition of the structures but also by what was found inside them. Stone furniture and hearths suggested that the buildings were once homes. The sands that had hidden the ruins had also helped preserve them.
pages.brief: George Petrie kneels at the excavation on the flat, treeless Orkney island, wind pulling at his coat as he brushes sand from four ancient buildings with thick curved stone walls. Inside one, stone furniture and a hearth stand where the sand has been cleared away.

pages.text: The ruins at Skara Brae are thought to consist of stone houses, passages, and what may have been a workshop. Petrie spent over ten years carefully digging and writing about what he found at the site. He thought the stone houses were part of a settlement dating back to 500 bce. In 1868, he published a scholarly article about Skara Brae. After Petrie concluded his work, the Skara Brae site remained untouched for years. Then several unfortunate events occurred. Around 1913, thieves raided the site and stole valuable artifacts. In 1925, another terrible storm struck the area, and strong winds damaged some of the stone structures. The Watt estate transferred the guardianship of Skara Brae to authorities to protect it from the elements. The authorities decided to build a seawall to help protect the ruins from the bay’s winds and waves.
pages.brief: Raised view of the excavated ruins: several stone houses joined by narrow covered passages, with one larger building at the edge that may have been a workshop. Petrie's trenches and heaps of dug sand lie around them, and the windy bay curves behind.

pages.text: Built to Last The seawall construction renewed interest in Skara Brae. Through the twentieth century, Scottish authorities continued to excavate the site. They unearthed another four buildings, bringing the total to eight. The excavations revealed many interesting details about Skara Brae. It seemed the structures had been partially buried on purpose. The back of each house was built into a midden—a heap of shells, bones, broken pottery, and trash. Such construction may seem strange, but it made sense for the Orkney climate. Stone houses built into the ground were sheltered from the wind and rain. The homes’ doorways were all connected by stone-covered passages. This feature was also due to the environment. People could move between houses without being hit by the island’s constant winds. The village had a water drainage system and even primitive indoor toilets. Each home had a similar design. There were no windows, which helped protect people from the wind, rain, and cold. The claylike soil from the midden reached over the walls to form a roof. A low doorway opened into a single large room with a central hearth that gave off heat and light. Smoke exited through a hole in the roof.
pages.brief: Cutaway of a Skara Brae house: thick stone walls sunk into a midden of shells, bones and broken pottery, clay soil roofed over the top, a low doorway, no windows, and smoke curling from a hole in the roof. Covered passages link it to the neighbouring houses.

pages.text: On one wall were stone shelves that served as a storage unit. A stone seat was in front of an object that scientists think is a dresser. Although the significance of this object is unknown, it is thought to have been an important part of each household. On either side of the hearth were stone box beds. One building at the edge of the settlement had a larger hearth and no beds. Experts think it may have been a gathering place or shared workshop. Because trees cannot grow on the islands, nothing was made of wood. The builders of Skara Brae used the sturdiest materials available to them—sandstone and turf. dresser seat bed bed hearth The homes at Skara Brae were attached by passageways. Each house also had a door that could be locked with a bar made of bone.
pages.brief: Inside a Skara Brae house: one large room with a central stone hearth burning, smoke rising through the roof. Stone shelves line a wall, a stone seat faces a stone dresser, and box beds stand on either side of the fire. The low door has a bone bar.

pages.text: Life in an Ancient Village The sands of time not only preserved the stone structures but also kept the items inside them intact. The artifacts told much about how the people in the settlement lived. Clumps of native grass and other plants were used as cushions to make hard stone beds more comfortable. Tools, animal bones, and other artifacts showed that these people fished, raised sheep and pigs, and grew wheat and barley.
pages.brief: Neolithic villagers at work: clumps of grass heaped on a hard stone bed as a cushion, stone tools and animal bones on the floor, people fishing from the shore, sheep and pigs nearby, small plots of wheat and barley on the treeless, windswept island.

pages.text: Do You Know? The site at Skara Brae is so famous that it even attracted the interest of fictional scientists! Indiana Jones gave a lecture about Skara Brae in the 2008 movie The Kingdom of the Crystal Skull. The residents of Skara Brae were creative as well. Finely crafted pottery, buttons, and jewelry show that these people had an appreciation of beautiful things. Balls and dice discovered among the ruins suggest that they also enjoyed having fun and playing games. What the ruins did not include is equally interesting. No weapons were found at the site. The knives found there were used only as tools. Skara Brae seems to have been a peaceful agricultural community. There was also no indication of what eventually happened to the community. Nothing indicates that a struggle took place. The ruins also do not suggest that a natural disaster such as an earthquake sent people fleeing for their lives.
pages.brief: Objects made by the people of Skara Brae laid out on flat stone: finely crafted pottery, bone buttons, jewellery, a carved stone ball and dice. No weapons among them, only simple knives shaped as tools. Soft light across the stone surface.

pages.text: Experts have several theories explaining why residents may have abandoned the settlement. Some claim a terrible storm similar to the one in 1850 drove them away. Others guess that perhaps blowing sand accumulated on the land, making it harder to farm. Another theory suggests that the residents of Skara Brae may have simply moved away to more productive fields. For now, most scholars agree that they just don’t know why people left. Scotland’s Pompeii The ruins at Skara Brae are often called “Scotland’s Pompeii.” Although both Skara Brae and Pompeii are well- preserved ancient villages, there are big differences. Pompeii was devastated in 79 ce by the eruption of a volcano. Thousands of people and livestock were quickly buried by a carpet of thick ash. Skara Brae was buried by sand, but this process was gradual and not due to a single terrible event. That is why no intact skeletons have been found at Skara Brae. Pompeii Skara Brae.
pages.brief: Two scenes: a fierce storm with high waves and shrieking wind driving people away from the low stone houses; and drifting sand piling against empty doorways and covering the pathways, burying the village slowly so the fields grow harder to farm.

pages.text: Older Than Old Scientists in the mid-1900s were not certain why Skara Brae was deserted. They were, however, fairly sure they knew when it was first occupied. They thought that Skara Brae came into existence around 500 bce. By 1970, though, new technology had been developed that proved them wrong. Scientists had come up with an accurate way to figure out the age of certain materials, called carbon dating. By measuring the amount of carbon that is present in something, experts can determine just how old it is. Scientists did this with some of the plants and fibers buried at Skara Brae. They discovered that the settlement was much, much older than people had thought. Skara Brae, it turns out, was actually built around 3200 bce during the Neolithic period, or Stone Age. This meant the site was older than the Egyptian pyramids! Carbon dating also showed that the site had been inhabited for six hundred years. Carbon Carbon is an element common to all living things. Carbon-12 and carbon-13 are stable forms of this element. This means they do not change over time. Carbon-14, however, is not stable. It decays as time passes. Carbon-14 is measured in the carbon dating process. carbon.
pages.brief: Scientists in a laboratory measuring carbon from burnt plants and fibres taken from Skara Brae, instruments and glassware before them, comparing the result with the Stone Age village as it stood around 3200 bce, older than the Egyptian pyramids.

pages.text: Skara Brae was a prehistoric Stone Age village. Its perfect condition gave experts a better understanding of how Neolithic people lived. During the Neolithic period, people began growing crops and caring for animals. The well-preserved site was one of the first human farming settlements in Britain. It had a strong, self-sustaining culture. Neolithic Scotland Skara Brae is just one of several Neolithic sites in Orkney. The islands have many prehistoric structures. A large, multichambered tomb called Maeshowe rises on West Mainland. The Standing Stones of Stenness form a ring a short distance away. Two large slabs seem to act as a window through which Maeshowe can be seen. Maeshowe The Standing Stones of Stenness.
pages.brief: Neolithic farmers in Orkney tending wheat, barley, sheep and pigs beside low stone houses. On West Mainland nearby, the great chambered tomb of Maeshowe rises, and the ring of the Standing Stones of Stenness stands a short distance away, two tall slabs framing Maeshowe.

pages.text: Skara Brae Today The Neolithic village of Skara Brae was an important historical find. In 1999, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) classified it as a World Heritage Site. This means that Skara Brae was officially recognized as an important historical site. It is legally protected by international treaty. Because of its importance, thousands of visitors travel to Scotland’s Orkney Islands each year. Guided tours allow them to visit the homes of people who lived fifty centuries ago. Historians continue to study the site and share what they learn about this ancient village. Perhaps one day they will discover why the people of Skara Brae abandoned their settlement by the sea. Skara Brae has attracted thousands of visitors who hope to explore a prehistoric village up close.
pages.brief: Modern visitors on a guided tour walk the stone passages of Skara Brae, coats pulled against the wind, looking down into the open house interiors while a guide gestures toward a hearth. Green turf, grey sea and wide Orkney sky surround the protected village.

pages.text: Skara Brae Through the Ages 3200 bce Neolithic village of Skara Brae built Skara Brae abandoned 2600 bce Terrible storm hits Orkney; Skara Brae ruins uncovered George Petrie publishes research on Skara Brae 1913 Thieves raid Skara Brae Skara Brae now protected by Scottish authorities 1925 Storm damages ancient ruins Seawall constructed 1926 Carbon dating reveals true age of Skara Brae UNESCO declares Skara Brae a World Heritage Site 1970s.
pages.brief: Scenes of the same stone village across the ages: newly built and lived in, then empty and buried; a storm peeling grass from a mound; scholars digging; a seawall rising along the bay; and today's visitors walking among the ancient houses by the sea.

books.title: Temperate Deciduous Forests
books.art_why: Real forests, seasons, plants, animals, and people can be photographed today.

pages.text: A Blaze of Color Fall is a special time of year. The weather gets cooler, and many people feel more comfortable being outside. In some parts of the world, this season has special appeal beyond the weather. As temperatures start to cool down, the first colorful hints of autumn appear on trees. Before long, brilliant displays of yellows, golds, oranges, and reds paint the countryside. Some people only need to step outside their door to see these glorious landscapes. Others may fly thousands of miles to view them. One thing is certain: this amazing event is not to be missed. Brilliant fall colors are one of the greatest shows on Earth. They’re also a telltale sign of temperate deciduous forests. Leaves change color in a forest in Germany. Word Wise The word deciduous comes from a Latin word. It means “to fall off.” Deciduous trees lose their leaves in winter. They are sometimes referred to as leaf-shedding trees. To shed means to give off as part of a normal life process, such as a snake shedding its skin or a cat shedding hair.
pages.brief: A forest in Germany glows with autumn color, with tree leaves in brilliant yellows, golds, oranges, and reds as cooler weather arrives. The countryside is painted by these colorful leaves, showing the first hints of fall in a temperate deciduous forest.

pages.text: Autumn leaves color the landscape in Quebec, Canada. The Temperate Deciduous Forest Biome Different types of environments cover Earth’s surface. These regions and the communities of plants and animals that live there are called biomes. Grasslands, rainforests, deserts, and oceans are examples of biomes. So are temperate deciduous forests. Many factors play a part in creating Earth’s biomes. Two important ones are latitude—how far a location is from the equator —and elevation, or height above sea level. Both help determine how warm or cool a place is. Climate, land, and water are also important building blocks of biomes, as are plants and animals. Temperate deciduous forests are large areas where deciduous trees grow. The leaves on these trees change color in fall and drop to the ground in winter.
pages.brief: Autumn leaves color the landscape in Quebec, Canada, spreading across a broad forest area. The scene shows a temperate deciduous forest biome, where deciduous trees grow in a large region and their leaves change color in fall and drop in winter.

pages.text: Earth’s Temperate Deciduous Forest Regions About 7 percent of Earth’s land is temperate deciduous forests. Australia, New Zealand, southern South America, and Washington State have some areas with deciduous trees. They aren’t considered part of this biome, however. Temperate deciduous forests are located in the northern temperate zone. This latitude band is in the Northern Hemisphere between the cold polar zone and hot tropical zone. Much of the eastern third of the United States is in this biome, as well as a small part of Canada. Large areas of temperate deciduous forest are also found in Europe, Japan, eastern Russia, China, and Korea. Temperate deciduous forests may border many other biomes. They may be located next to grasslands, semiarid deserts, taiga (cold forests), or subtropical forests.
pages.brief: Earth's land areas show the northern temperate zone with large temperate deciduous forest regions across the eastern United States, Canada, Europe, Japan, eastern Russia, China, and Korea, bordering grasslands, semiarid deserts, taiga, and subtropical forests.

pages.text: A beech forest in Germany comes to life in spring. Snow decorates bare deciduous trees in winter. Climate and Soil Temperate deciduous forests are located in regions that receive both very warm and very cold weather. As a result, this biome has four seasons, each with its own unique personality. Winters are cold, often with low precipitation, although it varies from place to place. Temperatures and precipitation both rise in spring and reach their peak in summer, which can be quite humid. Autumn is cool and crisp, with a drop in precipitation. Temperatures throughout the year generally range between –30°C (–22°F) and 30°C (86°F). Temperate deciduous forests have the second- highest precipitation per year of any biome, after rainforests. Roughly 75 to 150 centimeters (30–59 in.) of precipitation fall each year. In winter, precipitation often falls as snow, sleet, or hail.
pages.brief: A beech forest in Germany comes to life in spring with new growth, while a second view shows bare deciduous trees decorated with snow in winter. The forest shows the biome’s four seasons, with cold winters and warmer, humid summers.

pages.text: In late fall, leaf litter covers the ground in a temperate deciduous forest. Soils in temperate deciduous forests tend to be deep, dark, and fertile. This is a result of trees dropping their leaves in autumn. The leaves build up on the forest floor, creating a dense layer of leaf litter. Fungi, bacteria, and other underground organisms break down this leafy layer, releasing nutrients into the soil. mixed forest in fall mixed forest in winter Do You Know? In some temperate regions, the soil contains more sand and fewer nutrients. Forests in these regions often have a mix of deciduous and evergreen trees. Evergreens can live in weaker soils. They lose and grow their leaves throughout the year instead of once each year. Forests with both kinds of trees are often referred to as mixed forests.
pages.brief: In late fall, leaf litter covers the ground in a temperate deciduous forest. Deep, dark, fertile soil lies beneath the leaves, and a mixed forest is shown in fall and in winter, with both deciduous and evergreen trees.

pages.text: The shape and texture of the leaves of deciduous trees make them easy for plant eaters to digest. Plants Temperate deciduous forests are also known as temperate broadleaf forests. Most of the trees in this biome have wide, flat leaves instead of thin needles. Leaf shape is an adaptation that helps the trees survive. Because the leaves have a large surface area, they capture a great deal of sunlight for photosynthesis. In this process, plants make food from sunlight, water, air, and chlorophyll, a chemical. Forests in this biome generally have five levels of plants. The canopy includes the tallest trees, which receive the greatest amount of sunlight. The fertile soil nourishes many hardwood trees, including oak, elm, maple, hickory, beech, and ash. Some sunlight gets through the dense canopy, which allows many species of plants to grow in the lower levels.
pages.brief: Wide, flat leaves of deciduous trees fill a temperate broadleaf forest, where the tallest trees form a dense canopy. Oak, elm, maple, hickory, beech, and ash trees grow in fertile soil, and sunlight filters through the canopy to lower plant levels.

pages.text: The level under the canopy contains shorter trees, such as dogwoods, along with saplings— young, slender trees. Beneath them is the shrub level, which may include rhododendron, sumac, and honeysuckle. Next comes the herb level, which contains ferns, grasses, and wildflowers. Mosses, fungi, and lichens grow on the forest floor, or ground. They also grow on tree trunks. In addition to leaf shape, trees in temperate deciduous forests have other adaptations that help them survive. Dropping their leaves and becoming dormant in winter allows them to conserve energy and withstand the cold. Thick bark also offers trees protection from low temperatures. Plants in lower levels of the forest have adaptations, too. For example, ferns and wildflowers grow quickly in early spring before the canopy fills out and blocks too much sunlight. Rhododendron shrubs thrive under the canopy of a forest in Wales. Ferns grow in a birch forest.
pages.brief: Under the canopy, shorter dogwoods and slender saplings grow above a shrub level of rhododendron, sumac, and honeysuckle. Ferns, grasses, and wildflowers fill the herb level, while mosses, fungi, and lichens cover the forest floor and tree trunks. Rhododendron thrives in a Welsh forest, and ferns grow in a birch forest.

pages.text: Why Leaves Change Color The leaves of deciduous trees mainly conduct photosynthesis in spring and summer. They use sunlight and chlorophyll, a chemical mostly found in leaves, to turn water and carbon dioxide gas into a sugar that gives the trees energy. Leaves are green because they’re full of chlorophyll. They also contain orange, yellow, or brown chemicals that are hidden by the green chlorophyll. In fall, when the weather gets cooler and trees receive less sunlight, photosynthesis slows down. Leaves stop making chlorophyll, so they lose their green color. As a result, the hidden colors start to show. When the weather gets cold enough in fall, the temperature starts to drop below freezing. The trees shed their leaves before the sap inside the leaves begins to freeze. They do this to protect themselves from damage. Deciduous trees are bare in winter. They use the food they stored in spring and summer to survive. When spring comes and temperatures warm up, new leaves grow.
pages.brief: Deciduous tree leaves are green with chlorophyll in spring and summer, then lose their green color in fall as photosynthesis slows. Hidden orange, yellow, and brown colors begin to show, and the trees shed their leaves before freezing weather, leaving bare branches in winter.

pages.text: Animals Many different kinds of animals live in temperate deciduous forests. This is in part because of the many kinds of plants available to eat. Another reason is the variety of habitats with water, including lakes, ponds, rivers, and streams. Predators include bobcats, foxes, mountain lions, timber wolves, and coyotes. Large herbivores include white-tailed deer as well as moose in some areas. Rabbits, squirrels, and chipmunks are among the smaller herbivores. Omnivores include skunks, raccoons, opossums, and black bears. Eastern gray squirrels feed on the nuts, buds, and flowers of deciduous trees. Snakes, frogs, toads, and turtles are common, as are woodpeckers, cardinals, hawks, owls, and many other birds. This biome is also home to many insects and spiders. Before regal moths become adults, they eat deciduous leaves.
pages.brief: Many animals live in a temperate deciduous forest with lakes, ponds, rivers, and streams. An eastern gray squirrel feeds on nuts, buds, and flowers of deciduous trees, while a regal moth, before becoming an adult, eats deciduous leaves among the forest plants.

pages.text: Animals in this biome have adaptations to help them through the harsh winters. They need more energy to stay warm but have a harder time finding food since trees are dormant. Some animals, such as squirrels, store food for the winter ahead of time. Others, such as black bears and American toads, hibernate so they won’t need as much energy. Another way to survive the winter is to reduce heat loss. Red foxes grow a thicker coat of fur and often stay protected from the cold in dens. Mice and other rodents stay warm under a blanket of snow. Woodpeckers live in deciduous forests in the eastern United States all year long. A red fox stays warm in its den on a cold winter day. Woodpeckers and most owls are year-round residents of this biome. Many songbirds only live here during the warmer months. In winter, they migrate to warmer places where food is more plentiful.
pages.brief: A red fox stays warm in its den on a cold winter day, its thicker coat protecting it from the cold. Woodpeckers live in deciduous forests of the eastern United States all year long, while mice and other rodents stay warm under a blanket of snow.

pages.text: Hikers in South Korea enjoy the fall colors. People People have lived in temperate deciduous forests for many thousands of years. Most of this biome has been changed a great deal from its original condition. For at least five thousand years, people have been making use of its resources. These include fertile soil for growing crops and hardwood trees for fuel and building. Today, these forests are one of the most populated biomes in the world. People continue to use their resources, although in some places the forests have grown back. Temperate deciduous forests are popular recreation spots. Hiking, boating, fishing, camping, and wildlife watching all bring people to this biome. In addition, the fall colors are an irresistible attraction.
pages.brief: Hikers in South Korea enjoy the fall colors in a temperate deciduous forest. People use the forest’s fertile soil for crops and hardwood trees for fuel and building, and they come for hiking, boating, fishing, camping, and wildlife watching in this popular recreation spot.

pages.text: Magnificent Beauty Temperate deciduous forests stand out in every season. Frost, snow, and sunlight turn bare forests into winter wonderlands. In spring, the awakening of dormant trees and flowers provides welcome signs of new life. Summer heat and rain bring an explosion of green growth. Vibrant fall colors change landscapes into beautiful works of art. If you have a chance to visit a temperate deciduous forest, especially in fall, be sure to go. Gazing at the brilliantly colored trees or walking on a carpet of crunchy leaves is an experience you’ll never forget.
pages.brief: A temperate deciduous forest stands out in every season: frost, snow, and sunlight turn bare winter trees into a wonderland; spring brings new life; summer heat and rain bring green growth; and vibrant fall colors change the landscape into beautiful works of art.

books.title: Seahorses
books.art_why: Real seahorses exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: Seahorses.
pages.brief: Seahorses float in clear blue ocean water among soft seagrass. One seahorse faces forward while another turns slightly, showing its curled tail and horse-like snout. Sunlight filters down through the water around them.

pages.text: A pair of seahorses stay together for life. Strange Creatures A strange marine creature hides in beds of seagrass. It’s a fish that dances yet can barely swim. It’s an animal that can look ahead and behind at the same time. It’s the seahorse, a delicate and unique ocean marvel. The scientific name for seahorses is hippocampus. That name comes from two ancient Greek words: hippos, meaning “horse,” and kampos, meaning “sea monster.”
pages.brief: A strange marine creature hides in a bed of seagrass: a seahorse, a delicate fish that dances yet can barely swim. Its eyes look ahead and behind at once. A pair of seahorses stay together nearby, and the seahorse’s name comes from ancient Greek words.

pages.text: Honshu pipefish Funny Kind of Fish Seahorses are closely related to pipefish— skinny fish with long snouts—and have some of the same features. They both have small fins and eyes that move separately. Neither one has teeth. In other ways, though, these fishy cousins are quite different. Pipefish look like skinny tubes. They’re longer than they are tall. Pipefish hold themselves horizontally, as most fish do. Seahorses are just the opposite. They hold themselves upright as they move through the water.
pages.brief: A harlequin ghost pipefish and a Honshu pipefish swim horizontally through the water, their skinny tube-like bodies and long snouts visible. Nearby, a seahorse holds itself upright. Both kinds of fish have small fins, eyes that move separately, and no teeth.

pages.text: Another big difference is in the body parts that give seahorses their name. Seahorses have bumps called spines that run along the top and back of their head like a horse’s mane. Their snout looks like the muzzle and nose of a horse. They also have a long tail. All of the more than forty types of seahorses have this body structure, but their size varies. The tiny pygmy seahorse measures about 2 centimeters (just under 1 in.) The Pacific seahorse can grow up to 31 centimeters (1 ft.) long. Seahorses also come in different colors, ranging from purple to gold to white. They often change color as well. Parts of a Seahorse coronet eye pectoral fin snout keel dorsal fin tail.
pages.brief: A tiny pygmy seahorse sits beside a much larger Pacific seahorse, their colors ranging from purple to gold to white. A close view shows a seahorse’s coronet, eye, pectoral fin, snout, keel, dorsal fin and long tail, with horse-like spines along its head and back.

pages.text: Where Seahorses Live AUSTRALIA seahorse range seahorse range Seahorses live in warm waters in most parts of the world. Where Seahorses Live Seahorses live in warm waters along coastlines around the world. They nest in kelp forests and beds of eelgrass in places that have steady currents. These weedy areas are full of tiny plankton and shrimp larvae, foods seahorses like to eat. The moving waters bring them food, which is important since they can’t swim great distances to hunt. Seahorses sometimes move to deeper water during storms to avoid rough waves. Usually, though, they stay within a set area. A female’s territory may be up to 100 square meters (1,076 sq. ft.). A male’s range is only a fraction of that size.
pages.brief: Seahorses live in warm coastal waters around the world, among kelp forests and beds of eelgrass where steady currents bring tiny plankton and shrimp larvae. A coastline near Australia shows their range. Seahorses stay within set areas, sometimes moving to deeper water during storms.

pages.text: A Denise’s pygmy seahorse, one of the smallest kinds of seahorses, is found in Indonesia. Unique Adaptations A seahorse has an unusual body for a fish. It has an exoskeleton—a hard, armor-like covering with skin on top of it. Its exoskeleton helps the seahorse defend against predators and protects its internal organs from harm. Attached to its back is a small dorsal fin that flutters as fast as a hummingbird’s wings. That fluttering fin is not strong enough to move seahorses away from hungry crabs or sea rays quickly. Seahorses are not fast swimmers. In fact, the tiny pygmy seahorse is one of the slowest-moving fish on Earth, with a top speed of only 1.5 meters (5 ft.) per hour. For the most part, seahorses are drifters, letting ocean currents carry them along.
pages.brief: A Denise’s pygmy seahorse, one of the smallest seahorses, floats in the warm waters of Indonesia. Its hard, armor-like exoskeleton covers its body, and a small dorsal fin flutters rapidly. This tiny fish drifts with the current, one of the slowest-moving fish on Earth.

pages.text: Having a prehensile tail comes in handy for these seaweed dwellers. Seahorses can wrap their prehensile tail around something and grip it as a hand can. Seahorses use their tail to hold themselves in place. Hanging on to seagrass keeps seahorses from being swept away by swift currents. Camouflage is an important part of seahorse defense. Seahorses have adapted to survive by using color to blend in with their surroundings. Seahorse skin has special groups of cells called chromatophores. The cells change color according to signals from the body. Two cousins of seahorses— leafy and weedy seadragons—have growths that look like leaves. These growths make them especially hard to see in a kelp forest!
pages.brief: A seahorse wraps its prehensile tail around seagrass, holding itself in place against a swift current. Its skin blends with the surroundings as chromatophores change color. Nearby, leafy and weedy seadragons drift in a kelp forest, their leaf-like growths making them hard to see.

pages.text: Looking for prey is easy thanks to a seahorse’s unusual eyes. Its eyes work independently and can look in two different directions at once. When a seahorse spots prey, it points its snout toward its target and uses it like a straw to suck in food. A seahorse can eat only what will fit through its thin snout since it has no teeth and can’t chew. Eating Like a Horse! Seahorses can take in only the smallest bits of food, so they must eat often—up to fifty times a day!
pages.brief: A seahorse hovers among weeds, its eyes working independently and looking in two different directions. Its snout points toward a tiny bit of prey, ready to suck it in like a straw. Because it has no teeth and cannot chew, it must eat often, up to fifty times a day.

pages.text: A pair of tiger-tail seahorses mate. Dad Moms Seahorses are unique not just in how they look but also in how they reproduce. Males and females take roles that are quite different from those of other animal species. It’s the male seahorses, or stallions, that give birth! Seahorses and pipefish are the only animals that do this. First, a seahorse couple pairs off and dances together for several days. In this mating dance, they circle each other or swim side by side, changing colors to communicate. They may grasp each other with their tails. Some seahorse pairs bond for life.
pages.brief: A pair of tiger-tail seahorses mate, circling each other and swimming side by side in the water. They change colors to communicate and may grasp each other with their tails. Seahorses are unique because the male, or stallion, gives birth, and some pairs bond for life.

pages.text: A stallion has a pouch, not unlike a kangaroo’s. When the time is right, the female places as many as 1,500 eggs into the pouch. The stallion fertilizes the eggs and holds them in his pouch for about forty-five days. During that time, the female checks on him to make sure all is well. A male with a pouchful of eggs guards his territory. He puffs himself up to look as large as he can to scare off predators. Over time, the eggs develop into baby seahorses called fry, which look just like their parents. When the fry are ready, the stallion squeezes them out of his pouch into the water. Then they swim off on their own. Depending on the species, seahorses can give birth to more than a thousand babies at a time. However, only about one in twenty will survive to become adults. Those that do may live up to about five years. A male seahorse gives birth.
pages.brief: A male seahorse, or stallion, carries eggs in his pouch among the seagrass while a female checks on him. He puffs himself up to guard his territory. Later, baby seahorses called fry squeeze out of the pouch and swim off on their own.

pages.text: Surviving Against All Odds Only a small number of fry grow into adults. That number may not be enough to sustain seahorse populations, however. Adult seahorses are in danger, not just from natural predators but also from humans. Boats, especially those used for commercial fishing, present a real threat to seahorses. These boats may drag nets or anchors across the ocean floor, which uproots sea plants important to seahorse survival. The anchors may also destroy seahorse habitat, reducing their numbers. Since seahorses are not distance swimmers and have limited ranges, they are less likely to seek out new habitats once their home is destroyed. Another threat comes from people who hunt seahorses. People haul them in using nets. Seahorses are in great demand for several reasons. They are used for traditional medicine, and they’re also collected and sold as ornaments. People bring them ashore and place them in the hot sun to dry out. Their bodies are sold to companies that use them as decorations.
pages.brief: A commercial fishing boat drags a net and anchor across the ocean floor, uprooting sea plants that seahorses need. People haul seahorses in nets and lay them in the hot sun to dry. Because seahorses stay in limited ranges and cannot swim far, they struggle when their habitat is destroyed.

pages.text: Live seahorses are also sold as pets. Their unusual appearance makes them a popular addition to aquariums. Seahorses do not last long living in home fish tanks. Most die within weeks because of stress or disease. Conservationists have found that the best way to help seahorses is to educate people about them. Not only are they beautiful creatures, but they are also important to ocean ecology. Their feeding habits help to keep a healthy balance of sea life around coral reefs and grass beds. A Seahorse City A retired schoolteacher named Roger Hanson was a regular diver off the California coast. He wanted to study and protect the seahorses he saw on his dives. He created a “seahorse city” on the ocean floor with pine branches and palm leaves. He built this safe environment far from the beach to give seahorses a place to live without the risk of being trampled. Daphne, a Pacific seahorse that lives in Roger Hanson’s habitat (main); Roger Hanson (inset)
pages.brief: Roger Hanson, a retired schoolteacher and diver, swims near his seahorse city on the ocean floor, built from pine branches and palm leaves. Daphne, a Pacific seahorse, lives among the branches. In another scene, a live seahorse sits in a home fish tank, sold as a pet.

pages.text: Look but don’t touch! A scuba diver respectfully observes a long-snouted seahorse near Singer Island, Florida. Conclusion Seahorses are amazing ocean dwellers. They are shy creatures that hide among the weeds and try to stay out of sight. If you are lucky enough to spot a seahorse in the wild, move slowly. Do not disturb it. Take a quiet moment to admire and appreciate its unique beauty, then go on your way. These beautiful creatures are a delight to see in oceans all over the world. Their gentle nature and unusual characteristics make seahorses among nature’s most unusual treasures.
pages.brief: A scuba diver respectfully observes a long-snouted seahorse near Singer Island, Florida. The diver moves slowly and keeps a quiet distance, watching the shy creature hide among the weeds. The seahorse stays out of sight as the diver admires its unusual beauty without disturbing it.

books.title: Robots
books.art_why: Robots and real-world machines can be photographed today.

pages.text: Tireless Workers Imagine working at a job picking up nails and putting them into boxes as they pass through an assembly line. Imagine that this is the only thing you do all day and night. You never get to take breaks to eat, sleep, or go to the bathroom. This kind of job is very repetitive, which makes it difficult to stay focused. After a while, you’d be tired, cranky, and exhausted. But robots can do this job perfectly every time, without complaining.
pages.brief: A robot arm works at a factory assembly line, picking up nails and placing them into boxes as they move past. The robot keeps working through the day and night without taking breaks to eat, sleep, or rest.

pages.text: This robot swims like a fish and has a video camera inside. What Are Robots? The word robot comes from the Czech word robota, which means “forced labor,” or hard, boring work. In fact, many robots today are factory robots. Many are simple robot arms. Some can grip pieces of metal, while others weld them together. Still others drill or spray-paint parts. Robot arms with a lighter touch sort items, from chocolates to tiny screws. Robots are machines with mechanical bodies, information sensors, and computer brains. Most robots can move or have moving parts. Some robots look like people, but robots come in many shapes and sizes. Some walk on legs. Others use wheels or tracks to move. Some robots fly like insects, swim like fish, or even crawl like snakes.
pages.brief: A fish-shaped robot swims underwater with a video camera inside it. Factory robot arms grip metal pieces, weld, drill, spray-paint parts, and sort small items such as chocolates and tiny screws. Other robots move on legs, wheels, or tracks, fly, swim, or crawl.

pages.text: Inside a Robot color camera Motors control movements of the head, neck, legs, and tail. computer brain microphone speaker speaker rechargeable battery infrared sensor floor sensors This baby dinosaur robot needs many parts to work. Many robots use video cameras and microphones to act as their eyes and ears. Robots are programmed to perform certain tasks, either on their own or by remote control. The program plans every step of the robot’s task. Most robots cannot do anything that they have not been programmed to do. Robotics Robotics is the science of designing, building, and operating robots. Some schools and summer camps offer robotics programs where students work together to create their own robots. Teams of high school students around the world participate in yearly competitions to see who can build the best robots.
pages.brief: A baby dinosaur robot is shown with its color camera, motors, computer brain, microphone, speakers, rechargeable battery, infrared sensor, and floor sensors. Students in a robotics program work together to create their own robots, while high school teams compete to build the best robots.

pages.text: Simple or Complex Simple robots can perform basic tasks such as moving car parts on an assembly line. For this job, the robot only needs one arm, a sensor that tells it where the parts are, and a program to control its movements. As robots get more complex, they need more programs in their computer brains. Robots are usually built to be good at doing just a few things. It is much easier to build ten robots to do ten different things than it is to build one robot to do all ten things.
pages.brief: On an assembly line, a simple robot with one arm, a sensor, and a control program moves car parts. More complex robots have more programs in their computer brains. The page suggests ten robots built for ten different tasks instead of one robot trying to do all ten.

pages.text: Danger Zones Some robots are built to go places that are too dangerous for humans. After an earthquake damaged a nuclear power plant in Japan, officials sent in robots to check the damage. The radiation from the nuclear accident would have killed any living creature that entered the damaged plant. Volcanoes can also be very dangerous. Eight scientists died while studying a volcano in South America in 1993. A robot was built to get samples of gases safely from a volcano in Alaska. The eight-legged crawler robot successfully brought back the samples, though it was damaged during the mission.
pages.brief: After an earthquake damages a nuclear power plant in Japan, robots enter the radiation-filled building to check the damage. At a volcano in Alaska, an eight-legged crawler robot collects samples of gases, even though it is damaged during the mission. The page also remembers eight scientists who died studying a South American volcano in 1993.

pages.text: Robot Exploration Remote-Operated Vehicles (ROVs) are often used to investigate places on Earth that are hard for people to reach. ROVs use lights, cameras, and scientific instruments to search for new life forms living deep in the oceans. The remote-controlled Nomad robot explored the Atacama Desert in Chile. It traveled 215 kilometers (134 mi.) in forty-five days while collecting rock and soil samples. Nomad went on to successfully search areas of icy Antarctica for rocks that fell to Earth from space. The Hercules ROV recovers an object from the seafloor.
pages.brief: A remotely operated vehicle uses lights, cameras, and scientific instruments to search for new life forms deep in the ocean. The Nomad robot travels across Chile’s Atacama Desert, collecting rock and soil samples, then searches icy Antarctica for space rocks. The Hercules ROV recovers an object from the seafloor.

pages.text: The Spirit and Opportunity robotic rovers worked many years longer than expected on the surface of Mars. The Spirit and Opportunity robots explored the surface of Mars. These identical robots were programmed to act as geologists—scientists who study rocks. They had tiny rock drills, microscopes, and instruments that can tell what rocks are made of. Scientists controlled these robots by sending radio signals through space. Robots don’t need food, water, or air. They don’t age or get bored. They don’t even need a return trip home. For these reasons, much future space exploration will involve robots rather than people.
pages.brief: The identical Spirit and Opportunity rovers explore the surface of Mars as robot geologists. They carry tiny rock drills, microscopes, and instruments that identify what rocks are made of. Scientists send radio signals through space to control them, since robots need no food, water, air, or return trip home.

pages.text: Tiny Robots Scientists are researching and developing tiny robots. Some of these are smaller than the width of a human hair. Such tiny robots might one day be used by doctors to inspect sick or injured bodies from the inside. Groups, or “swarms,” of tiny robots working together could perform surgery to heal wounds or track down and destroy cancer cells.
pages.brief: Scientists research and develop tiny robots, some smaller than the width of a human hair. In the future, doctors might use them inside sick or injured bodies to inspect and heal. Groups, or swarms, of tiny robots could work together to perform surgery, heal wounds, or track down and destroy cancer cells.

pages.text: Robotic People and Animals People have tried to build humanlike robots for decades. Some robots have two arms and legs to move and work as people do. Some robots even have faces and hair to appear more like us. These robots may look like people, but so far they are not very good at acting like people. One problem is that it’s hard for robots to do many different things the way people can. In fact, the more automatic a task is for a human, the harder it is to program a robot to do it. Each of us learned to walk, but after that, we do it by instinct.
pages.brief: Humanlike robots with two arms, two legs, faces, and hair are built to move and work as people do. They may look like people, but they are not very good at acting like people. The page explains that automatic human tasks, such as walking by instinct, are hard to program into a robot.

pages.text: To get around this problem, scientists begin by programming a robot to only deal with one very simple task, such as rolling or walking on many legs. Then they add other simple programs one by one until the robot can do many different tasks successfully. This idea began with robots that imitate insects. These tiny bug-bots move and react just like insects and can send signals to each other. Several companies have built robot dogs as expensive toys and companions. These dogs bark, move, and perform tricks. More advanced models can recognize their owners’ voices and faces, and respond with actions or flashing lights.
pages.brief: Scientists program a robot to handle one simple task, such as rolling or walking on many legs, then add more simple programs one by one. Tiny bug-bots imitate insects and send signals to each other. Robot dogs act as expensive toys and companions; they bark, move, perform tricks, and advanced models recognize owners’ voices and faces.

pages.text: Robot Intelligence True artificial intelligence, or AI, involves human-level intelligence. It involves the ability to learn, react to new information, and make decisions independently. Scientists are still working on creating computers and robots with real AI. Some robots are able to adjust their own programming as they gain experience. This kind of machine learning allows robots to improve the way they work over time. Do You Know? Smart cars, also known as self-driving cars, use many of the same technologies as robots. Smart cars use cameras and sensors to sense what’s going on around them. Their computer brains calculate the best direction and speed to travel safely. Mechanical parts steer the cars and control their speed.
pages.brief: Scientists work on true artificial intelligence, which would let robots learn, react to new information, and make decisions independently. Some robots already adjust their own programming as they gain experience. Smart cars use cameras, sensors, and computer brains to calculate safe direction and speed, while mechanical parts steer and control speed.

pages.text: The Future of Robots Robots are already a big part of modern life, and they are becoming more common every day. Robots work in many factories, vacuum people’s homes, and mow their lawns. In some areas, robots deliver meals from restaurants or fly through the sky carrying packages from online stores. As robots continue to improve, we can expect them to keep changing the way we work and live. sidewalk delivery robot lawn-mowing robot flying delivery drone vacuum robot.
pages.brief: Robots already work in factories, vacuum people’s homes, and mow lawns. In some places, sidewalk delivery robots carry meals from restaurants, and flying delivery drones carry packages from online stores through the sky. The page shows a sidewalk delivery robot, a lawn-mowing robot, a flying delivery drone, and a vacuum robot.

books.title: Deserts Dry
books.art_why: Suggested by keyword check; desert scenes include ancient and historical elements suited to drawn illustrations.

pages.text: Dunes are actually found in only a few deserts. Introduction Shut your eyes and imagine that you are standing in a desert. What kinds of things do you see around you? Camels, cactuses, and sand dunes? This is what most people think of when they imagine the desert. But deserts are far more rich and varied than the sandy landscape you might imagine. A desert is any area where more water evaporates, or dries up, than falls as rain. Deserts can be hot, cool, or cold. In fact, both the North and South poles are considered deserts because all of the water there is frozen. Deserts make up almost one-third of the land on Earth, covering mountains, canyons, and glaciers. In this book, you will find out more about the surprising inhabitants of three amazing deserts: the Sahara, the Gobi, and the Atacama.
pages.brief: A person stands with eyes closed, imagining a desert with camels, cactuses, and sand dunes. The scene widens to show hot, cool, and cold deserts, including polar ice, mountains, canyons, and glaciers. The image suggests deserts cover almost one-third of the land on Earth.

pages.text: The Sahara On many maps of Africa, the entire top third of the continent is colored yellow or pale beige. This color represents the vast, dry land of the Sahara Desert. It is by far the largest desert in the world. This is where we get many of our images of the desert. Great, ocean-like landscapes of yellow sand dunes cover one-fifth of the Sahara. The Tuareg people, in their blue, flowing robes and turbans, lead caravans of camels across the sandy desert to trade salt. But the Sahara is much more than sand. Many people in the Sahara Desert still rely on camels.
pages.brief: The top third of Africa appears as a vast pale yellow desert. Tuareg people in blue flowing robes and turbans lead a caravan of camels across great yellow sand dunes. They carry salt to trade, while other people in the Sahara rely on camels.

pages.text: It might surprise you to learn that the world’s largest desert contains one of the world’s longest rivers. The Nile flows along the eastern edge of the Sahara, bringing life-giving water to crops and cities along its banks. This river allowed the great civilization of ancient Egypt to survive among the dunes. In ancient Egypt, as today, people carved irrigation channels. These channels carried water from the riverbed to thirsty crops, animals, and people. There is also water hidden deep underground in the Sahara. In some places, it seeps close to the surface, creating an oasis, or a small spot of green land. A pyramid built by ancient Egyptians But don’t get the idea that the Sahara is moist and pleasant. In some areas, no rain falls for years, the temperature can get as high as 136°F (58°C), and powerful winds whip up sun- blocking dust storms. The Sahara is home to thorn trees, shrubs, and low-growing grasses. Several kinds of antelope survive here, as do many rodents, birds, and reptiles. One kind of reptile, a skink, is known as a sandfish because it can “swim” through the sand.
pages.brief: The Nile runs along the eastern edge of the Sahara, with green crops and cities on its banks. Ancient Egyptian irrigation channels carry water to fields, and a pyramid stands nearby. In the distance, an oasis and a dust storm show the desert's extremes, while a sandfish skink swims through sand.

pages.text: A worker walks through a plant where gas is made from oil in Algeria. People have lived in the Sahara for centuries. Northern Africa is a natural trading area for people from Africa, Europe, and Asia. Rich ancient cities survived on irrigated crops and the wealth of spices, fabrics, and precious metals and gems passing through. During the Middle Ages, northern Africa was a center of art, writing, science, and learning. Today, a treasure lies hidden under the Sahara. The desert holds the world’s largest reserves of oil, a liquid that many people depend on heavily for fuel and energy. Some countries of the Sahara have become incredibly wealthy from selling oil. Unfortunately, many nations have fought wars over this valuable resource.
pages.brief: A worker in Algeria walks through a plant where gas is made from oil. Beyond the plant, an ancient northern African city shows its trading past, with spices, fabrics, and precious metals. Underground, the Sahara's vast oil reserves lie beneath the desert, a treasure that has brought wealth and conflict.

pages.text: The Gobi is more remote than the Sahara. The Gobi Mongolia and northern China lie deep within the immense continent of Asia. They are home to the high, dry Gobi Desert. It might surprise you that the Gobi is cold—it can get as low as –40°F (–40°C). Like the Sahara, the Gobi Desert was often crisscrossed by traders bringing goods to and from Asia. But unlike the Sahara, the Gobi is too harsh and remote to support cities.
pages.brief: The high, dry Gobi Desert stretches across Mongolia and northern China deep inside Asia. A trader's caravan crosses the remote landscape, but no cities rise here. The air feels cold, as low as -40°F, and the harsh, remote land offers few signs of settlement.

pages.text: Many parts of the Gobi are high, dry, and mountainous. The soil is rocky and salty, so there are few plants other than tough grasses and shrubs. But these grasses are enough to support grazing animals such as Mongolian horses, antelope, and gazelle. Also feeding on the grasses are many kinds of gerbils and another small rodent called the jerboa. Do You Know? Normally, naturally occurring salt in the soil gets dissolved by rainwater and carried in rivers to the ocean. This is why the ocean is salty. But in the desert, there is little rain to dissolve the salt, and the rivers dry up before reaching the ocean. So, most salt stays in the soil. In some places, rivers carry salt into temporary marshes or lakes. When those dry in the desert air, they leave behind huge areas of salt. These areas are known as salt pans.
pages.brief: High, rocky, salty ground stretches across the Gobi, with only tough grasses and shrubs growing. Mongolian horses, antelope, and gazelle graze on the grasses, while gerbils and a jerboa feed nearby. In the distance, a dry salt pan shows where a temporary lake has evaporated and left salt behind.

pages.text: Most of the people who inhabit the Gobi are nomads, people who move from place to place, often in search of food. Some of these nomads rely on horses for almost everything they need to live—meat, milk, hides for tents, and transportation. These nomads, who live in Mongolia, are excellent horse trainers. They rope and race horses as well as any rodeo rider.
pages.brief: Mongolian nomads move from place to place in search of food. They rely on horses for meat, milk, hides for tents, and transportation. Skilled horse trainers rope and race their horses across the open Gobi, moving with their tents.

pages.text: The Gobi has very few natural resources such as oil. But there is a fascinating sort of treasure here—fossils. The dry climate and lack of humans have preserved delicate fossils for millions of years. Today, scientists flock to the Gobi for new discoveries. It was here that the first dinosaur eggs were found, and where the fossil of a feathered reptile led scientists to believe that birds may be related to dinosaurs. Archaeologists digging for fossils in the Gobi.
pages.brief: Archaeologists dig for fossils in the dry Gobi Desert. The climate and lack of humans have preserved delicate fossils for millions of years. Scientists examine a dinosaur egg and a feathered reptile fossil, discoveries that suggest birds may be related to dinosaurs.

pages.text: The Atacama is one of the highest deserts. The Atacama Just west of South America’s Atacama Desert is the largest body of water in the world—the Pacific Ocean. The Atacama lies along the Pacific Coast, squeezed in a narrow band between the ocean and the high Andes Mountains. Temperatures in the Atacama are pleasant, between 50° and 70°F (10°–20°C). One would think that being near the ocean would give the Atacama some moisture. However, this desert is possibly the driest place on Earth. In some places in the Atacama, it may have never rained in human memory.
pages.brief: The Atacama Desert lies in a narrow band along South America's Pacific Coast, squeezed between the ocean and the high Andes Mountains. The Pacific Ocean stretches to the west. Temperatures are pleasant, between 50° and 70°F, yet this is possibly the driest place on Earth, where some places may never have rained in human memory.

pages.text: Some moisture does visit the Atacama. In the spring, snow on the Andes melts and flows in rivers across the desert to the Pacific. But these rivers don’t fill with water often, and they are usually steep, narrow, and quick-moving, so the water does not have a chance to spread out and sink in. The only other reliable form of moisture is fog that rolls in off the cold ocean. Many plants have developed clever ways to catch this fog. Some plant leaves gather droplets of fog and direct them toward their roots. Small “cloud forests” of these plants can grow in sheltered areas along the coasts where the fog is thick enough. Other than the cloud forests, almost no plant life grows in the Atacama. Some plants exist as dormant, or inactive, seeds. These spring to life after a rain shower, which may come only once every ten years. There are few animals in the Atacama besides rodents and insects. The chinchilla, a popular new pet, lives here. Llamas and alpacas, furry relatives of the camel, can also be found in damp areas near rivers and high in the mountains. Llamas.
pages.brief: Fog rolls in from the cold Pacific Ocean onto the Atacama. Plants catch droplets on their leaves and send the moisture toward their roots, forming small cloud forests in sheltered coastal areas. Nearby, dormant seeds wait in dry ground, while a chinchilla, llama, and alpaca live near damp river areas and high mountains.

pages.text: But what the Atacama lacks in animals, it makes up for in minerals. The Andes are volcanic mountains. Their volcanic activity brought copper, nitrates (an ingredient in fertilizer and explosives), and sulfur to the surface. Salt is also abundant here in marshy lakes. Mining companies build entire towns for workers who dig up these minerals. Port cities spring up along the shore where the minerals are shipped around the world. All food and water must be trucked in or shipped by boat. Because of the desert’s unforgiving climate, miners are some of the very few people who have ever made their homes in the Atacama. Trucks carry ore out of a mine in the Atacama desert.
pages.brief: In the Atacama, mining towns rise beside volcanic Andes mountains rich in copper, nitrates, sulfur, and salt. A truck carries ore out of a mine. Port cities along the shore ship minerals around the world, while all food and water must be trucked in or brought by boat for the miners.

pages.text: The city of Tucson, Arizona, lies in the Sonoran Desert. Conclusion So, what can you find in the desert that you might not have expected? Lakes of salt, dense fogs, and underground oceans of oil? Ancient civilizations, expert horse herders, and mining towns? You may have thought of deserts as empty, lifeless places. But for thousands of years, plants, animals, and humans have known deserts as sources of life, riches, and wonder.
pages.brief: The city of Tucson, Arizona, lies in the Sonoran Desert. Around it, surprising desert features come together: salt lakes, dense fog, underground oil, ancient civilizations, expert horse herders, and mining towns. Plants, animals, and humans have known deserts as sources of life, riches, and wonder for thousands of years.

books.title: Bears
books.art_why: Bears exist today and are best shown with real photographs.

pages.text: What Is a Bear? Bears are intelligent, curious, powerful animals that have always fascinated people. They have thick fur, short legs, and small ears. They also have stubby tails, long claws, and jaws that can crush bone. Bears have a strong sense of smell and can even smell and find food packed inside plastic bags. The smallest bear is the sun bear, which weighs 36 to 63 kilograms (80–140 lbs). The largest bear is the polar bear. Male polar bears can weigh as much as 680 kilograms (1,500 lbs). Many bears are known for hibernating, or sleeping, often for months at a time. Bears that hibernate do so to survive the cold winter when there is not enough food. They eat large quantities of food during the warmer months to store enough fat to last without food during the winter. Even though bears are famous for hibernating, many bears do not hibernate. Polar bears and giant pandas cannot get enough food during the warmer months to go without food in the winter. Sun bears and sloth bears, which live where food is plentiful year-round, also do not hibernate.
pages.brief: A large male polar bear stands on snow near the North Pole, showing thick fur, short legs, small ears, stubby tail, and long claws. In the background, a brown bear sleeps curled in a den.

pages.text: A bear mother and her cub Growing Up Most adult bears are solitary and like to roam on their own. The exceptions are during the mating season and when mothers care for their cubs. Bears usually have one to three cubs at a time. Bear cubs are very small, blind, and helpless at birth. They stay in a den with their mother for several months after their birth. Male bears do not help raise cubs. In fact, sometimes they kill and eat the cubs. The mother bear must fiercely protect her cubs while they are young and weak. Cubs stay close to their mother for up to three years. During that time, their biggest task is to learn how to find food. Then they are on their own.
pages.brief: A mother bear lies curled inside a dark den with one to three tiny, blind cubs nestled against her. She keeps them close and protected. Outside the den, a male bear is shown at a distance, kept away by the mother’s watchful posture.

pages.text: Kinds of Bears The following pages introduce the eight kinds of bears. Their comparative sizes are shown in the illustration below. List of bears, from largest to smallest: • Brown bear (Grizzly): length: 2.1 m (7 ft), weight: 250 kg (550 lbs) • American black bear: length: 1.5 m (5 ft), weight: 113 kg (250 lbs) • Asiatic black bear: length: 1.5 m (5 ft), weight: 113 kg (250 lbs)
pages.brief: Three bears stand side by side in a natural setting, arranged from largest to smallest: a brown bear, an American black bear, and an Asiatic black bear. Their different body sizes and coat colors are easy to compare, with the brown bear tallest and the black bears smaller.

pages.text: Polar Bears The polar bear is the largest bear and the largest land-dwelling carnivore on Earth. It is easily identified by its white or yellow-white fur that camouflages it in the snow. Polar bears are fantastic swimmers because they have partially webbed front paws. A thick layer of fat keeps them warm, even in extremely cold water. Polar bears live near the North Pole. They are powerful hunters, eating mostly seals and walruses. Because food can be hard to find, they may not eat for days at a time. Do You Know? Polar bears have black skin under their fur. The black skin absorbs the sun’s energy and helps keep the bears warm. polar bear.
pages.brief: A polar bear stands on ice near open water, white fur blending with snow. It watches a seal on a nearby floe. Its broad front paws are visible, and its powerful body is built for swimming and hunting in the Arctic cold.

pages.text: Brown Bears Not all brown bears are brown—they are divided into ten subgroups based on coloring. It ranges from light tan to reddish brown to very dark brown. One famous subgroup is the grizzly bear. Its name comes from its gray-tipped fur, which looks frosty, or grizzled. The largest brown bear, the Kodiak bear, lives in Alaska. Brown bears have the largest range of any kind of bear. They live in western North America, parts of Europe, and much of northern Asia. Brown bears vary in size depending on where they live and what they eat. Fish, especially salmon, is a staple in the diet of many brown bears. The diet of a grizzly bear is among the most varied of any living animal. Grizzlies eat meat, fish, insects, eggs, berries, roots, leaves, and grass. brown bear.
pages.brief: A large brown bear stands in a rushing river, water splashing around its legs, as it catches a salmon. Its fur ranges from light tan to dark brown, with gray-tipped hairs. Behind it are western North American mountains, forests, and grassy banks where it finds fish, berries, roots, and insects.

pages.text: Giant Pandas The giant panda is one of the most well-known animals in the world. It is easy to recognize because of its thick black-and-white fur and distinctive eye patches.
