Giant pandas live in the forest-covered mountains of China. They feed almost exclusively on bamboo and depend on the health of bamboo forests to stay alive. Giant pandas are extremely rare, with only about 1,000 left in the wild. Do You Know? The giant panda has an extra “thumb” on each hand. It is not really a thumb, but instead a special wrist bone, covered with a pad, that helps the giant panda grasp bamboo stems. giant panda.
pages.brief: A giant panda sits among thick bamboo in a forest-covered mountain in China. Its black-and-white fur and dark eye patches are clear as it grips a bamboo stem with a special wrist bone. More bamboo stalks surround it, showing the food it depends on.

pages.text: American Black Bears The American black bear—often black but sometimes lighter—has a light-colored muzzle. Scientists recognize separate subgroups of American black bears based on coloring. These include the cinnamon bear (reddish brown), the Kermode bear (white), and the blue, silver, or glacier bear (bluish black or dark gray). American black bears live in much of the North American continent. They can be found in Alaska, Canada, and northern Mexico. Black bears are true omnivores, eating a wide variety of plants as well as honey, fish, insects, and dead animals. They are very good climbers. American black bear.
pages.brief: An American black bear with a light-colored muzzle climbs a tree in a North American forest. Its claws grip the bark. Around it are plants, honeycomb, fish, and insects, showing the wide variety of foods it eats. The bear’s black coat and sturdy body are clearly visible.

pages.text: Asiatic Black Bears The Asiatic black bear, sometimes called the moon bear, is black except for a light-colored muzzle. It also has a patch of light fur shaped like a crescent moon on its chest and unusually large ears. Asiatic black bears live in mountainous regions of many Asian countries. They often anger farmers by eating crops and killing sheep, goats, and cattle. These bears have a diverse diet that also includes fruit, insects, and small animals. Asiatic black bear.
pages.brief: An Asiatic black bear stands in a mountainous region of Asia, its black coat, light muzzle, large ears, and crescent-shaped chest patch visible. It is near a farm field with crops and a sheep or goat, showing how it sometimes eats farmers’ crops and livestock. Forested slopes rise behind it.

pages.text: Spectacled Bears Spectacled bears have brown or black shaggy coats. They also have light markings on their faces that sometimes look like eyeglasses, or spectacles. They are the only native bear in South America, living in forested mountains, grasslands, and coastal deserts. Like most bears, they are omnivores and will eat almost anything, including dead meat. They especially like fruit, sugarcane, and corn. Spectacled bears often climb cacti to eat the fruit at the top. Do You Know? Each spectacled bear has a unique pattern of eye markings on its face. spectacled bear.
pages.brief: A spectacled bear with shaggy brown fur and light facial markings climbs a tall cactus in a South American landscape. Its unique eye markings look like spectacles. It reaches for fruit at the top of the cactus, with forested mountains, grasslands, and coastal desert in the distance.

pages.text: Sloth Bears The sloth bear is a type of small bear with a long, shaggy coat and a lighter-colored face. It moves slowly and often hangs from tree branches, similarly to another mammal called a tree sloth. Sloth bears live in the forests and grasslands of India and the neighboring island of Sri Lanka. Their favorite food is termites. A sloth bear has a long snout that it uses to suck out these insects from their nests. These bears also eat fruit, berries, and honey. When feeding, they make a loud sucking noise that can be heard from far away. sloth bear.
pages.brief: A sloth bear with a long, shaggy coat and lighter face hangs from a tree branch in India or Sri Lanka. Its long snout reaches into a termite nest, sucking out insects. Fruit, berries, and honey are nearby in the forest and grassland setting.

pages.text: Sun Bears The sun bear is the smallest member of the bear family. Mostly black, it gets its name from the light-colored patch of fur on its chest that is shaped like a rising sun. Sun bears live in lowland tropical rainforests in Southeast Asia. They feed on both plants and animals. They have unusually long tongues to help them remove insects from hard-to-reach places. Sun bears are sometimes called honey bears because of their love for honey. Sun bears like honey so much that they will fight angry bees to get it—and eat the bees, too! sun bear.
pages.brief: A small sun bear stands in a Southeast Asian tropical rainforest, its black coat and light chest patch shaped like a rising sun clearly visible. It reaches with a long tongue toward a honeycomb, bees buzzing around it. Plants and insects fill the lowland forest.

pages.text: Bear Survival Stories about bears attacking people are frightening. But bears are in greater danger from people than people are from bears. Because of human activity, bear populations are shrinking. Over half of all bear habitats worldwide have been destroyed by humans for farming, mining, and forestry. Five kinds of bears are endangered, and the other three are decreasing in numbers. Another threat to bears is hunters, who kill bears for meat, sport, or the use of body parts for medicinal purposes. Other people hunt bears because they consider them to be pests that threaten crops or livestock. Conservationists and wildlife biologists are working to save bears from extinction. Many people are trying to protect bear habitats and stop hunting so that bears can continue to survive in the wild. Scientists put a tag on this brown bear’s ear to track it and learn about its behavior.
pages.brief: A brown bear stands in the wild with a small tag on its ear. A conservationist or wildlife biologist watches from a safe distance, holding tracking equipment. Around them, forest and open land show the bear’s habitat, while the scene suggests protecting bears from hunting and habitat loss.

books.title: China: Past, Present, and Future
books.art_why: Modern China, its people, cities and wildlife can be shown in real photographs, and the book is not about one named famous person.

pages.text: China: Past, Present, and Future.
pages.brief: A sweeping view of China that brings past, present and future together: ancient stone walls and temple roofs in the foreground, busy modern city towers behind, and open sky above. The scene feels broad and welcoming, like the opening of a country study.

pages.text: Past, Present, and Future.
pages.brief: A wide landscape of China with a historic temple on one side, a modern city skyline on the other, and a path leading toward distant hills. Old and new buildings stand together under a broad sky, suggesting change over time.

pages.text: China: An Amazing Country! Asia is home to one of the biggest and most diverse countries in the world—China. There are at least fifty-six ethnic groups, or groups that have their own shared cultures. However, the majority of China’s population is Han (HAHN). Each province, or part, of China has its own distinct culture.
pages.brief: A lively outdoor market in China with people from different ethnic groups in varied traditional clothing, including Han families, chatting and shopping together. Regional buildings with curved roofs frame the square. The scene emphasizes many cultures living across China’s provinces.

pages.text: China has an incredible mix of people, landscapes, and wildlife. It is the third largest country in the world (only Russia and Canada are bigger). And it has the largest population in the world. In fact, one of every five people in the world lives in China—that’s more than 1.3 billion people! Gobi Desert rice paddy Yangtze River Do You Know? China has more than 1,500 rivers—including some of the biggest rivers in the world. The longest river in China is the Yangtze (yank-SEE), which is the third longest river in the world. (Only the Amazon River in South America and the Nile River in Africa are longer!)
pages.brief: A split landscape of China: dry Gobi Desert dunes on one side, a green rice paddy on the other, and the wide Yangtze River winding between them. In the foreground, a dense crowd of diverse Chinese people stands together, suggesting the country’s huge population.

pages.text: China is also a country alive with art, music, dance, food, and celebrations. And it’s known for amazing cultural sites—from temples and palaces to statues, canals, and the longest hand-built wall in the world. Chinese people have a long, rich history of inventing things. Ancient inventions include paper, printing, kites, and the abacus—a popular counting tool. More recently, Chinese people have invented the fastest trains in the world. abacus Maglev train porcelain pot kite.
pages.brief: A lively scene of Chinese culture: dancers and musicians perform near a temple and palace, a canal and long wall stretch behind, and a fast Maglev train speeds past. Nearby are a kite, an abacus, a porcelain pot, and sheets of paper and printing blocks.

pages.text: The Great Wall of China.
pages.brief: The Great Wall of China winds over rugged mountain ridges under a clear sky. Its stone walkway and watchtowers follow the hilltops into the distance, with steep green slopes on both sides. The wall looks long and hand-built, stretching far beyond the view.

pages.text: Chinese Wildlife One thing that makes China special is that it has many different kinds of natural places. There are rugged mountain peaks, rocky deserts, tropical forests, and lush valleys. Because China is such a big country with so many different habitats, it has many different kinds of living things. There are giant pandas in the bamboo forests of central China. There are tigers and monkeys in the tropical forests in the south. And there are all kinds of animals and plants that live in and near China’s many rivers and streams—including the giant salamander.
pages.brief: A rich wildlife landscape: rugged mountain peaks and rocky desert in the distance, tropical forest and lush valley in the foreground. A giant panda sits among bamboo in central China, while a tiger and monkeys hide in southern forest, and a giant salamander rests in a clear stream.

pages.text: Giant Panda Pandas are seen as national treasures in China. Giant pandas live in the steep bamboo forests of China, feeding almost nonstop on these tall, quick-growing grasses. Many pandas will spend more than sixteen hours a day chewing bamboo, eating about ten thousand pounds in a year. Unfortunately, China’s population has grown so quickly that many plants and animals are losing their habitats. For example, scientists say there are fewer than 1,600 pandas left in the wild. The bamboo forests where pandas live are being cut down for farming and houses.
pages.brief: A giant panda in a steep bamboo forest, sitting and chewing a thick bamboo stalk. Around it, bamboo grows densely on the hillside. In the background, a patch of forest is being cleared, with small farm plots and houses nearby, showing the panda’s shrinking habitat.

pages.text: Celebrating Chinese Culture: Food, Festivals, and More In addition to many natural treasures, China has a rich culture filled with special celebrations, art, music, dance, sports, and food. If you visit China, one of the first artistic things you might notice is the writing. The official language of China is Mandarin, which uses more than six thousand characters. Each character stands for a word or part of a word. Chinese Characters Here are the Mandarin characters for: fire mountain forest woman.
pages.brief: A calligrapher demonstrates Chinese writing with a brush, making bold strokes on a sheet of paper. Nearby, an ink stone and brushes sit on a low table in a warm study. The focus is on the careful hand movement and the expressive strokes.

pages.text: Lunar Calendar Each Chinese year is named after one of twelve animals. It repeats every twelve years. Look at the calendar to find the animal name for the year you were born. If you visit in late January or early February, you might be lucky enough to take part in the celebration of the Lunar New Year. This is one of China’s most important festivals and is celebrated throughout the country. To celebrate the Lunar New Year, people take part in colorful parades, wearing bright clothing and watching lion and dragon dance performances. Fireworks are also a big part of the festivities.
pages.brief: A Lunar New Year parade in a Chinese street: performers in bright clothing carry a lion dance costume and a long dragon puppet through a crowd. Fireworks burst overhead. Nearby, a circular calendar shows twelve animals in a ring.

pages.text: Sports are also important to many Chinese people. You’ll probably see a lot of people playing table tennis (Ping-Pong). China has trained some of the best table tennis players in the world! You’ll also see a lot of bike riders, since most people get around by bike. Food and Chinese culture go hand in hand. If you’ve eaten in a Chinese restaurant, then you know there are many flavors and spices that make Chinese food special. Different regions of China are known for different kinds of food. For example, food from the provinces of Sichuan (SEECH-wahn) and Hunan (HOO-nahn) is very spicy and often uses chili pepper oil. You might also notice that Chinese people often use two utensils: chopsticks and a soup spoon.
pages.brief: A busy Chinese street and park: two people play table tennis at an outdoor table while cyclists ride past. In the foreground, a family eats at a table with chopsticks and soup spoons, and bowls of spicy food with chili pepper oil steam nearby. The scene feels lively and everyday.

pages.text: Rice and wheat are common foods in China. Rice is grown in flooded fields called paddies. In many parts of China, rice is served with all meals and is an important part of the diet. You’ll also see people eating noodles, soups, fish, soybeans, and other foods. Do You Know? Chinese people eat three times more fish than Americans. In fact, the average person in China eats more than 20 kilograms (45 lb.) of seafood each year.
pages.brief: A flooded rice paddy in China, with green rice plants reflecting the sky and a field of wheat nearby. In the foreground, a family meal shows bowls of rice, noodles, soup, fish, and soybeans on a table, with chopsticks ready. The scene connects farming to daily food.

pages.text: China: Past, Present, and Future China has a long and rich history, which has helped shape the country today. Most historians think the country was settled more than 5,500 years ago. That makes China one of the earliest civilizations in the world still thriving today. The capital of China is Beijing (bay-ZHING). It is a city of around 21 million people. Beijing is the center of government. It is also known for its many tourist sites, like Tiananmen (tee-AHN-un-men) Square, also named the Gate of Heavenly Peace—a large square in the city’s center that is used for special events.
pages.brief: A view of Beijing as China’s capital: a huge public square filled with people, with the Gate of Heavenly Peace at one side. Around the square rise modern government buildings and city streets busy with residents. The scene suggests a long history meeting a bustling present.

pages.text: China also has many other thriving cities. Shanghai (shang-HI) is the largest city in China and one of the biggest ports in the world. Guangzhou (gwahng-JOH) is a major port city known for its businesses and manufacturing. Even though many of China’s more than a billion people live in cities, most people still live in rural towns and villages. Many of them farm or herd sheep and goats in the grasslands.
pages.brief: A split scene: Shanghai’s busy port with ships and tall buildings, and Guangzhou’s manufacturing district with factories and businesses. In the foreground, a rural Chinese village and grassland appear, where a family farms and herds sheep and goats, showing where most people live.

pages.text: Land of the Silk Moth Most of the world’s silk is produced in China. Silk comes from the caterpillar of a silk moth—the only domesticated insect in the world. The caterpillar spins a silken cocoon, and people harvest the silk threads from the cocoon. Chinese people discovered silk about 2640 bce and kept it a secret for almost three thousand years. Today, China has the second largest economy in the world. It is a leader in making and selling many products to other countries—from toys to televisions and textiles, such as silk. It also has a huge tourist industry and hosted the 2008 and 2022 Olympics in Beijing.
pages.brief: A silk moth caterpillar spins a pale cocoon on a leaf, while an adult carefully harvests silk threads from another cocoon. Behind them, modern China appears: a factory making toys and televisions, a textile display, tourists, and a Beijing Olympic stadium.

pages.text: But China faces big challenges. Under the Communist government, everyone had a job working for the government. Then the government made big changes. It began to “open up” China’s economy. It allowed more businesses that are not run by the government. Now, it is harder for the people of China to find jobs. Many people are jobless. Do You Know? The Communist government discourages religion, so most people do not belong to organized religious institutions. However, many people believe in the teachings of Buddhism, Taoism, and other religious thinking that promotes harmony and compassion.
pages.brief: A Chinese city street with job seekers waiting outside an employment office, while small private shops and businesses line the road. Nearby, a calm temple courtyard shows people reflecting quietly, suggesting Buddhist and Taoist traditions of harmony and compassion.

pages.text: As China’s population grows, people will need more water, energy, food, and other resources. The country faces the challenge of providing enough jobs and resources for its population while still protecting the environment and people’s rights.
pages.brief: A wide view of a growing Chinese city beside farmland and a river. In the foreground, people collect water and electricity workers maintain power lines, while farmers tend crops. The scene shows the need for water, energy, food and jobs while keeping the environment clean and protecting people’s rights.

books.title: Plight of the Polar Bear
books.art_why: Real polar bears, Arctic tundra, sea ice, and Inuit life exist today, so photographs can show them accurately.

pages.text: Introduction The vast tundra of the northern Arctic is a harsh, unfriendly place for most living things. But one of Earth’s most magnificent creatures, the polar bear, has managed to thrive in the tundra—that is, until now. Word Wise The word tundra comes from a language spoken by several thousand Native people in the northernmost regions of Europe. It means “treeless plain.”
pages.brief: A vast, treeless Arctic tundra stretches under a cold sky, with no trees to break the wind. A single polar bear stands on the open plain, showing that this harsh northern place is its home.

pages.text: Tundra: Winter Versus Summer During much of the year, the temperature in the tundra is well below freezing. Winter lasts for more than six months. For several weeks during that time the Sun never rises above the horizon. The soil just below the surface remains frozen throughout the year. There are no trees to slow down the cold winds that sweep across this icy land. This makes conditions even more harsh. Word Wise The word used to describe the frozen soil of the tundra is permafrost. It is a combination of the words permanent and frost.
pages.brief: Dark winter settles over the treeless tundra, where the sun stays below the horizon and cold winds sweep across the land. The ground below the surface stays frozen, and no trees stand to slow the icy wind.

pages.text: Plover Summer in the tundra is quite different from winter. The Sun does not set for several weeks. Often it just peeks over the horizon. During this season, the average temperature remains above freezing. The snow has a chance to melt, and low- growing plants such as mosses, lichens, grasses, and small shrubs grow. Millions of insects hatch and fill the air, ground, and pools of water. Those insects attract huge numbers of birds that migrate to the tundra and make it their summer home. Even mammals that moved south to escape the harsh winter return to feed each summer.
pages.brief: Summer in the tundra brings a sun that does not set, melting snow and low plants such as mosses, lichens, grasses, and small shrubs. Clouds of insects fill the air, ground, and pools, while migrating birds and returning mammals gather to feed.

pages.text: The polar bear lives there year round. It is well suited to the tundra. But in recent years polar bears have been struggling to survive. The tundra’s harsh conditions are not the reason. The rapid changes happening to Earth are the reason. Do You Know? Some scientists believe that polar bears cover their black noses with their paws to make themselves harder to spot as they hunt for seals.
pages.brief: A polar bear stands on the tundra year round, well suited to the cold. It lifts a paw toward its black nose as if hiding it while hunting for seals. The scene suggests recent changes on Earth are making survival hard.

pages.text: Built to Survive Polar bears are adapted to life in the Arctic. Their fur is waterproof, so the icy waters in which they swim don’t make them cold. Though each strand of hair is actually clear, they appear to be all white. This helps them to blend in with the snow, making it easier for them to stalk their prey.
pages.brief: A polar bear moves through snowy Arctic surroundings, its white-looking fur blending into the snow, though each strand is actually clear. The fur is waterproof, so icy water does not make the bear cold, and the white appearance helps it stalk prey.

pages.text: Do You Know? Polar bears have a very good sense of smell. They can smell a dead, rotting seal from 32 kilometers (20 mi) away. Seals are an important part of the polar bear diet. Polar bears’ main food is seals, but they also eat walruses, smaller whales, and some land animals. They do most of their seal hunting during the winter months when ice forms over the Arctic Ocean. By blending into the snowy scene, a polar bear poised to pounce may not be spotted by a seal. Polar bears will wait patiently for hours near a hole in the ice where seals come up for air.
pages.brief: A polar bear waits patiently beside a hole in the sea ice, watching for a seal to come up for air. Its powerful nose can smell a dead seal far away, and seals are its main food during winter hunting.

pages.text: Polar bear paws can be up to 30 centimeters (12 in) in diameter. The claws, pads, and hair on a polar bear’s paws keep the bear from slipping on the ice. Adult polar bears need to eat a great deal of food to survive. They store fat to get them through the seasons in which they are not hunting. They have large stomachs and will eat nearly 45 kilograms (100 lbs) in a single meal. That would be like eating 400 quarter-pound hamburgers at one time! Two layers of fur and a thick layer of body fat insulate polar bears from very cold temperatures. They even have fur on the bottoms of their large paws.
pages.brief: An adult polar bear stands on the ice, showing huge paws with claws, pads, and hair that grip the slippery surface. Two layers of fur and thick body fat keep it warm, and its large stomach can hold an enormous meal.

pages.text: Polar bears are excellent swimmers. They have been spotted hunting seals up to 80 kilometers (50 mi) out to sea. They swim with their heads above water by dog-paddling at over 9 kilometers (6 mi) per hour. Bears use their huge paws like large paddles to move through the water. A thick layer of blubber helps them remain afloat. 3+5+2=10–4+10÷2=14 x2–3=25– 3+9x2÷8=3–2+7–5 x3=9+4–1÷4=3x5–3 Math Minute A polar bear swimming at an average speed of five kilometers per hour leaves the shore to swim to an ice floe. The bear swims to four more ice floes. It rests 10 minutes on each ice floe before swimming to the next one. When it reaches the final ice floe, it waits patiently near an air hole for a seal to surface. The bear swims a total of 30 kilometers. pages.brief: A polar bear swims through open sea with its head above water, using huge paws like paddles. Its thick blubber keeps it afloat as it moves between ice floes, where it rests before continuing toward a seal's air hole.

pages.text: Shrinking Ice The polar bear has only one enemy— humans. The greatest threat is not caused by people hunting polar bears. Instead, it is what humans are doing to the environment that poses the greatest threat. Scientists know that Earth is getting hotter and hotter. This warming of Earth is known as global warming. Global warming is caused by pollutants that are being released into the atmosphere. More pollutants are released each year as Earth’s growing population burns more and more gasoline, oil, and coal.
pages.brief: Human activity sends pollutants into the atmosphere as a growing population burns more gasoline, oil, and coal. The warming of Earth, called global warming, is the greatest threat to polar bears, not hunting. Smoky pollutants rise into the sky above the Arctic environment.

pages.text: Global warming causes changes that make life difficult for plants and animals around the world. Where polar bears live, global warming is causing ice to melt. That might not seem like a big deal for some animals—but it is for polar bears. Polar bears depend on the sea remaining frozen for most months of the year. When the sea freezes over, polar bears walk onto the ice. They search for holes where seals are likely to come up for air. The longer the sea is frozen, the longer polar bears can hunt. And the more they eat, the more food they store as fat for the short summer season when they fast. Do You Know? Polar bears are an important source of food and clothing for the Inuit people who live in the Arctic region. Changes in weather and decreases in polar bear population caused by global warming threaten the Inuit way of life.
pages.brief: Melting sea ice leaves a polar bear on a smaller frozen patch, searching for a seal's breathing hole. Longer frozen seasons let bears hunt and store fat for summer, while shorter ice makes life harder. In the distance, Inuit people rely on polar bears for food and clothing.

pages.text: When hunting seasons are shorter, polar bears can’t store as much fat. Scientists estimate that each lost week means a loss of 10 kilograms (22 lbs) of body fat for the summer. This is a big problem for polar bears because more and more polar ice is melting. As a result of their shorter hunting season, polar bears are dying at alarming rates. Scientists estimate that they could go extinct by 2100. Do You Know? The melting of polar ice caps due to global warming is one reason the oceans are rising. In time, this will flood vast stretches of coastline in many parts of the world.
pages.brief: A thinner polar bear stands on shrinking sea ice surrounded by open water. Shorter hunting seasons mean less stored fat, and scientists warn the bears could become extinct by 2100. In the background, rising oceans threaten to flood stretches of coastline in many parts of the world.

pages.text: Due to their lower body weight, female polar bears are giving birth to fewer cubs. This is a very serious problem for the survival of an animal that has an average of only two cubs every 28 months. During the summer, polar bears in search of food are also going into areas where humans live. In some places, these bears are captured and put into bear compounds until the winter ice returns. They are then released so they can hunt and restore their body fat.
pages.brief: A female polar bear with a single cub stands near a human settlement, showing fewer cubs born because of lower body weight. In the background, a bear compound holds captured polar bears until winter ice returns so they can hunt and restore body fat.

pages.text: Other Problems Global warming isn’t the only bad effect of human activity on polar bears. Many pollutants reaching the air and water are toxic. These pollutants often end up in the blubber of seals. When bears eat these seals, they also eat the toxins. How Pollution Reaches Polar Bears 1 Toxic chemicals end up in Arctic air and water. 3 Polar bears eat Arctic seals whose body fat is full of stored toxic chemicals. 2 Arctic seals eat fish that have high levels of pollutants in their bodies.
pages.brief: Toxic chemicals drift in Arctic air and water, then pass into fish. Seals eat those polluted fish and store the chemicals in their body fat. When a polar bear eats such a seal, it also takes in the toxins, adding another danger beyond global warming.

pages.text: Think About It Many creatures share Planet Earth. You are one of these creatures. Make a list of all the things you can do to slow global warming and help save the polar bears’ environment. Think about the effect you can have if you convince others to do the same things. Another threat to polar bears comes from the desire of humans to use more and more fuel. To meet this desire, oil and gas companies want to drill in Arctic regions where polar bears live. Much of this drilling would happen where female polar bears build dens in which they give birth to their cubs. This drilling could hurt the polar bears’ survival.
pages.brief: An Arctic oil and gas drilling site stands near snowy ground where a female polar bear has dug a den for her cubs. The drilling equipment shows human demand for more fuel, while the mother bear and cubs stay close to the den they need for survival.

pages.text: Polar bears need frozen sea to hunt for seals. Conclusion There is no question that the world’s polar bear population is shrinking. In the Western Hudson Bay region of Northern Canada alone, the population has dropped a lot. In 1995, there were over 1,200 bears there. In 2021 there were fewer than 620. Many groups are worried about the plight of the polar bear. They are taking steps to protect these magnificent creatures before it’s too late.
pages.brief: A small group of polar bears stands on sea ice in the Western Hudson Bay region of Northern Canada, where the population has fallen sharply. Conservation groups work to protect these magnificent creatures, hoping to slow the shrinking of the world's polar bear population before it is too late.
